SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with Quentin Jackson
Reel One of Seven

Washington, D. C.
June 1976

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS

This is Sunday, April 10, 1976.
I'm sitting here with a dear friend of mine, Quentin Jackson. We've known one another for many, many years.
And, Quentin, I just want to say that amongst all musicians you are considered, without any question of a doubt, one of the greatest instrumentalists in the terms of our craft as sidemen that ever existed in the history of orchestral and jazz playing. I don't think there's anybody that has come through or played in as many great bands, any instrumentalist or jazz musician, as you have starting back where you started and to the most modern orchestras of today.
So, Quen, I've now said my little piece and from now on it's all your conversation. I'd just like to ask you, you know, where you were born and when.
I was born in Springfield, Ohio, January 13, 1909.
And your mother's name?
Was Imogene Jackson. My father's name was Dudley Jackson.
Uh-huh. Where did you -- What town? Springfield, huh?
Springfield, Ohio.
Uh-huh. How many was in the family?
Just myself and two sisters.
Uh-huh, and were you older or they? In what order?
I'm in between. I'm in the middle.
What were your sisters' names?
Dorothea was my older sister's name and Marguerite was my younger sister's name.
Uh-huh.
We're very far apart.
Uh-huh.
Marguerite was -- my older sister, rather, was born in 1903. I was born in '09 and Marguerite was born in '17.
Oh, this is interesting.
Uh-huh. You know, --
Excuse me. And what about the schools? I notice in all of the books that tell about you you began playing piano and ______. How did that happen?
Well, you know, my mother played --
Uh-huh.
-- just for her own amusement.
She did.
And she used to get the Etude every month and she played a little light classics. And so I used to crawl upon the stool behind her and play what I heard her
play.
Uh-huh.

Well, and, oh, I imagine, oh, the first time I played before an audience I was four years old. I have a piece at home from the newspaper about me. They thought that I was a prodigy and that, gee whiz, one day Mrs. Jackson went into the living room and she heard someone playing the piano and she was astonished to see the little fellow at the instrument. And they had consulted several teachers and they said I was too young at the time.
And yet and still I played before the church audience in the church. One Sunday I played an old hymn called Power in the Blood, There's Wonder Working Power in the Blood of the Lamb.
Yeah, I remember that one.
That was the first thing I played. I was four years old.
So then they went -- they had me go to a teacher. His name was Professor [Brane.]
Professor [Brane.]
And I took some lessons from him. He was all right but I didn't like him. I didn't like his approach, [because]a kid, you know, a kid, if you don't approach a kid right, you'll get nothing from him.
So my mother changed teachers because -- There was

a teacher coming to teach my older sister piano -- her name was Miss Marguerite Williams from Yellow Springs, Ohio, from Antioch College -- and she would come up and give my sister lessons, so she would give me lessons, too.

But I did not like piano lessons. I did not like playing five finger exercises. I wanted to play more than that. That meant nothing to me. So the teacher one day had made the mistake of playing my lesson, so I didn't practice that week. But when she came back I played the lesson note for note just like she played it. So she told my mother that I hadn't been practicing, she said, because "Quentin played the right notes but he wasn't using the right fingering. So I know he didn't practice."
So after a while it went on like that, went on like that, and finally I started disliking piano as far as taking lessons was concerned, you know.
Yeah.

So I would go ahead and play what I wanted to play anyway and I got so I could read. Gee whiz, you learn to read in grade school. At home you learn to read music. You know, we used to have a singing period.
Uh-huh.
All the old songs like Love's Old Sweet Song and Annie Laurie and all those things you sang in school.
Sure, Just a Song at Twilight.
And you learned to read. Yeah, uh-huh.
Sure.

So then I didn't like that. So they started to having music in the schools, public schools, so I figured, I said, "Now I've got to have something to play." So I saw this violin in the arcade at home. $16. And I was at a job lighting gas lamps, so I bought --
How old were you then about?
12, about 11 or 12.
Uh-huh.

And I -- My mother, I used to give her my check every payday. But I saw this violin and she was standing upon a corner waiting for me to give her the check, but I had slipped around the arcade music store at home in Springfield and I got this violin. And it was a funny looking case. It looked like you put a dead person in.
A coffin.
Yeah, like a coffin,
Yeah, that was the ______.

A wooden case. So I had the violin in there and I came around and my mother looked and saw this violin case, so she tried to get mad because I didn't have the check, but she had to smile. So I took the violin home and I told Professor [Humberger,] he was supervisor of music at

home in the schools, and I told him I wanted to play the violin. So he sent me to a teacher, Mark Snyder. He used to play a second violin in the Cincinnati Symphony. And I took lessons from him and I got so I could play a lot of things on the violin. It got so I could play solos in front of the orchestra. I could play Souvenir, da-da-da-de de-de, things like that.
Sure.
The only thing whipped me was Caprice Vieuxtemps when I tried to tackle that.
That's Kreisler's. Yeah, he's --
That's right.
He's a tough man.
Oh, was he. He was beautiful. You know, I got to hear him in person.
Yeah, Fritz Kreisler.
Yeah. My mother used to take me to hear all the artists when they would come home. I heard Paderewski in person.
What kind of auditorium did you have to hear?
Just Memorial Hall.
Memorial hall.
Yeah, we called it Memorial Hall where they had all the concerts. I heard Fritz Kreisler in
person. I heard Caruso when I was six years old.
Wow.
I heard Schumann-Heink. I heard Galli-Curci, Alma Gluck. My mother used to take me to hear all these people, you see.
Uh-huh.
Because I loved music.
Where was your mother from, Quen?
She was born in London, Ohio. Oh, maybe the town is about maybe 14 or 15 miles from Springfield going towards Columbus, that way. Just a very little town.
Uh-huh.
And her father was a horse trader in that town.
My dad came from Danville, Kentucky.
What was the first, your first interest in getting to hear an orchestra where you figured you wanted to play in an orchestra? How did you get to there?
Well, McKinney had a band called Synco Cinco Septet. They only had seven pieces. And they used to rehearse out to Milt Senior's house, you know.
Uh-huh.
And I used to go out there and listen. And Claude Jones was playing with the band at the time and he finally married my sister.
Uh-huh.
And Claude usually -- he played such great trombone. To me I thought he was the greatest trombone player that ever lived.
I almost still do.
Well, me, too.

So he used to come home all the time, you know, come through Springfield, and he said, "Gee whiz, Quent," he said, "you've got such a good musical background, why don't you take the trombone? Because there's very few good colored trombone players. This would be a good instrument for you." So I thought over this thing and thought over this thing and finally the guys at home, my buddies, they got a band together and they had nine pieces. They needed a trombone to make ten pieces.

So at that time I was working for an undertaker. His name was Elmer [Burns]. I used to drive the ambulance and I used to play the organ for the funerals and things, you know, then jump out and drive the funeral car. And Elmer [Burns] had a brass trombone, he played in the Elks band. So I told Elmer, I said, "Elmer," I said, "why don't you tell me about this trombone? I'd like to know how it works and how do you play it. I'd like to know about this."
So he took me and showed me the positions on it, showed me how to put my lip on it and how to attack the notes,
you know, how you get from one note to the other. But he made the mistake of telling me it read the same as a bass clef of the piano.
Oh, I see.
So the trombone parts in those days were simple. You know, it's more like little fill-ins.
Yeah.

So I took all the trombone parts home that the guys had to the orchestrations and I would go in each position till I would find the note because I'd look on there and I knew how the note was supposed to sound, and I'd go to each position till I found that note. Then I'd remember where I got it.
Uh-huh.
From then on I started playing with the band, started to practicing with the band.
What band was that?
A little band at home called the Buckeye Melodians.
Uh-huh. Who was the leader? Was that Wesley Helvey's band there?
No, no, no, that came later.
Oh, I see.
That is a story.
Buckeye Melodians, huh?
Yeah, that came to Springfield, Ohio.
Uh-huh.
Later on Earl Warren, you know, the saxophone player, his father later took it over after I left home. And Earl was just starting to play at that time, just starting to learn to play saxophone.
Oh, yeah.
So there was a drummer, Gerald Hobson. Gerald Hobson used to come and play with our band. He lived in New York a long time and I used to like to listen to him telling me stories of New York.

And I was singing, too, so he told me, he said, "You know, Quentin," he said, "you got a good chance to make it in music." He said, "I'm going to Cincinnati and if I see anybody out there that wants a trombone player, I'll tell him about you because I think you got a good chance." So he went to Helvey's Troubadours in Cincinnati.

So I had left Elmer [Burns] and I was working for the big undertaker at that time, Patterson. So I'm sitting there one night to answer the telephone in case any calls come in and I get this call from Cincinnati. I said, "Who in the devil knows me in Cincinnati?" And it was Wesley Helvey. He said, "You know, Quentin," he said, "how would you like to join my band?" I told him I'd love to.
He said, "Do you belong to the union?" I said,
"Sure, I belong to the union. I belong to the little local at home." Paid 75 cents a quarter dues. That was 1929.

So Helvey said, "Well, I'll come through and pick you up tomorrow." Well, I had a little horn I had bought out of a pawnshop for nine $6, [Kenon] It was a silver horn, had a -- oh, the bore was so small you called it a pea-shooter in those days.
So I took my little horn and Helvey met me. I had him meet me in front of the Brick, it was a place where the guys used to hang out, because I wanted everybody to see me leaving home.
Oh, called the Brick. The place was called the Brick?
Yeah, yeah. You know, they served near beer in there.
Yeah.
Guys -- there was a pool table in there, that sort of thing, you know, in a small town.
Sure.
So I had him meet me in front of the Brick so all the guys could see me leaving home. I got my little valise and everything.
Sure.
So they took me to Buffalo. My, it was big. I'd never been no place no further from Springfield
and Cleveland, Ohio, and you'd go up there on excursion, go up to Lunar Park and come back home.

So Helvey and those guys they saw that little horn I had and they told me, he says, "No, you can't play that here. You've got to get a better horn." So I went down to the music store in Buffalo and I got another horn. I got a second-hand Holton. It was one of the best horns I ever had.
It's a great horn.

Uh-huh. And so I joined Helvey's band and our headquarters was Cincinnati. Then I run into a trombone player, Floyd Brady. We called him Little Stump, and he took me under his wing and I learned more from him --
By the way, he's still living, isn't he?
Sure.
We see him in New York all the time.
That's right. That's right. He's still got a trombone under his arm, and his upper teeth is gone but do you know he can still play without those teeth?
Yeah.

And he taught me more than I could have learned from a teacher. He had the Auburn instructor in those days. He had a lot of Miff Mole solos, you know, that he used to practice with. You know, books of Miff Mole

solos, and I learned so much from him, you know.
So I stayed with Helvey until January of '30.
That's when I went to Zack White. Whyte,
Let's see, Zack White. [Right.]
Uh-huh, and Zack White had a very good band. Si Oliver, you know, was the arranger in the band.
Wow.

And he played the trumpet then. He was playing the trumpet in the band.
It was a nice little band. There was a lot of bands out there in the West, though, that to me that -- you know, someone could play it better, like Speed Webb. Speed Webb came to the Paradise Ballroom in Cincinnati and made us sound bad.
Who's this? Speed Webb?
Yeah. But the band, the guys he had in that band -- Teddy Wilson was with that band at the time.
Yeah, Teddy. Who else was in? Anybody else you remember?
Sure. The trumpet section was Reynauld Jones and Steve Dunn from Cincinnati and Roy Eldridge.
Wow.
And the trombones was Gus Wilson, which was Teddy's brother, and Vic Dickinson.
That's Teddy Wilson's brother?
Dickenson
Yeah, and Vic Dickinson.
Wow.

And the saxophones was Leonard Gaye, Smoke Richardson, and Chuck -- I forget Chuck's last name. He was from Detroit. And of course Teddy on the piano and Bowles was on bass. I think Bowles later went to Chicago to live.
Uh-huh.
And the drummer's name and guitar name I can't remember either. But they were very good. The drummer used to drum like the old Walter Johnson style, very smooth.
But they had a lot of good arrangements because Gus was writing then, you know. Gus was a very good arranger.
That's Teddy's brother Gus?
Yes, a very good arranger. And, gee whiz, they had -- the soloists they had, oh, wow. But --
Those are still great names, all those powerful names.
Are they, are they?
Yes, yes, indeed.
But, you know, Milt, I've been lucky. I've never played with what I could call, what you call a real sad band. I've never played with a sad band in my life. I've been that lucky.

Well, you've always been such a great asset to every orchestra you've ever been with. I don't know whether you know it, brother, but you are considered amongst musicians a musician's musician, a complete musician. And any band or any group of musicians that get together and talk about sidemen or instrumentalists they refer to you as the most complete musician. You certainly are the most knowledgeable one for this background that you have. And I want to ask you about that. How did you come about -- I know I've worked with you in Cab's band and I've worked with you in studio recordings and whatnot and I know that you have the capacity to know everybody's part in the orchestra, not only your part but everybody else's part in the orchestra. And it has always been known that in Duke's band sometimes a guy would be late showing up. There was quite a bit of tardiness in the band. And you could take your trombone and play the alto part. How did you acquire that sort of a talent?

Just hearing, just listening, because I love to listen to parts. I love to listen to -- I love big bands. You know, I've never had the pleasure, really, to play with a small band but my ears I've always kept open and I like to listen to different parts, you know, different guys' parts, you know. That's how I come to play the plunger,
you see. Tyree wanted to go home. He wanted to come home to see Gloria once in Chicago --
Oh, that's when you were with Duke?

Yes. -- and so he goes to Duke and he never even asked me -- because you know how Tyree and I was, you know. We was very close, very, very close. People don't know, really, how close we were, you know. Tyree goes to Duke and I come to work the next night and here's this mute and plunger in front of my chair, and I said, "Oh, no." So Duke told me that, you know, "Tyree told me that you could play anything. So he told me that you could do this." And do you know that night he called Trans-Bluecency on me, he called Turquoise Cloud and all those things on me. I didn't even need to read the music because I heard every note Tyree played on those parts and I went out there and played it, --
That's remarkable.
-- you see? And you like to hear different saxophone parts. You know these parts, you see.
But most other people have never been able to do that. I notice that you, just from knowing you, I notice you hear, which is part of being a complete musician, you hear the whole band.
Oh, yes.
The whole [ ] of the band, which is
really what a musician should do.
Uh-huh.
I just want to get back to a little bit of the early days first. You've given me a lot of things about the different members of the orchestra.
Let me ask you, how did you, how did the name Butter -- how did you get that name?
Oh, Don Redman when I first joined McKinney's Cottonpickers, I was young and I looked tender, you know, --
That was about 1936, huh?
No, no. I joined McKinney's Cottonpickers December 7, 1930.
Oh, 1930. Oh, yeah, that's right.
Yeah, uh-huh. I joined -- yeah.
And they looked at me and, I don't know, they looked at me and I don't know whether my complexion had anything to do with it or not, but Don said I looked like butter.
Ah, ha, ha, ha. It was the complexion, yeah.
And I was plump, too, you know. Being plump and all that, you know, I was -- oh, I weighed about 210 then, you know. And, gee whiz, I was 20---- when I joined that band I was 21 years old, --
Wow.
-- you know. And I come in the band to sing because George Thomas, the saxophone player, he was killed in an automobile accident.
Oh, yeah.

And how that happened, I was with Zack White's band and, of course, McKinney and them knew me, you know, from Springfield because the band originated there when it was Cinco's Septet before it got to be McKinney Cottonpickers.
What was it? Before it got to be McKinney's, what was the band called?
McKinney's Cinco Septet. There were seven pieces.
Oh.
It had Claude Jones on trombone and a guy named Chauncy -- I forget his last name -- was on trumpet until they got Nesbitt. They got Nesbitt from a carnival.
Yes, but what was Nesbitt's full name?
John Nesbitt.
John Nesbitt. He played trumpet, right?
And a fantastic arranger.
Uh-huh.
And just two saxophones, just Milt Senior and Wesley Stewart. Wesley Stewart played violin, too.
Uh-huh.
And June Jim Cole, they got him on, too.
Oh, yeah, June Jim Cole. Todd
And, of course, Claude Rhodes was the pianist. McKinney didn't do nothing but take care of the business.

Originally there was four pieces before it got to be the Septet. McKinney was a drummer and Milt Senior's father had a little orchestra around home. So Cuba, they got Cuba Austin also a drummer, they got him from a carnival that came through. And McKinney formed this Septet.
And then McKinney didn't play anymore? He just managed?

No, he was just the manager. And as the story goes with that band, they used to go up to Manitou Beach, Michigan, every summer to [Clark's Lake] and play. When Jean Goldkette Gene Galkit heard the band up there he liked what he heard, so he was getting ready to build this million dollar ballroom called the Graystone in Detroit. So he liked the band, so he figured with himself that he could do something with this band, so he sent and got Don Redmon to come, and Don Redmon at that time was playing with Fletcher Henderson and, also, Don, back in 1925 and '26, had wrote worked for Jean Goldkette's Gene Galkit's
orchestra and Paul Whiteman, --
Wow.
-- you see. He was one of the forerunners of big band dance arranging. That was before Fletcher Henderson and all those guys.
And it seems as if Fletcher Henderson is given more credit for that than Don.
I know but Don was writing for Fletcher before Fletcher was writing himself.
If you listen to the original arrangement of 'Sugarfoot Stomp,' that's Don Redmon. 'Bean Koo Jack' and all those things, Don Redmon made those arrangements, you see.
That's beautiful.
You know. But Don was, he was the type of guy, he was a very quiet guy, and so nobody really got to know about him. They've never exploited him to that extent.
Yeah.

McKinney kept him in the background, in a way. Jean Goldkette So Gene Colkit sent him, sent and got him, Fletcher, to come to Detroit and he took this band and he augmented the band and made it 11 pieces and the band sounded so nice and,
I guess, well, being a black band, too, if you listen to it on the air, you couldn't tell whether it was a black band or white band, in a way. So they --
[Intonation was] makes it so good.
That's right, and so they nicknamed it Cottonpickers, so they'd really know that it was a black band.
Ah.
They named it McKinney Cottonpickers.
That's beautiful.
That's right.
Yeah, but that's beautiful. Well, let's go on now. We'll find out what Butter is and everything.
Yeah.
You can carry that on if you want to from there. I'll get back to --
So --
Oh, okay.

So going back to McKinney Cottonpickers, that turned out to be one of the greatest dance bands in the country at that time. It had the reputation. And Gene Goldkette also got them a contract to record for Victor. I think it was one of the first colored bands to record for Victor, you know.
How far did you guys travel with
From coast to coast.
Is that so?

That's right, that's right. We did a lot of one nighter's around New England. In fact, I joined the band in New England, you know. That's where I joined them. I was playing in Zack White's band in Wheeling one night so the guys asked me to come up and sing. So I said sure I'll sing. So I went up and I sang the "Kiss Waltz" because the band played waltzes in those days too, you know.
Right.

They played all kinds of music for the dance public. So I sang the "Kiss Waltz" and I sang it in the key of D-flat. When I got to the ending I got up on a high D-flat and I held it and I broke the dance up. So McKinney said, well, and said -- Todd Claude Rhodes, rather, came to me and said, "McKinney wants to talk to you." He said, "Mack wants to talk to you." I said, "Okay." So I said I wonder what he wants to talk to me about. The great McKinney Cottonpickers and I'm with Zack White and he wants to talk to me? I never even dreamed that he would want me in the band. So I got in the car with him, we were riding up the street in the car, and McKinney told me, he said, "You know, Quent, how would you like to join the band?" He said, "You know, George Thomas" -- they called him Fathead. Well, that
was his nickname.
Pathead, George Fathead Thomas.
Yeah.
What did he play, brother?

He played alto. Very good alto saxophone player. In fact, when Don wasn't playing lead he played lead when they only used three saxophones. Naturally Don would play lead when they used four, you know. In fact that was one of the first bands to have four saxophones.
McKinney's?
That's right. Don created a lot of things when it came to music, as far as that goes.
Anyway, so I told him I would love to join the band. So he said, 'How much money would you like to have?' And I said, oh, my, I got scared then. I don't want to ask him for too much.
Right.
And I thought of asking for enough, so I told him, well, I said, well, 'Would $50 a week be too much, Mr. McKinney?'
50 bucks a week?
Yeah. Mr. McKinney is what I called him, you know. So he said, 'Well, I'll give you 60.'
Wow.
Like he said this poor guy, you know,

because the rest of the guys was getting 75 and 80 and 90. You know, like that in that band. So he said, "You join me. You can join me." I said sure and he told me when to join him in Baltimore and he said, "I'll call you and if you need any money, let me know," you know. So I said, "Well, --
What year was that Butter?
Well, you (unintelligible)
This was December 1930.
How much was a dance hall? How much did it cost to get in to dance in those days?
50 cents.
Wow.
75, you know. It's according to the band.
You would have to have at least a thousand people to have a good night.

Oh, sure, but they always had a good night. In those days when McKinney's band played anyplace it was packed all the time, every place you played. In fact, there were so many ballrooms over the country in those days, you see, --
call that didn't have
Yes, didn't have radio and there was no television. It was just radio.
Just radio, and we used to broadcast. When we'd be in the Graystone, you know, which we would go in there and stay for weeks and months, we would broadcast over
WJR all the time, you see.
[ ] station in Detroit.
Uh-huh, yeah, yeah. We used to broadcast over WJR and that's what you had. That was the greatest publicity in the world right there is to be on the radio.
Yeah. So you got your 50 -- you got your $60 a week instead?

Yes, I did. So I said, gee whiz. Now he called me and said, "I want you -- Do you need any money?" And I said, well, "Sure." So I had talked to Clarence Paige, one of the saxophone players in Zach's band, and I'm young, I don't know, I'm dumb, I'm fresh from Springfield. I didn't know what to ask him for. So Clarence said, "Ask him for $100. He's got plenty of money." So I asked McKinney for $100. And do you know he sent me the $100.

So he sent me a train ticket and I got on the train -- I had never been on a train before because in Zach's band we traveled in automobiles and some of those cars if you would see them, you wouldn't believe. Those cars. I drove the baggage car, a little baggage car. It was a four cylinder Dodge. It couldn't go over 50 miles an hour and I drove it once all the way from [Camden], Ohio, to Philadelphia over the mountains.
Wow.
That's right. But you're young then. You don't think about those things.
Sure.
You make it.

So, anyway, I got on the train to go to Boston. I didn't know nothing about going to the diner so -- I ate so much -- I had all this money. I ate so much candy and peanuts till I almost got sick till I got to Boston.
I get to Boston and I go to meet the band and everything. I saw -- this was when I first met Don Redman, you know, to really meet him.
Right.
So they told Jimmy Dudley to --
Jimmy Dudley?
Yeah. He was the alto saxophone player in McKinney's band.
Yes, that's right.

Yeah, and Edward Inge had taken George Robinson's place by then, you see. And, of course, Prince Cuffee Robertson was still there. And Edward Cuffy was the other trombone. He came in Claude Jones' place in 1929 when Claude left McKinney's to go to Fletcher.
Wow.
You see. And so they had rehearsal and I went on playing my part, the second trombone part, and
Don, I heard Don tell the rest of the guys, he said, "Oh, he can see, can't he?"
I thought to myself, sure I can see. I don't need no glasses or nothing, you know.
Ha, ha, ha, ha.
I didn't know what he meant, you know.
That's one of the good advantage of that young training of that violin and piano.
Oh, definitely.
Yeah, sure.
I advise any kid, if he's going to take music, please try to learn the piano --
Right.
-- as much as he can because that is the foundation. That's the foundation of any instrument that you want to learn.
That's right.
Is the piano.
That's right.
It teaches you so much.
So I sang, went on and sang with the band and I got so, just like we was speaking it before, I got so that I didn't have a lot of second trombone parts, you know.
Uh-huh.
So I listened to the band and I started

making up parts, you know. So one night I'm sitting there, you know, just calmly and I didn't have no part to something, you know, and Don Redmon was a big kidder but I didn't know it at that time. He got a lot of kick out of me, you know, being young and I didn't know. So he come over to me and he said, "Hey, you, why aren't you playing in there?" And I said, "Well, Mr. Redmon, I haven't got a part to that." He said, well, "Play in there anyway." So I grabbed up my horn and I made up a part anyway and played. But it was a great experience and I learned a lot from Edward Cuffy, too, because
Cuppy was a trombone player, right?

Yes. I used to practice with him and I learned a lot from Mr. Redmon because Mr. Redmon knew every instrument in the band and if you didn't know, he would take your horn and show you. He could. You know, he knew just how to write because he knew how every position on the trombone, how it laid, trumpet, alto saxophone, and all that. I've seen him take a saxophone player's horns and they have a tough passage and he would watch them finger it and he would tell them no. He said, "You finger it this way," you know, and it would be a faster way of fingering, an easier way. I've seen him do that, you know.
And then that's when I started to playing the second trombone and I started to really learn how to play low notes, and I love low notes, you know. And I learned a lot from Mr.
Redman to that extent, you see. He was like a teacher.
Did you get to do some singing now in McKinney's band?

Oh, definitely. Oh, yeah. And in fact I made three records. I made -- the first one I made was 'Come a Little Closer' and then later on I made 'Do You Believe in Love at Sight' and 'Wrap Your Troubles in Dreams.' McKinney didn't put my name on that record, I don't know why. To this day I never understood why he didn't put my name on there. Every place that you can buy the record it says vocalist unknown.
Oh, that's wild.
But --
Is your name on the other two records, though?
My name is on 'Come a Little Closer' but 'Wrap Your Troubles in Dreams' is on one side and 'Do You Believe in Love at Sight' is on the other side of the 78.
Uh-huh.
So that's the record that I didn't get my name on, you know.
Oh, I see.
And when I made that record at that time, too, Bennie Carter had came to take Don Redman's place because Don had left to get his own band.
Who were all the guys in that band -- this, again, I'm trying to recapture this band of McKinney's -- when you joined it?

When I joined the band the trumpets were Langston Curl -- he was playing first trumpet. Joe Smith was out but he came back -- and Buddy Lee, George Oliver Buddy Lee. And, by the way, he's Jonah Jones' cousin.
I see.
Uh-huh. And the saxophones was Edward Inge and Jimmy Dudley and Prince Robinson. Jim Larson was the drummer and Dave Wilburn was the guitar player and Escudero was the bass player.
Bass player, yes.
Now, Escudero left, oh, not long -- I hadn't been in the band too long and Don sent to New York and got Billy Taylor to come in Escudero's place.
Uh-huh.
That was a fantastic bass player, Milt.
Yes.
That's when I started fooling with the bass fiddle, when Billy Taylor was there.
Yes.
He had this metal bass --
Right.
-- and I used to watch him. Then I
found out that it fingered just as on the back of a violin, you see.
Oh, that's why you came in on that thing. I see.
Yes, because I know you had and I (unintelligible) did some things later.
Yeah, I know. So --
Beautiful.

-- so I used to fool with Billy's bass and then he had a tuba. Well, then I got to fooling with this tuba, too, and I found it dawned on me that the B-flat instruments were all relative. All the notes he made open on the tuba I could make closed on the first position on the trombone, you see.
Oh, yeah, you compared the --

Oh, definitely, you know. And your second valve was my second position, the third valve was the first -- is the first valve -- the third position, rather, and your fourth position was your first and second valve. Your fifth position is your second and third valve and your first and third valves is the sixth position, and all three valves down is the seventh position in the trombone. And it's the same way with the tuba.
Yeah, you really wiggled it out.
That's beautiful.
Yeah.
That's beautiful.
So after you find this out, then you say, oh, gee, you know, I can play this.
How long did you stay with that band then, Brother?

Well, I stayed with that band from December 7, 1930, to about May 1932. And there was a little discrepancy in the band then. Don had left the band and Bennie Carter came but Bennie wasn't that interested in the band either. So Bennie did some writing and all that. So Rex Stewart had come with the band at the time. Buddy Lee had left and went to New York with Don.

So Rex left and went to New York and he called me back and he said, "Fletcher would like to have you in his band." He said, "Why don't you come to New York?" So Bennie Carter was going, coming to New York, too, he and Hilton Jefferson because Hilton Jefferson was in the band, in McKinney's band at the time, too.
Is that so? Hilton Jefferson in the band?
Oh, sure.
I didn't know that.
He come in when Inge left. You see,
Inge came to New York with Don.
I see. So tell me about that switch. Now, when Inge left Hilton Jefferson took Inge's place in the McKinney's Cottonpickers band?
That's right, that's right.
And when Don Redman left, Bennie Carter --
Bennie Carter came over, you see.
I see, uh-huh.
When the switch first started, first, Cuppy had left and they had sent and got Big Green in Cuppy's place, Charlie --
(trombone player,)
Big Green, Charlie Green.
Yeah, see. And they got Doc Cheatham in Langston Curl's place because Langston went to New York with Don, see. And Buddy Lee went to New York with Don, you see?
Uh-huh.
So that's when they got Rex. But Joe Smith stayed with McKinney, --
I see.
-- you see? And later on Cuppy came back because Big Green didn't stay. And Bennie Carter took Don's place in front of the band.
Right.
But --
Then you left to come to New York with -- who'd you come to New York with? Don Redman or who?

Well, I came to New York actually in the beginning to join Fletcher. Now Fletcher wanted me to play violin. He wanted me to play trombone. He wanted me to sing and then double just playing [rhythmic] piano, you know, because I knew the piano, for $100 a week.
Uh-huh.

So I saw Don on the street and Don said, "What are you doing here?" And I told him. He said, "Oh, no, you don't want to go with Fletcher. Come with the old Pickers, you know. You know us." And he said, "Fletcher's not working that much anyway." So he said, "Why don't you come on in my band?" Well, that's all I wanted, --
Beautiful.
-- you know. Now, --
That was in 1932, right?
That's right.
So Fred Robinson and I used to come down to listen to the band. The night that Fred Robinson got --
Trombone player?
Yeah. -- he got wind of it and put in his notice.
Oops.
He put in his notice, see, in Don's band because he knew right then that I was going to have the job.
Uh-huh.
Now, a funny thing happened in the meantime. DoPreist Dupreez Wheeler's lip went bad and Calloway had me to play in the Lafayette Theater with his band and double at the Cotton Club.
What year was that?
That was 1932.
Really?
Yeah.
Let's see, that's interesting.
Yeah. So Cheatham Reuben was coming in the band in Ruben Reeves' place, you know, --
In whose band now? Cheatham was coming -- ?
In Calloway's band. He left McKinney.
Oh, yeah. Well, you didn't really stay, you were just subbing for DoPriest Dupreez Wheeler?
That's right.
How long did you sub for him at the Cotton Club?
Just a week.
Oh, just a week.
Just a week.
I see, but you were really with Don's band?

Yeah, but Calloway told me, he said, 'Why don't you come on over here with us?' He said, 'We're getting a lot of young boys up here now, you know, I'm changing men.' He said, 'You're going down there with them old men.' I told him -- I listened to Calloway's band and I didn't like his band at all there. I didn't like it at all. It was, oh, man, it was a horrible band to me, and I'd been used to playing Don Redmon's music, you know.
Sure. Good arrangements?
Oh, beautiful arrangements. So Calloway said, 'I'll give you $90 a week if you come on up to the Cotton Club.' I said, 'No, uh-uh, never mind.' I went down to Connie's Inn for 66.
Connie's Inn. Well, Don had to be in there, huh?
That's right.
Beautiful.

That's right. And what a beautiful band. We used to broadcast over the network, CBS. We used to broadcast three times a week, sometimes four, over CBS and then every night we broadcasted over WMCA, every night. We got
that exposure.
What kind of club was that? Connie's Inn, Brother?

Connie's Inn was a nice little club. It had a show. It had a floor show just like -- but it wasn't as elaborate as the Cotton Club's show but it was a good floor show. It had chorus girls in it and comedians and singers, you know.
Connie Immerman was the guy that owned it, wasn't it? A little fat guy, Connie Immerman?
Exactly. Connie Immerman.
Immerman, yes.
He had a brother, George Immerman.
Right.
Yes. Yeah, he had --
Where was that club located?
On a corner of 131st and Seventh Avenue, downstairs.
Yeah, right.
The little awning is still out there.
Right, and you go down the steps.
Go down the basement. That's right. The Lafayette Theater was next door.
Right.
And it was a beautiful little club

down there. I liked it. I liked it very much.
When we used to broadcast, though, we had to have
a funny setup. When we used to broadcast the rest of the
band would sit on the bandstand, but the six brass would have
to come out and stand on the other side --
On the dance floor?
-- in a semicircle.
Yeah. On the dance floor?
Yeah.
Right.

On a semicircle when we broadcast.
That's the only way they could get a good setup at that time,
and that's where we stood out there to make all the broad-
casts.
With that old spider mike.
Oh, my goodness.

That mike looked like a spider
wheel.
That's right, it did.
Yeah. Oh, that's beautiful.

But that's better than the mike that
I made my first recording in. It was made in a wooden box.
Oh, yeah?

Like a little wooden box with a little
mike in it.
Butler
Where was that, Brother?
At the old Victor.
The first recording?
We called it the church, with McKinney Cottonpickers.
What year was that?
That was 1930.
Uh-huh.

December 18. And that's where I made "Come a Little Closer", and you sang in this one mike. They had one mike is all. And it was a wooden box, a square wooden box and the little microphone was about I'll say not even two inches, maybe three inches in diameter. But it come over. How they did it I don't know, but it came over.

But, anyway, Don Redmon's band, going back to Don Redmon's band in Connie's Inn, after I joined that band I really started to learn the trombone because Don had three. He was the first one to have three trombones.
Who were the three trombones?
Claude Jones and Bennie Morton, --
Oh, yes, --
-- you see?
-- and you?
Yeah, I came in in Fred's place, and we used to have a lot of rehearsals, section rehearsals. We
Victor's studio in Camden, N.J., was a converted church.

used to go down at Connie's Inn in the afternoon and rehearse, and Claude Jones and Bennie Morton was using lip vibrato in those days and they taught me lip vibrato. And we had a beautiful section, beautiful, and, Milt, that's another thing. I've never played with a bad trombone section in my life, never. Never.
That's beautiful. Well, you're a nice man. Well, see, you improve so many great trombone sections.
Yeah, but I know nice fellows, too, and they could play. They could play the -- you know, they could play. Every one of them could play.
That's beautiful.
That's right. Every one of them, I could even name them and talk about them. They could play.
How long -- Now, what did you -- After you stayed at Connie's, with Don Redman at Connie's Inn, what was your next band?
My next band was Calloway.
Oh, yes. Well, that was about 19 -- was it -- ?
It was January 1940.
19 -- I thought it was -- 1940, huh?
That's right. I joined the band in
Springfield, Massachusetts.
Uh-huh. Well, I was in the band then?
Yes, you were.
Yeah, I remember --

You know, how that happened was Don's band was kind of going downgrade then and so we went -- it's a funny thing. We went to Cleveland to play a New Year's Eve dance. When we got to Cleveland the guy didn't have no money and we rode a bus in all that snow -- and there was a lot of snow -- to get to Cleveland, in all that snow.
So when I came back I was living in the Woodside Hotel in New York. A lot of musicians lived there, you know, in those days.
Yeah, that was the black musicians' hotel.
Exactly.
Like the President was for the white musicians in New York.
That's right, that's right. And, gee whiz, Count Basie's band stayed in there. Erskine Hawkin(s) band. I was standing out in front of the hotel when Erskine's band drove up from Alabama /state.
That's beautiful.
And I was there when Basie's band
checked in from Kansas City, too.
it was.
And that was about 1937, I guess
'36 was it? Yeah.
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
And when did Erskine come up from Alabama?
About a year later.
A year later?
Uh-huh, yeah. And --
Was Sam Taylor in that band?
No, no, he came later, way later. Sam came later.
Oh, it was another group.

Oh, man, it was a beautiful -- Erskine had a good band. They had a lot of head arrangements and they made a lot of tunes up among themselves, you know. That's the way that 'Tippin' In' was made. That's the way 'Tuxedo Junction' was made. There was about three writers to 'Tuxedo Junction' out of the band but, you know, a little discrepancy -- we won't go into that because --
Sure, sure.
-- it's personal.
Well, then, --
But anyway --
-- we were back there where you, Don's band was getting a little seedy and you was in Ohio and Cab --
That's right.
-- came through.
Cab? No. Cab -- I come back home --
Springfield?
-- from the trip. No. From the trip I came back to New York.
New York?
Yeah, from the trip to Cleveland.
Uh-huh.

And Choo Choo Berry was sitting in the lobby. So Choo Choo Berry told me, he said, 'Say, Brother,' he said, 'Calloway wants to see you.' And I said, 'Yeah?' And he said, 'Yeah,' he said, 'come over to the Adams Theater tomorrow.'
That's over in Newark, New Jersey?

Uh-huh. So I come over to the Adams Theater and talked to Calloway and Calloway said, 'How'd you like to join my band,' he said, 'after all these years? I tried to get you before.' He said, 'Now, do you want this job?' You know?
And I said, 'Sure I'll take this job.' And he told

me the salary and everything and he told me, he said, "You go to [Carnik] and get measured for your uniform," you know, and so forth and so forth, "and you give me the itinerary of the band." I said, "What?" I never had anything like this before, you know. And I said, "How much the uniform's going to cost me?" because I used to have to buy the uniform in Don's band.
"It shouldn't [cost] you nothing," you know. He said, "You go to [Carnik] and measured up for a uniform and meet me in Springfield on the 8th."
[Carnik] was a tailor that --
[Carnik], yeah.
-- made all the -- Carnik made all of the clothes for band musicians in the --
About 100 bands --
About 100 bands.
-- he made clothes for.
A very nice man, too.
Oh, wasn't he? Wasn't he?
He was a [ ] man.
He was a sweetheart.
We're going to take a break now because now I can join this conversation with you a little bit since you've come into where I came in with you.
That's right. [PAUSE]
Yeah, Butter Brother, so I up booked to Cab Calloway. When do you say it was, December the 8th?
No, January.
Yeah?
January the 8th, 1940, at --
Springfield?
-- Springfield, Mass. --
Uh-huh.
-- I joined that band. You know, I took DePriest Dupreez Wheeler's place and Ty --
He lives right near here.
Yeah? Oh, he does? Uh-huh -- and Tyree came in in Claude's place.

Now, it was supposed to be originally, it was supposed to be Keg was supposed to go. He was going to keep Claude and let Keg go for Tyree, but Claude started getting drunk or something is the way I heard it -- I don't know because I wasn't there -- and Claude and Calloway had some words and so, instead, he kept Keg and put Tyree in Claude's place.
Oh.
And I still came in DePriest Dupreez Wheeler's place, you see.
Oh, yeah.
And we worked out a very good section
because we was all, you know, friends, you know. And in fact in that band everybody was friends, you know.
So it was Claude Jones -- ?
No, Claude had left.
No. Keg --
And Tyree and myself.
-- and Tyree.
We only had three. That's right. And the trombones was Lamar Wright and Mario Bauza and Dizzy.
Oh, yeah.
You see?
Right. (Laughter)
And Chauncey was leaving when I came in the band. Chauncey was leaving and Hilton Jefferson came in.
Oh, yeah. (Candy)
You see, because Brown was still there and Foots was still there and Chu was there and Jacinto Chabania.
Yeah, Jerry Blake.
Jerry Blake.
The baritone sax player. Let's see, you say -- let me get this straight. I was wondering, who was leaving as Jeff came in?
Chauncey Houghton.
Oh, yeah, that's right, right.
Yeah.
I tell you something, Butter Brother, I bet you've forgotten.
What?
I remember once you all had -- that trombone section was so great -- and you all were having a section rehearsal, --
Yeah.
-- and I was -- Tyree, I was always clowning with Tyree and kidding him, and you guys, as you mentioned before in your statement that you had learned the lip vibrato from Claude.
That's right.
And you guys were playing lip vibrato and Tyree was still using the hand vibrato and you all were trying to sell him on --
To go back to it.

-- to go back to the lip vibrato so the section would sound the same. And so you finally got him to do it one day and we played the show and it sounded beautiful and you guys were applauding him and praising him and I went over to him and started to kid him. I said, 'See, I told you you were doing it wrong just using that hand.'
Well, Milt, --
And Claude Jones called me over and said, "Look, we just got this guy to do it right. If you say one more word to him, I'm going to punch you in your mouth."
Well, this is after Claude came back. That's when he come back to the band.
Yeah, yeah.
Now, I tell you what Keg -- you see, Keg and I both could use lip or hand. Tyree couldn't use hand at all, --
Right.

-- you see. So one day we, Keg and I was fooling with the hand vibrato and he was using lip and Keg and I got the same speed with our hand he was getting with his lip, and he couldn't do that. He couldn't do that to save his life. There's no way in the world he could do it. And he never -- he used the lip vibrato, so Tyree never could play a dead tone, --
Yeah.

-- never could. He never could play a dead tone. His lips had become so accustomed to lip vibrato until he couldn't. If you tell him to play like -- Later on in years, you know, guys started playing dead tones, you know.
Dead tones, yeah. certain effects, yeah.
Duke didn't like for you to play a vibrato unless it was in your solo, you see.
Ah, yes.
You know, saxophones yes, but not brass.
I see.
Yeah.
Well, I remember that band now because I was there with you. Let's see, the rhythm -- Who was that rhythm section? When I was there it was Ben --
It was Bennie Payne and you and Cozy Colezie --
Cozy Colezie. Was Danny Barker -- ?
-- and -- Danny Barker.
Danny Barker.
That's right.
Daniel Moses Barker.
You know, we just heard a tune of his.
Yeah.
'Save the Bones for Henry Jones.'
'Henry Jones, because Henry don't eat no meat.'
Not long ago we heard that, didn't we?
Right.
Yeah, yeah.
They're still playing it.
I know it.
He's doing very well in New Orleans now.
Oh, I know. I know he is.
He's got a great book out.
Uh-huh, and he's -- I don't know, he's been working for that man in that club I don't know how many years, you know.
Yeah. He was up a few months ago. I got to see him for a minute.
Oh, you did?
Yeah.

But, now, let's see, to get that band -- the one thing about that band, you tell me about it, you guys were so conscientious because Cab, not being what we call really a musician, he was a great entertainer and he always got good musicians because he was paying good money and he wanted to surround himself with good musicians, but he didn't really know how to rehearse a band. And I remember we used to all get together and have section rehearsal and you guys used to get it together and then when we got on the stage, --
Oh, definitely.
Tell me about that.
Well, I'll tell you, do you remember,
too, that a lot of times if a guy made an arrangement, whoever made the arrangement, sometime Calloway would have him just run it over.
Right.
Then we would take it from there, --
Right.
-- you see.
Right.
But the section rehearsal was the thing that really made you have a lot of precision, --
Right.

-- and you could feel each other. And I have to go back to Don Redman, too, that taught me how to play with a section. Don Redman used to say all the time, 'Listen to the first man and you cannot go wrong. If you listen to the way he phrases something and you phrase it with him, you will have a section,' --
Beautiful.
-- you see. You know, today there's so much individualism till the kids, I don't know, they just don't learn this.
Let's see, who did you say the saxophones in that band was?
The saxophones in that band was Hilton Jefferson, A. J. Brown, --
A. J. Brown.
-- Walter Thomas, Chu Ghee Berry, --
Chu Ghee Berry.
-- and Jerry Blake was on baritone.
Oh, yes.
What a good band. It was a good band.
It was a good band.
A good band.
A lot of fun.
Oh, we had so much fun with Dizzy there.
Yeah. Oh, yeah. Do you remember the cooking? We used to cook -- ?
Sure. Well, you know why. The reason that you guys cooked is because we used to play a lot of towns in those days that you couldn't eat in white restaurants.
That's right, that's right.
I know the way we could get good food was to -- was we were cooking in the theater --
That's right.
Excuse me -- because in those days all the RKO theaters had beautiful back stages. They all had kitchens.
Sure did.
They had playrooms for the kids.
Sure.
Each dressing room had individual tables with your adjustable lights, chaise lounge, white sunken tub and bath for you to take a bath then if you wanted to.
Right.
Each room was named after a state.
Right.
And we all used to have -- we had so many rooms around there that --
Yeah.
The trombone section, we usually stay together, you know.
Yeah.
Sometimes when you all was cooking -- I know you and Tyree -- but you and Walter Thomas, oh, my --
Yes, well Tyree --

I never saw a room like that. Let me insert this. That room was chaos and when we got ready to leave Milt and Walter Thomas just take it like this, papers and everything, and say, 'Shrump,' shrump it up like that and put it in a bag.
We put them in whoever bag it was in.
That's right.
That's the truth, and (Unintelligible)
Then get it out.
sort it out when we got to the next town.
That's right.
"These your socks? These your shirts?" But it was still chaos in that room.
It was, but that was a beautiful way -- That band traveled, I think, first class. I think it was one of the first bands that traveled first class.
Cab, yeah. Cab was always first class. We had the best accommodations.
That's right, that's right.
He -- As you mentioned before, when you walk in that -- he bought all the uniforms, --
Shoes.
-- and all he asked you to do was to keep them clean.
That's right.
He insisted on cleanliness. He bought the shoes, he bought the uniforms. I mean, several sets.
We had five, I remember.
At least. Sure, we sure did.
Five sets of uniforms.
That's right. He was really first class. There was no question about that. And the guys, the
men in the band -- the discipline was such and the guys were such gentlemen until if a stranger, a new guy, came in the band, if he was a little below, we'd just look at him --
That's right.
-- and he would straighten up.
Where'd he come from?
He'd have to straighten up because he couldn't survive in there, --
No.
-- because there was too much class for him.
That's right.
It was really a great thing to be a part of.
Well, you see, Calloway himself -- you know, I've always said, and it's been said a lot of times, a band is no greater than its leader, --
Right.
-- you see. Calloway had a lot of class.
Always.
A lot of class, you know, and he believed in discipline. If you're going to do it, do it right. If you don't, get out, --
That's right.
-- you know.
And he'd tell you in a minute. "Lay dead till Tuesday."
That's right. He'd tell you -- that's right -- "Lay dead and wait for Thursday." That was payday.
That was payday, Thursday. He was amazing.
But I'll never forget when a couple of guys was late or a couple of guys didn't act right, he looked at [ ] little boy in his place.
That's right.
Do you remember Buster Harding--
Right.
-- was the arranger, --
That's right.
-- and Buster Harding used to be in New York? And Calloway would call up Buster and we used to say Buster was head of the farm system.
Yeah. "Pull out another guy right away."
That's right.
I wonder -- tell me about some of the songs you sang in that band, Brother, because you --
Oh, gee whiz, I used to sing "Out of Nowhere." I used to sing Besame Mucho. I used to sing "I
Concentrate on You." I used to sing 'As Time Goes By.'
'As Time Goes By.' Yeah, I remember that one. Tell me about the --

And the first song that I sang, oh, gee whiz, I'll have to think that over. But I enjoyed every tune. Calloway used to -- it looked like he always gave me the tunes that he didn't want to do but they had to be played because they were popular tunes, --
They were popular tunes.
That's right. -- and tunes that I guess he thought he himself wouldn't do, you know.
Well, he didn't have the in-depth musically to do some of those intricate tunes like 'I Concentrate on You.'
Yeah, I know.
That's, of course, a hard one for a singer to sing.
And 'The Night We Called It a Day?'
Yeah.
And I used to -- Well, after Payne left, you know, I got the tunes that Payne used to do, a lot of them I got to do later on, --
Right.
-- you know, like Just Worrying for You --
That's right.
-- and 'Don't Worry About Me,' you know, and those tunes like that that Payne used to do when he left, you know.
Right.
Payne showed me a lot of things, you know.
Yeah, he was a [ ] .

You know, Payne and I was kind of close, you know. Payne, he admired what I could do, you know, and Payne used to talk to me. The only time that he didn't talk to me, if he got in a blackjack game with me he wouldn't talk to me.
Do you remember, Butter Brother, when Franz Francis Jackson came in?
Oh, yeah. Franz Francis Jackson came into the band to play tenor.
Tenor saxophone player?
That's right. He came in and he wrote this thing for bass only.
Yeah.
And you had these guys come up, you know, and they tried it over with you. So one day I asked you,--
It was written for two basses.

Yeah, uh-huh. -- so I asked you, I said, "Milt," I said, "let me try this with you." So Milt looked at me and he said, "All right," you know, and said, you know -- so I went up there and we had a ball.
We played beautifully.

Milt went all over the theater saying, "Do you know one thing?" He said, "John and all them bass players, come up here, man, and try to play this thing. And, Buddy, come up here, man, and no trouble."
We played it right away. We played it, too.
