On the train, was it?
Yes.
That's right. You sure do have a great memory. That's marvelous.

Yes, we did. Yes, we celebrated his birthday. And do you know still, before he died, he was out in California and the guys told me that I think, I forget the trumpet player's name offhand told Pop let me hear him play. So Pop said all right. He said, "I'll play a little "Tenderly," and took his horn out there and played"Tenderly" so pretty it'd make you sick. And that was when he was -- just before he died. He had to be in his eighties.
That's right, easy.
You know? And he said, "Son, this is the way it's supposed to go."
But one thing I remember about him -- this is not music -- but we used to get into card games and Pops used to cheat, you know, --
He sure did. He beat me.
-- and he'd cheat, you know, and the guys would tell him, "All right, I caught you cheating." He said, "All right, if you want me to quit, I'll quit," but he
had won all the money, you see. He'd have cards on up by the -- standing on the train, you know, --
-- up in the baggage rack. He'd have cards all up in the baggage rack.

I never shall forget what, I think, one of the last times he -- I quit gambling, so I never gambled hardly much since -- he beat me on the train playing poker and I put all my money and I had kings showing and he had kings showing and he had a king-eight high, and where that eight came from I'll never know. But it took every dime I had. I was so sure, I was so sure I had that money that I didn't know what to do. He was really a fantastic man and he really would cheat at cards. Pops used to always cheat.
Yeah, I know.
He was a phenomenal man even though he couldn't read, you know. But play cards, count money? Forget it. He was the champ.

There is one story that perhaps we should tell 'cause you and I both know about it, and this is your history, but I think certainly this great man that you and I worked with and respect so highly we should mention. Since he couldn't read, we used to write his letters for him and he sent his money periodically to this lady he was married to and he didn't get home for years --
That's right.
-- and when he finally retired, he went home and she put him out.
Yeah, I know. I remember that.
She put him out.
She did, she put him out after he sent that money all those years. That's right.

All those years. When he went to California his wife -- Russell Smith, his wife -- put him out. But the most beautiful part about the story is to be told, which is so rewarding. He was a veteran of the -- he was a veteran and he went to the veterans association and explained it to them and they took her to court and they made her sell the house and give him half of the money for the house. They also took her to court and the government lawyers defended him and made her give him the automobile because he was a musician and he needed it.
True.

They made her give him the furnishings in the house that a musician needed, like the hi-fi and the record player. And they took the money -- not only did they do that, but they took the money that they got for him and bought him a condominium with about five or six apartments in it --
Oh, yes.
: -- and gave him a place to stay and let him live off the income so that he'd live to his old age in comfort, because he had been a veteran which I think is kind of rewarding --
It is.
: -- that we can know that somebody has been taken care of.
But the reward is, too, you know, he wound up marrying her daughter.
: Right. That's what I heard.
That's right, he married her daughter.
: Right.
That's right.
: That's amazing. That was --
And they stayed together clear till he died.
: That's right.
That's right.
: Quite a story there --
Yeah.
: -- which we were all involved in.
Oh, definitely. Oh, there's so many stories involved in that.
: Did you know Pike Davis at all?
Pike Davis was -- I met him, too. He
was the first trumpet player with the Blackbirds. He always played first trumpet.
Right.
He was a legit trumpet player. I never heard him play jazz but a very good trumpet player, but he had a funny personality.
Is that so? I didn't know that.

You couldn't talk to him, you know. You didn't talk to him much. If you was a kid or younger musician, he wouldn't have much to do with you, you know. And he wasn't a guy that I hung around too much. But he always worked. He always worked, always. He was a -- he had a big name as being a first trumpet player. He always played shows, you know, legitimate shows.
Right.
Fantastic. They wouldn't go out on the road with the Blackbirds without him, you know.
Beautiful. That's just what I heard. I never got to know him.

But since we're on the trumpet players of yesteryear, and I know you've met some of them and I've heard so much about some of them and knew some of them with you, can you tell us a little about Rex Stewart?
Rex Stewart was one of the most fantastic trumpet players that I've ever known. He had so

many tricks and he was fast, very fast. You know, that's who Roy listened to in the beginning. That's who Roy kind of patterned after to adopt his style, you see. And Rex used to cover the valves up -- he would finger his horn and cover the valves up and use a lot of false fingering so the guys couldn't tell what he was doing, you know. And a very -- he had an enormous appetite.
Is that so?

Oh, yes, he did. But he wasn't a real fast reader either. They found that out in Duke's band. But he had such a good ear, too, you know. They'd bring the music in for their parts out there and Tizol used to turn around and tell him, "uh-uh, I heard what you played there," because Tizol had did the copying, you know.
Right, right.
But once he got it down, though, he could play. He was fantastic. He had a lot of tricks, to me. A lot of tricks. He --
Did you ever get to play with him at any time?
In McKinney's Cottonpickers.
Oh, yeah.
Sure. I got to play with him then and that's when I really found out, you know. He has a solo on the record I sang on, "Do You Believe in Love at Sight?"
He has a record -- he has a solo on there. And Bennie Carter made that arrangement, by the way.
Wow.
And --
We didn't mention Bobby Starks, did we? Can you tell me about him?
Bobby Starks. He was one of the cleanest, one of the cleanest trumpet players that I ever heard.
He was a short, kind of plump, round guy?
Yeah, he wasn't too plump but he was very neat. Neat as a pin. He was immaculate. And very quiet, never had much to say, but he didn't have to with what came out of the horn.
He was in Chick Webb's band, right?

Oh, definitely, definitely. He was in that great band that Chick had when he had -- to me it was one of the greatest bands he ever had is when he had Dick Vance, Bobby Stark, and Taft Jordan in the trumpet section. That was fantastic.
Can you think of any of the other trumpet players along that line that we haven't -- do you remember them -- that impressed you, any of them?
Oh, so many of them impressed me.
When I first heard Buck Clayton he impressed me. When I first went to California he impressed me.
Right.
Gee whiz. And, of course, going back to the thirties, --
Charlie Shavers.

Oh, Charlie Shavers, I don't even talk about him. You put Charlie Shavers up there and then talk about the other trumpet players. That's the way I feel about him. He was fantastic. To me he was one of the greatest all-around trumpet players that ever lived. To me. That's my idea of him, you know. There's an album of (unintelligible) the genius of Charlie Shavers.
Si Oliver did the arrangements on that?
I don't know.
I played for him before (inaudible) & of here.
Fantastic.
(unintelligible)?,
Yeah, yeah.
But there's so many trumpet players, you know, that you, that I have known. John Nesbitt was a great trumpet player to me.
Who did he play with?
McKinney Cottonpickers.
Uh-huh.

And he also was one of the arrangers. He did some beautiful arrangements for McKinney Cottonpickers, like the arrangement that the band had made on "Playing Dirt," "the Way I Feel Today," "Rainbow" -- no, not "Rainbow Around My Shoulders," he didn't make that one. But "Playing Dirt" he did make. And I have to talk about this record because at that time McKinney's band a lot of times couldn't get to New York to record, so Don would come to New York and get some musicians together to record under the name of McKinney Cottonpickers, you see.
Oh, I see.
He would come and he would get Leonard Davis and get Sidney DeParis and sometimes he'd bring Joe with him to make the record date, and he always used Claude on trombone.
Claude Jones, that is?
That's right. And he would use Bennie Carter, Jabetus McCord McCoy, Coleman Hawkins on saxophones.
Jabetus McCoy. We haven't mentioned him before.
Yeah.
What did he play, tenor or alto?
No, he played alto, because Hawk played the tenor on the recording.
Where was he from?
I don't know. There was two brothers. There was Cass McCoy and Joe Beatus McCoy.
Oh, yes, I remember Cass.

Yeah, that's right, that's right. And he would use Fats Waller on piano and he would use Kaiser Marshall on drums and he'd always use Billy Taylor on bass and he used Truehart on guitar. Truehart was a guitar player with Chick Webb, a great rhythm guitar player. A great rhythm guitar player he was. Fantastic. I think he was the only guitar player Chick ever had --
Wow.
-- until he died, you know. He died, like some of the other great musicians at that time, they died of tuberculosis.
Yeah.
Medical science hadn't got to that yet.
Yeah, they had no cure for it, just rest. We didn't have very many --
Just like I know you remember Blanton.
Jimmy Blanton, of course, yeah.
I remember when we was in California in '42 and you used to go to see him at the hospital. Every day you used to go see him.
That's right. That's right.
That's right.
Sure did.
Fantastic.
Unbelievable bassist. He died at 22 years old.
That's right, just a kid.

We lost so great many. And while we didn't talk about it, of course I just [ ] some few trumpet players because in the brass department -- I asked you about trombone players later, but if you can think of any that I haven't asked you about, you just --
Uh-huh. Well, Steve Dunn was a very good, beautiful trumpet player. He played like Joe Smith, you know. He was a very good trumpet player back there in those days. [PAUSE]
Uh-huh. This is Sunday -- what is this, Brother?
25th.
Of what?
April.

This is Sunday, April 25. This is a continuation of oral history of what most musicians consider -- Quentin Jackson -- the super sideman. Undoubtedly one of the most renowned sidemen in the history of jazz.
Butter

No, but I was offered one. In fact they told me I could have one in the Cotton Club when they moved downtown. Now Duke was in there at the time, and Freddie Jenkins, he had talked to Herman Stark and them. He said, "Why don't you get a band together and we'll put you in as the relief band?"
When was this, Brother?
Around 1939.

So Fred Jenkins was around New York at the time, so I said, "No, I don't want to be bothered with a band." I had seen what other band leaders went through and I wanted just to keep my mind on playing and singing. And I didn't -- You know, to keep a bunch of guys working and keep them happy and satisfied, that was a job in itself, --
It sure is.
-- you see?
Right.

And I love my friends and I wanted to keep all my friends, so I said the best way to do that is not to become a band leader. I'd rather play for somebody else and play with somebody else and enjoy that, which I did.
Yeah. That is one of the reasons we call you a super sideman. You, an instrumentalist, have played for all of the greats and made all of these great
musicians, these great band leaders, helped them to perform great orchestras. So this -- I just want to specifically say -- this is why we consider you the super sideman.
Thank you.
Instrumentalist.
I try.
Now, we were just talking, to continue what we were doing last week, we were talking about Don Redmon and his arrangements and we were talking about some of the instrumentalists.
Now what do you remember, Butter, about -- Did we talk about Seventh Avenue and what it was like and the rhythm club?
Seventh Avenue was a boulevard, a beautiful boulevard when I first came to New York.
What year was that?
I came to New York in May 1932. I joined Don Redmon June 6, 1932. I took Fred Robinson's place.
Fred Robinson was trombone, right?
Yeah. And a beautiful experience I'll never forget as long as I live because to me there was no band that sounded like that.
Who was in that band, Butter?
Well, the trumpets was Langston Curl and Shirley Clay --
Shirley Clay, trumpeter.

Yeah.-- and Sidney DeParis. Now, Shirley Clay, he got him from Earl Hines. And the trombones was Claude Jones and Bennie Morton and myself. And the saxophones was Rupert Cole and Edward Inge and Bob Carroll and, of course, Don himself. And Horace Henderson was on piano.
That's Fletcher's brother, right?
That's right. Manzie Johnson was the drummer and Talcott Reeves was the guitar player.
What a beautiful band. We used to broadcast over CBS three times a week and then every night we used to broadcast over [WMC.]
From where?
From Connie's Inn.
Connie's Inn?
That's right.
Three times a week?

Oh, yes, CBS, coast to coast. And we stayed in Connie's Inn until the fall, about, well, I'll say December and then we went on the road with that band. And fantastic that band was, it was so beautiful every place we went. And it was a band that you could dance to. Don knew the value of dance tempos, you see, whether it was a waltz, whether it was a fox trot in those days.
Don Redman,
(Unintelligible)?
Yes, yes.
You know, going back to McKinney's band, you know, that's what made McKinney's band such a great dance band was Don Redman, --
I see.

-- you see? Because he believed in playing music that people could dance to, and you'd always see the people just skim around the floor beautifully, you know, and relaxed because it was that type of band, that type of music.

So we come out of Connie's Inn and the next year, like 1933, we went on the road with a show with the Mills Brothers, one of the most fantastic shows, to me, road shows that has been ever put together. We had Ralph Brown who was a very good dancer in those days.
Sure, I remember Ralph Brown.

And we had a little comedy team, Red and Strugge. They used to do the lindy hop to 'Nagasaki'. And we had Myra Johnson. She used to be Fats Waller's vocalist. And we had Pete, Peaches and Duke, which was the neatest dance act I think I've ever seen, you know, and the Mills Brothers and, of course, the band.
That was a fantastic show. We played all the theaters all over the East Coast. We didn't go west.
Then after that that that broke up -- and John Mills got sick, you see, the Mills Brothers. That's when he died was that year. He got tuberculosis.
What year was that?
That's when John Mills died?
Yes, and when he got sick the show folded. Oh, we had a chorus line too.
Oh, boy.
We had a chorus line of 12 girls.
Name some of the theaters you played, Butter.
We played all the RKO theaters and we used to double back. Like when we played the RKO Palace in Cleveland, we would come back maybe three months later and play Loew's Orpheum in the same town.
Uh-huh. Well, a lot of times you played RKO theaters in ? What other towns
Oh, gee whiz, Cleveland. We played Youngstown, --
Akron?
-- Akron, and Boston.
Did you play -- ?
We played at the Metropolitan in Boston.
And where'd you play in Philadelphia? The Earl? Was it the Earl?
No, we didn't play the Earl Theater. No, we didn't play that. We played I think it was the Lincoln Theater then, which was a colored house in those days.
Oh, yes.
Sam Steeple owned the Lincoln. In fact he owned a chain of theaters in Philadelphia. He owned the Pearl Theater, he owned the Nixon Grand.
The Pearl Theater in Philadelphia is where a lot of great black stars got a start?

Exactly, out on Ridge Avenue it was. That's the first theater I ever played, by the way, with McKinney's Cottonpickers in my life. The first day I ever played in my life was the Pearl Theater in Philadelphia.
Name some of the great people that got started there. Dizzy -- I think Dizzy played there first.

I don't think Dizzy played there because I think the Pearl was closed when Dizzy came. When Dizzy came to Philadelphia he was -- when he was with Frankie Fairfax, I think the Pearl had closed then. But the Nixon Grand was open, the Lincoln was open, and they used to have all the -- have the black shows, you see, and the black bands. All the big bands used to play there.
So going back to 1933 with Don Redmon, after that

year of one-nighters, we played the first theater restaurant in New York. It was called the Casino de Paris. It was where theater -- CBS Theater number four is now on 54th Street. That was the Casino de Paris. Billy Rose was the manager and he run it for the Kings Beer people. In those days it was the Kings Beer people, if you understand.
: Sure.

A beautiful show. Two bands, Ben Pollack's band and Don Redmon. And we used to play the show together. The conductor was Charlie Drury, he used to conduct the show and he used to have a light that he would stand in the middle and he would conduct both bands. Sometimes both bands would be playing at the same time in the show.
: Oh, I see.
Ben Pollack had a very good band. And we started --
: You remember the guys who was in that band, Butter?
Well, I remember Charlie Spivak was in that band. He was playing first trumpet. Yank Lawson was in that band. Eddie Miller was the tenor player.
: Wow.
Ray Bauduc was the drummer. And Joe Harris. He only had one trombone. Joe Harris was the
trombone player. He later went to California. And I think Bob Zurkee was playing the piano and I think Bobby Haggart was playing the bass. I think he was playing the bass then.
Bob Haggart?
Yeah, uh-huh.
It was a band actually later that Bob Crosby took over.
Oh, it became the Bobcats?
That's right.
I see. Now what year was that again, just to -- ?
That was 1933, but the Bobcats didn't come into being, I think, till about '36 or '37 --
Right.
-- when Ben Pollôck --
Now this was Casino de Paris on -- ?
On 54th -- between 54th and 53rd Street. Let me see, --
On what -- What avenue was that?
No, it was on Broadway, between Broadway and Eighth Avenue.
Oh, between Broadway and Eighth Avenue.
Yeah, but the club extended from 54th to 53rd Street, you see.
I see.
You understand?
Sure.
It took up that block, in other words.
Oh, yes.
And it was a theater restaurant, and on the stage you would do the show.
That would be like where the Ed Sullivan Theater is now, right?
No, no, no.
That's 53rd and 54th.
Yeah, but the theater is more near Eighth Avenue to what I'm talking about.
Near Eighth Avenue. Oh, yes, the CBS Theater.
That's right.
I'm trying to pinpoint it down. I see.
That's right. That's right. And then, after the show, they would turn the panels around and make a big chrome semicircle and the people would go up there and dance on the same stage.
Oh, that's interesting.
Uh-huh. It had a beautiful show. It had Cardini in there, [Houdini Hindu] Smith and Dale. It
had a chorus line of 24 girls and it had 16 showgirls. And Max Baer, he opened it.
Oh, is that so?

That's right, and Max Baer, he wanted to be a playboy and so one night he didn't show up for the show and he was out with the girls, so Billy Rose fired him and that's when he got Bill Bojangles Robinson to come and take his place.
Wow.
Yeah.
And going back to the band, of course, that's when we added the fifth saxophone because Don played alto, too.
And you tell me that's the first time that you heard any band use five saxophones. Is that right?
That's right.
Who instigated that?
Don.
Don Redmon.
Just like he was the first one to have three trombones.
You never saw a band with three trombones before until -- ?
Never, never.
And then Don put five saxophones.
He also originated five sax, then?
That's right.
: And wrote for them?

That's right, he wrote for them and, of course, Donald Kirkpatrick, the piano player in the band, was a wonderful, wonderful arranger. He come in after Horace Henderson left. And he used to write for Chick Webb, too, and so he made a lot of arrangements for Don, beautiful arrangements. And sometimes Jerry Blake would play baritone. Other than that he'd play alto because we didn't use two tenors then. We used three altos. And then when Don would play alto, the lead alto, then Jerry Blake would play the tenor part, which would make five saxophones.

Sometimes he'd use a combination like soprano on top and the two altos and the tenor and the baritone. The baritone would play a lot of times what the bass clarinet would play today. They would write it that way, too, like sometimes there'd be soprano on top and then three clarinets, you see, and then the baritone on the bottom, and Jerry would play a kind of subtone effect so it would blend with the clarinets, you see.
: Wow.
And the soprano made a beautiful, beautiful sound.
: You know who the five -- Did you

Oh, I mentioned the three before. I mentioned Rupert Cole and Edward Inge on altos and Bob Carroll on tenor. And then we got Jerry Blake for the baritone, and he played alto, too, and played good solos and good clarinet, good clarinet. He was one of the most soulful clarinet players. Two good clarinet players in that band. Inge was a technician and then Jerry was really the [solo] man, actually, you would call it.
Uh-huh.

And, of course, we had -- Claude had left the band. Claude Jones had left the band and we got Gene Simon in the trombone section so we still had three trombones. And the same trumpet section, Sidney DeParis, Manzie Langston Curl, and Shirley Clay. And Manzie Johnson and --
Drums?
Yeah.
Manzie Johnson on drums.
Uh-huh, and Bobby Ysaguirre on bass.
Bobby Ysaguirre on bass, right.
Yeah, uh-huh. And Talcott.
I'd just like to mention we're having a little repast here because I don't want you to get too hungry, so we're having a little bite which we would like to include in the conversation, so --
Oh, definitely.
-- anytime you get ready to have your little bite, you go right ahead. I'll be thinking of something to ask you while you have your little --
Just go right ahead, because --
-- a little repast.
-- I'm kind of in to it now and --
Yeah, I want you to --
-- you know, I don't want to stop for too long.
-- keep right ahead because I want to ask you about the Savoy Ballroom and who was over there at that time, Butter.
Oh, good.
Yeah. And I wanted to ask you something about the Savoy Ballroom, and we can get into Bennie Carter and Russell Procope. So let's start with the Savoy Ballroom.
What year is this now? We're in 1933, right?
Yeah, uh-huh.
Could I go before I came to New York about the Savoy Ballroom because --
Yeah, sure, by all means.
-- [ ] that?
Well, you know, Fess Williams, --
Right.
-- he was a band from Chicago. He opened the Savoy Ballroom in 1926.
He did?
Yes, he did, Fess Williams. He opened the Savoy Ballroom.
Go right ahead, Butter.

And then Chick -- Chick Webb was in there, too. Chick Webb had an eight-piece band. He had two saxophones in there. He had Johnny Hodges on alto and Elmer Williams on tenor, and he had Cootie Williams on trumpet. I don't know who the bass player was.
Was it Elmer James? Maybe Elmer James?
No, no, this is before Elmer's time.
Oh, I see.
Yeah. I remember when Elmer James was there. But I know the horns, you see. And Jimmy Harrison was on trombone with him for a while.
That's who Chick had for the four horns. And then, of course, the rhythm, he had Bobby Johnson on the guitar. He always did have him. No, Truehart. He had Truehart.
Truehart.
Excuse me. Yeah, Truehart on guitar. But I don't know who the bass was at that time. And then

came Cecil Scott's orchestra. Cecil Scott originated in my hometown, Springfield, Ohio. He used to be just a trio. He played clarinet and his brother played drums, Lloyd Scott, and he had Don Fry on piano. They used to do little jobs around home, so finally they got the idea to have a big band.
So they got Bill Coleman and Frankie Newton for their --
Bill Coleman was a trumpet player, right?
-- trumpets. That's right. Him and Frankie Newton. Frankie Newton was a great trumpet player. And Bill Coleman is still playing trumpet in Europe.
Right. This is 1976 and he's still --
That's right.
-- playing well.

Of course Frankie Newton passed. And Dickie Wells was the trombone. Here was a trombone player that I don't think nobody would ever get his style. It would be useless to try to copy it. Dickie Wells played the most humorous trombone that I have ever heard.
Yes.

There was a lot of humor in his playing and he could play pretty if he wanted to, you know. He could play a beautiful melody. And he had an iron lip and a very good range. He was making D's and F's back there then.
In those days no other trombone player you would hear that was making them like that in his solos.

And he had John Williams on alto and, of course, Cecil himself played tenor, and Don Fry played piano, Lloyd played drums, and they had Hubert Mann, a banjo player from Pittsburgh. He played the banjo.
What a band they had. They made some records for Victor.
For Victor, huh?
Uh-huh, and they stayed together for a while.
What companies were recording most of the jazz musicians in those days?
Well, it's according. You had Brunswick, you had Victor, you had Columbia, you had Vocalion. Those were, really, the main companies --
I see.
-- at the time. They were the main companies.

Then, going back to the Savoy Ballroom later on, Chick was always the main band there and he enlarged his band, you know, and he always was the house band there. Then later Basie came and the Alabama State Collegians.
Well, Basie came about 1936 or '37, right.
That's right, and the Alabama State Collegians came before that.
Well, we haven't mentioned the Savoy Sultans. What about that band?
The Savoy Sultans was a little band. There was about -- they had two trumpets and three saxophones and rhythm and they didn't really play in tune. Musically they wasn't too much musically, but --
But they had a beat.

-- they would swing you into bad health. Any band that come up to the Savoy Ballroom, if you didn't outswing the Savoy Sultans, the dancers wouldn't even dance to your music. They'd wait till the Savoy Sultans started playing.
It wasn't academically a good band.
That's right.
But rhythmically it was out of sight.
Beautiful, rhythm like that.
I just want to interject that the drummer was called Razz. Alex Elliott Mitchell was his name.
That's right.
I remember him. I went to school -- he's one of the alumnis of the Wendell Phillips gang. It's comparable to the Austin High gang. We had Ray Monroe
and Nat Cole and --
Oh, yeah.
-- Eddie Cole and Lionel Hampton and Razz -- that's Alex Elliott Mitchell -- Razz, drummer, that came by the Wendell Phillips High School. This is in the black community.
Uh-huh.
And Cyril Haynes was the piano player, wasn't he?
Yes, he was.
Cyril. was
Yes, he was a piano player.
Who were the two trumpets, you know?
I'd have to think.
Greshon Moncyr Brother Moncour --
Sam, Sam.
Sam.
Yeah.
Greshon Brother Moncyr was the bass --
Was the bass player.
-- player.
His son is a good trombone player right now.
Right.
Greshon Gresha Moncyr.
Gresham?
: Gresham?
Uh-huh. And Sam -- I can't think of Sam's -- What a trumpet player he was.
: But they were rhythmic --
Oh.
: -- rhythmic. Hard for that lindy they had the beat that was just right.
Yes, they did.
: So what were you saying about -- ?
Al
Mel Cooper himself played alto.
: Oh, alto?
Uh-huh, he played alto.
: Cooper and his Savoy Sultans.
That's right.
: He was their leader?
Uh-huh.
And then Teddy Hill had a fantastic band up there, too.
: Oh, he played the Savoy, too?
Oh, sure, he was one of the main bands in the Savoy, like he was second to Chick Webb.
: Oh, I see.
What a band he had. He had -- his trumpets was Bill Dillard, Shad Collins, and Roy Eldridge.
: Wow.
x Massenberg
And Dickie Wells on trombone. Saxophones was Howard Johnson and Russell Procope and --
Alto sax?
Yeah, two altos. -- and Choo Berry was the tenor. And Sam Allen was the pianist and old man Fulbright -- I forget his first name -- he was the bass player.
Bass player.
He used to wear all them funny hats.
Yes.
That's right. And I think the guitar player was named Bobby Johnson, too. And Bill Beason was the drummer.
Bill Beason?
Uh-huh.
I see.
Bill Beason later was with the Kirby band.
Oh, yeah.
Uh-huh.
Oh, is that so. Beason -- Okay.
Bill Beason came after O'Neill Spencer.
Oh, I see. That's what I was checking, checking up.
x Richard (Dick)
Yeah.
Let's see, O'Neill Spencer was at --
That band was the most fantastic band. It was a beautiful band, Teddy Hill. And the trumpets, they could play so high, all of them, and Dickie Wells played right up high with them.
On the trombone?
Yeah, yeah.
Oh, that's beautiful.

-- beautiful. He was a body-builder.
-- barbell and whatnot.

And he could play --
-- the piano a little bit, too, didn't he?

The same way he does with the saxophone. He might not play the saxophone for two or three months and then pick the alto up and play it like he just laid it down. He's one of the most amazing musicians of our time.

That's right.
He was in Fletcher's band then.
What year was that again, just for -- ?
That was 1930.
Ah ha.
1930 I got to hear that band. I was with Zack White at the time and we wasn't doing anything so I got a chance when they played in Cincinnati.

That's right. The same time, the first time I heard Duke was that same year.

I didn't know that.
-- some records with Chick Webb playing
actually, Fletcher Henderson!
violin years ago.

That's 'Blue Lou'?
That's 'Blue Lou'.

Oh, that's all right.

Uh-huh.

I would like to ask you just right now, just to interject this. What do you attribute to that the young black musicians don't have -- we have this era of all these instrumentalists like Bennie Carter and Chick Webb and Don Redmon and Garvin Bushell and Sam Wooding that played all of these great, all these instruments, these academic instruments like the flute and piccolo and bassoon -- and in this era we don't have too much of that.

I attribute that to disc jockeys, to our booking agents, to the trend of music that they are putting in front of these people. There's not music, actually, that you can learn anything from. There's no more big bands where that you can learn to play with a section. Everything is so individualistic now, you see. And everybody, if you listen, they all sound the same. They sound the same. You can make a million dollars on one record and a guitar player can learn five chords and get rich.
That's absolutely so, but I find that --

But now they want to know. The kids want to know now. Now they want to know now. They're going through a nostalgic era right now. And if you play colleges and you go around and do clinics and things, they want to know why, where did this come from, you see.
These musicians played great jazz and they also, Buster Bailey, a tremendous clarinet, you know, --
Oh, yeah, he was wonderful.
-- and I'm teaching now and I find out, white or black, young people aren't interested in clarinet anymore.
Uh-uh.
And the super white musician and the
super black musician, the Hubert Laws and the Frank Wess and Seldon the Selden Powell, are the ones that are playing these instruments and they're making a tremendous living.
Yeah.

But I find it very difficult to interest the whole complexity of young black musicians into being academic, whereas in this era you mentioned that everybody seemed to have been academic. Coleman Hawkins played piano, you played piano, organ, trombone, violin, I played violin and saxophone and bass, tuba. And I was wondering, other than what you said just now about the media, how is it that we can't seem to get these young musicians into being tremendously academic and using this for their own advantages?
Well, they see these little rock-and-roll bands making all this money.
Right.

They listen to certain things on the radio, certain types of music on the radio, you see, and you must remember that when we come up in the era of big bands you had to learn to play academically in order to play together.
Right.
Now, today, you can play solos or play anything you want to, any type of horn you can play, and it
doesn't need it, you know.
It doesn't need togetherness.

That's right. That's right. The world is separated, Milton, if you want to know the truth, and music describes the world. There's no togetherness in the world. People don't dance together no more, They dances separately. Everybody's doing their own thing. So how are you going to have togetherness in music?
Thank you, Butter. I'm so glad --

no, Virginia (Norfolk).

[ getting] the band. What year about was that, Butter, approximately?

-- from all these different places.

Which is most interesting because in most historical jazz we only hear of the musicians coming from New Orleans, but we had these great territorial bands --

-- that played in their territory and people are beginning to recognize them and they begin to see, now that the Chicago era is over, everybody's beginning to flow to New York because this is the mecca now where -- entertainment mecca -- and they all began to flow into here.

Jonah's brother-in-law.

course, Coleman Hawkins.

I know.

-- and a couple of others. Yeah. He was a very good arranger. I don't know as he ever wrote anything for Tommy when he was there but he should have.

-- and we would like to talk about them and mention them --
Yes.

-- for posterity so people will know that there wasn't just a handful that won the awards but that a great number of musicians contributed to these bands to make them as great as they were. And I think this is one of the main things -- object in doing this kind of an oral history is to let the people know, the students of jazz and lovers of jazz know the great people that comprise the making up of these great bands. So I know, between you and I
we'll probably miss some which we really don't intend to miss but it's going to be hard because your memory is so beautiful. But I'd like to --
Of course, something's always coming to you, you know, that you can say. --
Sure.
-- about these people.
And so we keep rehashing things about different ones.
Uh-huh.
I'd like to get back to Detroit. There was a couple of brothers out there that played saxophone. One brother that played with Milton -- the organ player -- Milt --
Oh.
-- the organ player that's now around.
I know. He just lost his brother. His brother just died. Ted Buckner.
Ted Buckner is the one.
Ted just died.
Ted Buckner, yes.
Ted played with Jimmy Lunsford.
Ted Buckner.
A lot of solos he made with Jimmy
Lunsford people thought that Willie Smith played them, but it was Ted Buckner.
Ted Buckner.
He played the first chorus on the record, Jimmy Lunsford's record of "Margie."
Uh-huh.
That was him. A very good saxophone player.

And, you know, around Detroit they had a lot of good bands. When I was there at McKinney's band, they had a lot of good bands. Billy Minor had a good band around there, you know. And that's where Inge came from. That's where we got Inge, from Billy Minor's band.
Uh-huh.

But Ted Buckner and his brother both were fantastic musicians around there at that time, even. Ted Buckner played the xylophones with four mallets, would make some of these vibraharp players today look sick.
Yeah, this is --,
And it was said once that when he first joined Hamp he played Hamp's vibes and Hamp told him not to touch them anymore.
That's interesting.
That's right.
So if you can think of anything else.
I'm just trying to revive some that I know that I know you know.
Oh, yes. And, gee whiz, there was so many.
So many -- Let's take a little --
So many good saxophone players, and Albert Sears.
Al Sears. Let's don't forget him.
Al Sears. You know, Al Sears came from Zanesville, Ohio.
Uh-huh.

And he played with Zack Whyte before I joined the band. He played with Zack Whyte in '29. He played baritone, you know. He used to stomp his foot way high to get that rhythm, you know. He left there and went to Buffalo, like a lot of musicians.
Did you know Buffalo was a center for a lot of musicians back in the thirties?
Uh-huh.

Alphonso Trent's band went there and stayed. Jimmy Lunsford's band went there and made its headquarters there for a long time before it came to New York. Stuff Smith stayed there after Alphonso Trent got his band together.
Where was that -- ?
Buffalo.
In Buffalo, New York.
Yeah.
Yeah, Buffalo was a great town, --
Was it. A lot of good musicians around there.
-- a great town. Cozy Cole was around there.
That's right. Cozy Cole, he went there -- You know, Cozy Cole played with Willie Bryant's band used to be in the Savoy.
Uh-huh.

Bennie Carter was in that band. Ben Webster was in that band. Teddy Wilson was in that band Willie Bryant had at one time, you know. And Willie Bryant was an entertainer. He wasn't a musician but he liked musicians.
That's right, he was a dancer. He used to dance. He had a dance act at first.
Oh, yes, him and Leonard Reed.
Right.
They was with Toby's show years ago called the Whitman Sisters.
Right.
That's where I first saw them when I
was a kid in Springfield.
When you say a Toby show, what does Toby mean besides --
Theater Owners' Booking Association.
Theater Owners' Booking Association.
That's right. They booked different little theaters, one-night stands all around the South, with black shows.
Yeah, and so we had a little expression --
We called it Toby time.
Toby time.
Yes.
Theater -- What does it stand -- ?
Theater Owners' Booking Corporation.
Theater Owners' Booking Corporation.
Uh-huh.
But in the soul, in the black society we had another name called --
Booking Association.
Yeah, we had another name for it called Tough On Black Asses.
Yeah. It was.
Yeah, because there was a -- the right [was] playing all of these segregated places --
That's right.
-- and all of the things that it took to get through in the form, with the segregation policies at the time.
That's right. Blanche Calloway and, of course, Calloway himself, you know, his sister had a show that came home called Keep Shuffling. She had a show on Toby time.
Is that so?

And that's where I first saw Calloway. He was just a kid. And he and Blanche had an argument at home and that's when he got mad and went back to Chicago. He left and went back to Chicago. This is even before he was with Hardy's Alabamans.
Wow.
That's right. I told him about that, you know.
I'm sure -- he always admits that Blanche was his mentor. She was the one, because Blanche was his only sister and she was a fantastic performer --
Was he?
-- and bandleader and she was the one that helped him get into show business.
Do you know, I always knew that, if you ever saw Blanche work back in those days and how she used to
bend over and throw her hair around and shake her head, --
Right.
-- Calloway used to do the same thing.
That's exactly where he got it.
Oh, what a master showman.
Absolutely.
Let's take a little breather for a second so you can finish your repast there and then we'll go back into something else, get into some other --
Now, where are you on the notes, so we --
Yeah, yeah, here we are, Butter.
We've just taken our little break now.

I'd just like to mention we were talking about the great saxophone players, Don, Ed Inge and Don Byers and we named -- we didn't even mention Jacquet Jackett. Of course, that's coming up later, but when did you first run into Jacquet Jackett? In Cab's band? He came --
Oh, no, uh-uh.
No?
Uh-uh.
Illinois Jacquet Jackett, that is.
I first heard Jacquet Jackett with the first band that Lionel Hampton had in 1941. That's when I first heard him.
Well, he came in here with Lionel around that time.
Yes. And Lionel had a very good band there.
That's right.
And it was -- the two tenor players was like Mutt and Jeff, here was Dexter Gordon, and Dexter Gordon was so tall and Illinois was short, and they was the two tenor players in there.
Right.
And the alto players in the band was Marshall Royal and Ray Perry, and the baritone player was the co-writer of 'Open the Door, Richard.' I'll think of his name a little later.
But the trumpets in that band was Ernie Royal, Joe Newman, and Karl George.
Right.

And the trombone player, we called him Mushmouth. I forget his real name. And the trombone player was a beautiful trombone player. And, of course, Norman was the bass player. I think he's out in Frisco now.
No, not Norman. He was a football player. He lives in San Francisco. He --
Freckle face guy.
Yes, yes.
He was the bass player, anyway.
I can't recall his name.
And, of course, Milt Buckner was the pianist.
Right.
And the guitar player used to be with Nat Cole. He was the guitar player then.
Irvin Ashby.
Yeah, he was the guitar player.
Irvin Ashby.
Irvin Ashby. He was the guitar player with Hamp then.
I'm ashamed I can't recall the bass player's name, as well as I know him.
Uh-huh, that was --
He turned out to be a disc jockey later in San Francisco.
Uh-huh.

The last time I saw him, you know, he was playing with a relief band. We played a dance there -- a concert, rather -- and he was playing in the concert band, you know, and he played a little while in a club there, but --
Now, we went on to some arrangers. We started talking about -- of course we mentioned Don and we mentioned Don Redmon and we mentioned Bennie Carter and
Fletcher Henderson and Horace Henderson. But there was a young kid that Tyree Glenn was with -- talking trombone players, we haven't mentioned. We haven't got to trombone players yet?
Oh, no, we haven't.
But we were mentioning about Elton Hale Hill.
Yes.
A good arranger.
Yes, I knew Elton Hill when he was with Tommy [Myles] in Washington and then later he was with Eddie Mallory at the same time --
Eddie Mallory was married to Ethel Waters --
That's right.
-- and he was a musical conductor.
That's right.
And he's from Chicago.
Yes, I know.
He come out with a band out -- Jimmy Wade's or one of those bands out of Chicago.
Uh-huh, yeah, and he was also with the Hardy's Alabamans, too.
Right, [must] have been with Hardy's Alabamans.
That's right, and --
Coyle Les Corley was the guitar player.
Uh-huh.
Yes.
And Doc Cheatham was in that band and Calloway conducted the band.
Right.
In fact that's the band that Calloway came to New York with first, --
Uh-huh.
-- was Marion Hardy's Alabamans.
Uh-huh.
Now let's get on down into the trombone section, which is home for you, and you can --
Well, we haven't finished with the arrangers yet, by the way.
Oh, yeah, no, the arrangers. Go ahead.
Do you remember Jimmy Mundy Monday?
Oh, yes, by all means, yeah. Where did you first run into Jimmy?
With Earl Hines -- No, in Washington. He was playing with Tommy [Myles'] band in Washington. That's when I first ran into him. That was before he went to Earl Hines.
: How did he impress you?
He was a good tenor player. I thought he was a good tenor player.
: Uh-huh.
Yes, I did.
: Uh-huh.
And definitely a good arranger.
: That's amazing. He went on to great heights, writing for a right, with the Broadway shows and --
That's right.
And Norman -- what's his first name? He was a very good arranger, too. He used to play trombone with Tommy Miles. Wears glasses. You've seen him around. He arranges for the shows he has.
: Norm -- Fred Norman.
That's right. Fred Norman was a trombone player with Tommy Miles, too. He was in Tommy Miles' band even before Trummy Young, --
: Uh-huh.
-- you see. Now Fred Norman was a very good arranger.
: Oh, Trummy Young come out of Tommy Miles' band also? Is that so?
Oh, yeah, yeah.
: We haven't mentioned --
But Fred Norman -- going back to arrangers --
Uh-huh.
Fred Norman was a great arranger. Donald Kirkpatrick with Don Redmon was a great arranger, a very good arranger. And, of course, let's don't forget Buster Harding.
Oh, yeah, the little Ohio flash.
Yeah. Cleveland boy. I tell you about these Ohio boys --
Yeah, you guys contributed a great deal.
And Andy Gibson.
Andy Gibson.
Andy Gibson came from Zanesville, Ohio.
That's right.
Oh, we had so many lovely times. Andy Gibson made so many arrangements for Cab. He could write.
Did he.
He used to just write -- Instead of writing a score, he'd just write part by part.
Uh-huh, yeah.
He could remember the parts and just write from his head without a score.
That's right. Well, you know, that's
the way Sy Oliver did when he was with Zack White back in those days.
Oh, Sy was with Zack, huh?
Sure. Sy was doing the arranging Lurcefor then, even before Jimmy Lunsford, before he went to Jimmy.
Uh-huh.
And Sy used to write part for part like that.
Is that so?

Uh-huh, sure. In fact he showed me a little thing once. I was going to make an arrangement on 'Snake It Break It' Shaking and Breaking and Hang It on the Wall. And you write that way. You write your first trumpet part down, then your second trumpet to blend with that, then your trombone, and then you can get to your saxophones, to blend them in, you know, how you wanted to write countermelodies and things that go against that. You see?
Yes.
And I haven't forgot that.
Sy was truly a master at that, a tremendous master at doing that sort of thing.
Yes, that's right.
Sy Oliver, that is.
He had his own style. His style and his music sounds like no one else.
MR. : He was identifiable in Jimmy Lunceford's Lunceford's band.
That's right.
Also in Tommy Dorsey's band --
That's right.
-- and so many other bands. Anywhere you hear 'Margie,' a SI Oliver arrangement, you'd know immediately.
Exactly.
Because it had that swinging, swinging beat.
It had that driving beat about it, you know.
Right, and that little open space to give you time to breathe.
That's right.
Catch your breath and go back into the thing.
Uh-huh, yeah.
A truly great style.
Yeah, good arrangers, a lot of good arrangers around that, you know --
Uh-huh.
Of course we won't go into --
We've mentioned -- Who? Oh, what's
He wrote for Honi Coles.
Chappie --
Chappie Hill.
Chappie Willett.
Chappie Willett.
Chappie Willett.
Yeah. Gee whiz, Chappie Hill was a blues singer.
Yeah, Chappie Willett. I think he was from Philadelphia.
He was.
Yeah.
He used to do a lot of arranging for shows and for Cotton Club shows.
That's right.
And for dancers. He was a wonderful arranger for dancers. Yeah, he did Honi Cole's -- you know he did the music for Honi Cole's dancers when he was there?
That's right.
Yeah.
They were the Cotton Club Boys, the Cotton Club Boys.
That's right, uh-huh.
Extremely a good arranger for that.
That's right.
All right now, if we didn't think of any, we'll get back to some of them. Jimmy Munday, Elton Hill and Chappie Willett.
Calvin Jackson.
A great pianist.
And good arranger, too.
Uh-huh.
A very good arranger. He was writing for pictures for a while in California, you know.
Right, right.
Well, let's get back to our era now and start bringing the trombone players up.
Uh-huh.
Who basically really influenced you beside -- of course, you say your brother-in-law, Claude Jones, which was married to your sister.
Uh-huh.
And who were some of the great guys you admired, great trombone players, of that era, Butter?
Jimmy Harrison.
Jimmy Harrison. Tell me about him. Elucidate.
Jimmy Harrison was -- he could do more with five notes than any trombone player I ever heard. He was
a great swing trombone player. He would make you pat your foot. There was a lot of guys that, I think, stole from him. I have to say they stole from him.
Sure.
I tell you, the closest to me that played like him was -- oh, Bennie Morton was one of them.
Uh-huh.
And Teagarden used to listen to him, too, you know. And the trombone player that was with Chick. I think even he played as nearest, I'll call his name.
Uh-huh. What do you think of Teagarden? How do you -- ?
Teagarden to me is one of the most flexible trombone players in the business. I have to put it that way.
I agree.
Very flexible, very flexible.
Big sound.
That's right.
Mouthpiece for each.
Oh, yes, he can make his own. He made his own mouthpieces. He made his own mutes. You know, he was a mechanic, too, like --
Yes, he carried his lathe with him.
That's right.
And, of course, going back to the old trombone players, Charlie Green. I'll never forget him.
Yeah, Big Green.
Big Green. Big Green, there's nobody in this world I think could play blues as soulful as he could yet still turn around and play a most beautiful waltz you want to hear.
He did a lot of stuff behind Bessie Smith, didn't he?
He did almost all her records. He played trombone on all her records.
She even had a song made for him or something.
Oh, that's right.
Play the Horn or something?
Play that Horn, Play that Slide Trombone. Play it, Charlie.
Uh-huh.
I made that same record with Dinah Washington.
Is that so?
Yeah.
Oh, that's great.
Yeah, Dinah Washington Sings Bessie Smith.
: Yeah.
And we did that on there. She used my nickname, Butter. She said, 'Play it, Butter. Play that slide trombone.'
: Oh, that's nice.
Uh-huh.
: That's most interesting.
And, of course, Wilbur DeParis to me was a good trombone player, a very good trombone player. He was a what you call all-around trombone player. Vic Dickinson. Vic Dickinson left home before I did.
: He's from Ohio, too?
Sure, he's from Xenia, Ohio.
: Is that so?
Oh, yes, down there where Wilberforce University is. Yeah, he's from Xenia.

Then there was a little trombone player named Stump Brady, Floyd Brady. Floyd Brady, I took his place with Zack Whyte's band, and when I first left home when I went to Cincinnati he was the first person to ever give me any kind of a lesson and let me practice with him. He was a very little guy.
: He's still around.
He's still around. He doesn't play
much now.
: No.
But he left Zack Whyte and went to Andy Kirk and the 12 Clouds of Joy, and that's how I got in Zack Whyte's band.
: I used to hear Keg Johnson always mentioned him and how much he admired him.
Oh, yes.
: Stump Brady.
Oh, yes. Well, Stump, you know, Stump played with them a long time, with Andy Kirk. Then he came to New York, of course, with Teddy Wilson and that beautiful band.
Now, let me see --
: Well, we've got Big Green. What about J. C. Higgenbotham?
J. C. Higgenbotham, when I first heard him, he was another one. He used to play a lot of execution and all at once he changed and went to playing a lot of blues, you know.
: I see, uh-huh.
And J. J. -- well, of course, we're going way back.
Dickie Wells. I want to talk about Dickie Wells for a while.
Sure, please do.

Dickie Wells came through my home with Cecil Scott. I thought he was the most phenomenal trombone player I had ever heard. He was making a lot of glisses and he was -- he could almost do a conversation with the horn. Then later on when I heard him, he had left Cecil and he went with Teddy Hill. Then later he went with Basie and stayed with Basie a long time. He did a lot of good recordings with Basie, a lot of good recordings.
Is that so?
And, of course, Vic got a chance to play with Basie, too.
Right.

Dickie liked to kid a lot, you know, and he used to kid Vic a lot. One time they were sitting on the stage and Vic was sitting there -- he had stayed up all night and he was asleep, you know -- and Dickie shook him and said, 'Hey, it's your time to play.' And it wasn't his solo but he grabbed his horn up and started playing.
Oh, that's funny.
Oh.
It sure was.
And, of course, I want to talk about Lawrence Brown.
Yeah, but before we get to Lawrence,
I'd like to get -- I know you -- before we get -- that's the Duke Ellington era and I know you knew him before that.
Oh, way before that.
Well, okay, good. Starting talking about Lawrence Brown.
Lawrence Brown. I met him when I was with the McKinney Cottonpickers and he was playing in Sebastian's Cotton Club with Les Hite.
Uh-huh.

Now, Les Hite used to play with Louie whenever he came to Sebastian's Cotton Club. He used to use his band. Les Hite also recorded with Louie. He made 'Song of the Islands'. That's where the first vibraphones was played on Lionel Hampton. They got him a vibraphone to play and that was Lionel playing the chords on 'Song of the Islands' that Louie made back there.
Is that so?
That's right. And they got these vibraphones for Hampton and asked him could he play them, you know. He said sure, so he played the chords.
Well, he always played a one-finger piano, so he just jumped --
Sure, that's right.
And then Lawrence, you see, Lawrence made a record that nobody knew about way back there, I think about 1930, * actually 'Memories of You'; Song of the Islands, made earlier * get Hamp!
called 'Charlie's Idea.' It was really 'Tiger Rag.' Nobody ever heard a trombone player like that. Nobody knew who he was or anything because nobody ever went to California. But --
'Charlie's Idea?'
'Charlie's -- It was what they called Charlie's Idea of Tiger Rag,' really, is what it was. It was 'Tiger Rag.'
Do you know what band he played it with?
I don't know -- oh, Paul Howard.
Paul Howard.
Paul Howard was the name of the band, that's right.
And Lawrence Brown, 'Charlie's Idea'.

Yeah. I never heard nothing that fast. I never heard a trombone player like that, not like Lawrence was playing in those days. Now, when I met him in Sebastian's Cotton Club, he was working with Les Hite. Now, in between dance sets of the show, there was a piano player named Harvey Brooks and Lawrence used to take his trombone and go around to the tables and play tunes. Whatever tune that the people wanted to hear Lawrence would play a tune for them. He could play that soft.
Like a violin player, --
Yeah.
-- like a strolling violin player.

That's right, and could play that soft and had that much control. And Lawrence tried to get McKinney to get Lawrence then -- Excuse me -- but McKinney couldn't see three trombones and Don had the idea for it then. So when Don finally had three trombones in New York and Duke found out Don had three, Duke immediately when he went to California grabbed Lawrence Brown so he would have three.
Wow.
So Duke is the one that got him, not McKinney.
Oh, boy.

And I have never worked beside a man that played as consistently and as beautiful as this man played. He had so much soul -- I have to say a soul. He could play blues, he could play melody, and he could almost cry on the trombone. He made such beautiful records.
Well, there's no question, you worked with and knew essentially all of the great trombone players.
That's right.
Your brother-in-law, what did -- what do we have on Claude Jones, your brother-in-law. He influenced you to take up trombone. Claude Jones.
Well, Claude Jones, you know, he was
going to Wilberforce University and he was a drummer in the Wilberforce orchestra.
Wow.

And McKinney had this band and for some reason or other in that orchestra they had a trombone. And McKinney didn't have no trombones, so Lawrence -- I mean, Claude -- gee whiz -- Claude Jones started fooling with the trombone while he was in school down there. And he got to playing with the Synco Cinco Septet which later became the McKinney Cottonpickers.
What's the first name of the McKinney Cottonpickers?
Synco Cinco Septet.
Synco Cinco.
There were seven pieces.
Seven.
Seven pieces, and they used to play up to Manitou Beach, Michigan, every summer. The guys would get out of school and they'd go up there and play.
What school were they getting out of?
Oh, different schools.
Xenia?
Like Springfield. Some of the guys -- a couple of guys were still in high school, like Dave Wilburn, you know, and Claude was going to Wilberforce, you

know, and the guys used to play little gigs around there. So they got this job up in Manitou Beach, Michigan, to Clark's Lake. They used to go up there every summer. So Jean Goldkette heard this band, the seven pieces, and he liked what he heard. So at that time Don Redman was writing for Jean Goldkette. He was making arrangements for Jean Goldkette's orchestra, also writing for Whiteman. And I think I told this story before, I'm not sure, and he got Don to come out to Detroit and to take this band and enlarge on it to an 11 piece band, and he made it the house band in the Graystone.
And in those days, in order for -- you know, you're a black band, so they got to give you a name so that the people really know you're a black band.
Right.

And the band sounded so pretty on the radio and everything, you wouldn't recognize it as a black band, really, because they had so much finesse, so much quality. So they called it McKinney Cottonpickers, and the guys hadn't even been South. The band started in Detroit. And Jean Goldkette got them a contract with Victor Records. They named them the house band of the Graystone and they broadcast on WJR.
To me it turned out to be one of the greatest dance bands in the business. In fact, --
What year was that when Jean Goldkette
did that?
Oh.
Beautiful.
Now, let's get -- What about my best buddy, Keg Johnson?
Keg Johnson. I first knew Keg in Chicago. He was playing around there. He had played with Louie.
Right.
That's when I first heard of Keg. Keg had a phenomenal lip, too.
Yeah, a thin sound but a very --
Well, now, I can't say he had a thin sound. I wouldn't say that about Keg.
Well, you know better.

But I'll tell you something about Keg. Keg, he was like -- he had a nervous temperament inside. A lot of people didn't know that. Because he could play you more things up in the dressing room on the trombone and he would get down on the stage --
Right.
-- and he would start to play something and he would tighten up, --
Right.
-- you see.
He was a teacher. He could inspire and help anybody --
Couldn't he?

-- where they're almost -- I mean, he solely -- I could say almost singlehandedly Keg Johnson was responsible for any improvement I ever made in my life. But I was never able to help him improve because he couldn't accept things like that.
Well, you know, he helped me.
Right. Everybody.

He got me to go to my first teacher I ever went to when I went to Jerry [Chimmer] in Chicago when we was playing in Chicago in 1941. He got me to go to Jerry [Chimmer.] He also got me to go to Donald [Reinhardt.] Keg did this.
But Keg could play a lot of trombone. He could do anything that he wants to do with the horn and he could play anything that you would put up in front of him.
And he was great behind a soloist.
Oh, definitely.
Oh, he could --
Definitely. Definitely.
I think that was his best thing where he would stay in the background and let somebody be singing and he'd just put those little things in behind them. It was always beautiful.
Yeah. Well, you see, because he was not there by himself, you see. That [added] a little thing, too, you know.
Right, right.

He had a beautiful sound to me, and we had a very good section. The section blended. You know, I've never played with a bad trombone section in my whole life and that was one of the great trombone sections, to me, that we had in Calloway's band with Keg and Tyree and myself.
Well, I don't think it could be a bad trombone section if you were in there, anyway. If anybody listened to you in any kind of a way, it couldn't be bad.
[Yeah]
And what about --
Tyree used to tell me he'd like to have me in his left ear.
Yeah. I was just going to ask you about our fat friend, Tyree Glenn from Corsicana, Texas.
Oh, what a beautiful trombone player. That's right. Well, you know, Tyree didn't like for anybody to say it, you know, but Tyree used to be with the minstrels.
He used to be with Jimmy Perkins' minstrels and played banjo.
Wow.
And he used to get mad whenever I told anybody. He used to get made at me for telling them.
Then he was with an orchestra called Johnson's Happy Pals in Richmond.
Right, right.
And that's when he knew -- Billy Eckstine used to say that Tyree came up to Tommy Miles' band and all he had was a tuxedo suit in a straw bag. Well, you know how Billy used to kid him, --
Sure.

Billy Eckstine. And he came to Tommy Miles' band then and that's when I first met him. And he used to come backstage of the theater and used to worry Claude and I to death to teach him different things. Claude showed him lip vibrato. Claude taught him lip vibrato. And then I used to map out little solos for him --
Yes.

-- at times, you know, and when he came to New York he'd come to my room and then say play such and such a tune for him. I played 'Stardust' or 'Body and Soul'. I go to the Savoy and listen to him and Tyree played what I played up in the dressing room -- I mean up in my room.
Right.
And he developed a style from that, --
Yes, he did.
-- developed his own style, you know, and --
He's got a warm sound.
Oh, well, Tyree was a warm guy inside.
Just beautiful, just happy.
A beautiful, very warm guy.
All happiness, all fun.

Yeah, he liked to kid. He always was kidding. He used to like to kid me all the time. He's always kidding me. He caused me to cuss Calloway once, you know, and I never did cuss at Calloway. That time on the Strand Theater and Tyree kept on kicking the stand in front of me and Calloway caught me kicking it back at him and told me I shouldn't be doing that on the stage, and that's when I got mad because he got on me and didn't say nothing to Tyree.
Yeah, he was a [funster].

Can you explain some of the scenes on the stage with Cab Calloway, like Cab would be singing a ballad, and Tyree and Dizzy, two Peck's bad boys, what would they be doing when Cab would be singing a ballad?
Well, Dizzy would be liable to get up and go into his dance like he used to do when Cozy played a
drum solo.
Yeah.
Dizzy would get up and go into his dance behind him and make all kind of things.
Yeah, and look out at the audience and wave at someone.
That's right.
Do you remember the --

Tyree used to be turning around and put them big eyes and mug at him and do things like that and would be talking to me, you know, and ask me different questions, get me to talk about somebody and then turn around and say -- and I'd get on him -- and he'll say, "See, he'll talk about you the same way," Tyree would tell everybody.

Do you remember Cab would be singing something like a beautiful ballad, 'I Got You Under My Skin,' and the trumpets were on the left of the bandstand facing the theater, and the trumpets would be to the right of him.
Uh-huh.
And Tyree would act like -- Dizzy would act like he was in a football -- he was out playing football. Remember that?
Uh-huh.
And he would throw a pass, and Cab was singing a ballad and people were listening to Cab sing, and
all of a sudden Dizzy would act like he was making a pass --
Yeah.
-- and Tyree would act like he was catching it.
I know.
And as he caught it, J. C. Heard, which was the drummer, would hit the bass drum --
Yeah -- No, it was Cozy Cozie.
Was it Cozy Cozie?
Yeah.
-- like he -- he'd just tap the bass drum like it was caught and the people would laugh.
Yeah.
And the laugh in the middle of a beautiful ballad, --
I know.
-- Cab didn't understand exactly what was going on.
No, he didn't.
He'd look around and it would be all peace and tranquillity up there.
Oh, definitely. Everybody would just sit there just like nothing ever happened.
Oh, that's amazing.
Oh, there was a lot of fun in that
band. You know, Tyree used to do that with me and with Jonah.
Uh-huh.
He'd tell me, "Butter, catch the football," and he'd reach back at Jonah's head like he was going to throw it.
Like he was going to throw it because Jonah's head was long.
And then Jonah would mock me holding his head up like I used to do singing and tried to mock me singing.
Yeah.
That's the only way he'd get back at me, you know.
Right.

How about Dupreez Wheeler? Did you know him? He played trombone and bass trombone. I think he was one of the first bass trombone players I ever saw. He had a bass trombone and -- for me -- in Cab's band.
Oh, yeah? I never saw it. I didn't even know DePriest Dupreez had one.
Yeah.
I never saw it. Because the first bass trombone player I ever saw in a jazz band was with Stan Kenton. That was the first one I saw.
Well, DePriest Dupreez had one, with that
trigger on that thing.
Uh-huh. I didn't know he had that.
: Yeah.

Well, you know, I worked in Dupreez's place once when I first came to New York. I worked in his place at the Lafayette Theater and doubled at the Cotton Club. I used to talk to him when I was seeing him but very seldom I seen him because Calloway's band was always on the road and always gone.
: Uh-huh.
And when I come to take his place in the band, he was gone, too. He had left. Because I joined the band in Springfield, Massachusetts, and he had left.
: Uh-huh.
Yeah.
I'd like to ask you this. Like in bass, we always afforded Jimmy Blanton as having revolutionized bass playing.
You did,
: Yeah.
As far as solos was concerned.
: Right.
Well, who would you say was comparable to that in jazz trombone, that really just turned it around from what Big Green and Claude and --
I would say J. J. Johnson.
Hello. Hello.
J. J. Johnson.
I agree.
Yeah.
I would agree very much.
I call him the master right today whenever I see him.
Right.
He tells me I'm crazy but I still call him the master.
Well, how did that strike you when you first heard J. J. play?
I'd say -- Well, the first time I heard J. J., you know, was with Bennie Carter. That's the first time I heard J. J.
Uh-huh. Oh, he was in Bennie Carter's band?
Sure, uh-huh.
About what year was that?
Oh, God. It was in the forties, if I'm not mistaken. It was in the forties. Bennie Carter brought a band to the Apollo Theater.
Uh-huh.
And that's the first time I saw Al
Grey was with Bennie Carter, too.
Wow.
That's right.

But that's the first time I saw J. J. and then J. J. went with Basie. Of course he went to 52nd Street and he played with Basie too. And he was writing then, too, you know. J. J. was a very good arranger.
Uh-huh.
But J. J. to me was the first modern trombone player, to me, that had something before -- that changed the style of all trombone playing.
Yeah, a revolution.
Yeah, like the bop era.
Right.
He fit into that era which to me was -- to me I would call it modern.
Right.
And nobody to me played like J. J. clear till this day if you listen to J. J.'s records or listen to J. J. play. To me, still, he's the greatest modern trombone player today, especially among us.
Right. Among the black --
There's a couple of white trombone players I know that, you know, --
Yeah, we didn't mention enough of
the white trombone players. We just touched on Jack Teagarden. We haven't mentioned -- just to digress -- we haven't mentioned Tommy, --
We haven't mentioned Tommy, we haven't mentioned Jack Janney. [handwritten correction: 'Janney' struck through, 'Jenney' written above]
Jack, yes.
We mentioned Jack Teagarden.
Yeah.
And, of course, -- oh, there was a lot of good trombone players.
Miff?
Miff Moe was the first, he was the first one I noticed. [handwritten correction: 'Moe' written above 'Hoe']

Of course, when I joined McKinney's band and Don had told me about Tommy because Don, when Don was writing for Whiteman, Tommy Dorsey and his brother Jimmy was in Whiteman's band. That's when I first heard about Tommy Dorsey. I didn't know nothing about him because he, you know -- Miff Moe was -- [handwritten correction: 'Moe' written above 'Hoe']

Well, black and white bands didn't get to see one another enough. We would play together but we could hear them and appreciate their great talent, of a guy like Teagarden and a guy like Miff Moe. [handwritten correction: 'Moe' written above 'Hoe']
Well, with Don's band we got to play across from Isham Jones. [handwritten correction: 'Isham' written above 'Eisam']
Yeah.
Cass Long

We got to play across from Cass Long and that's where we got to know Peewee Hunt -- he was playing there. They didn't have but two trombones when I first played across from Cass Long and Billy Rausch. Billy Rausch was a beautiful trombone player, a beautiful trombone player.
And when I first played across from Isham Jones, Jack Janney was playing trombone with Isham. You know he later played with Artie Shaw?
Right.
Then later had his own band, you know, before he died.
Right.
He was a very good trombone player, I thought, of the white -- Billy Rausch was a very good trombone player.
But I never listened to too many. There was so many good white trombone players but they weren't exactly soloists.
But Jack Janney was.
Oh, he was a beautiful melodic trombone player. Will Bradley.
Will Bradley, right.
Originally Wilbur Schwichtenberger Putzenberger.
Yeah.
Buddy Morrow.
: Yes.
Today, even.
: Right, that's right.
I call him the iron man because Buddy Morrow used to play -- he had a band and he used to play the parts and the solos and never give out.
: An amazing man.
That's right.
: Amazing man.
Right. Today he's amazing.
: Right.
Then, if we want to come up to the modern era of the white trombone players, my favorite is Carl Fontana --
: Uh-huh.
-- and Frank Rosalino.
: Uh-huh. I think we've got [a little] kid here in New York who came in and kind of upset New York for a while on Trombone named Urbie Herbie Green.
Oh, I don't even mention Urbie Herbie. I don't mention him because to me Urbie Herbie is the tops over everything.
: That's right, but we want to just get him on record because --
Oh, no, I never mentioned Urbie Herbie Green,
for some reason or other, because you can't say enough about Urbie Herbie-Green.
Right.
Urbie Herbie Green's the greatest all-around trombone player in the business --
I think so.
-- from coast to coast.
I mean academically, jazz-wise, --
Any way that you want to mention.
That you want to mention.
That's right.
And we got another young trombone player that's coming up today, to me, that is right -- he's right on the verge, and that's Bill Watrous.
Bill Watrous, right.
Yeah, that's my son.
Uh-huh.
That's what he calls me, father.
Yeah? That's nice. I think --
Because we work together so much, you know.
I think he's a lovable young man and has such potential. His powers -- I don't think he even knows his own strength, as we say.
Well, you know, the kidsshould take
after him. You know, Bill Watrous practices five and six hours every day, legitimately. That's what the kids should learn to do instead of learning to play a solo, you see.
Yeah.
And that's the reason that he produces like he does, and he's doing a lot of clinics around the country now, too, and I hope he is selling the kids.
I'm sure he is.
Of course, the last time I talked to him he told me he was trying. And he tries to tell me about kids talking about me, that kids -- that I had been with Thad Jones, I played clinics.
Well, he was the one that would go around and tell them about you, --
Yeah.

-- that you are truly without a doubt the super sideman. Here's a man, Quentin Jackson, that in all the annals of his history, 50 or 60 years in jazz, that never had a band but has -- excuse me -- helped make so many great bands greater because of your presence with the band. And being highly respected. The reason I'm saying this is because all of these trombone players mentioned to me you and about how you influenced them. J. J. Johnson.
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
And we haven't mentioned one of the
old guards of the -- 'Margie.'
Trummy Young?
Trummy Young.

Trummy Young, the only reason that he didn't get to stay on the New York scene too much because he wanted to live in Hawaii. He left this country to go to Hawaii and live. He had his own band in Hawaii in a hotel there. And he left to come out with Louie.
Right.
Then the people noticed him a little more because he hadn't been noticed since the Jimmy Lunceford days --
Right.
-- when he made solos on 'Margie' and things like that.
[ ] 'Traveling Light?'
Uh-huh, yeah.
That's his tune.

And, you know, so he got back, he was with Louie, and the people got to notice him again and then he got tired. He wanted to go back home to his family and he went back to Hawaii where he is right now.
He's very happy. I see him every year, once a year.
Oh, sure.
Eddie Bert Burt, a trombone player, you know. There's another very good trombone player.
That's right.
He corresponds with Trummy all the time.
They're very dear friends.
Yes.
Let's hold it for a second, Butter, just to get our breath together.
Okay. [PAUSE]
We've got to wind this up, too. Yeah, we're still on these trombone players. Before we forget it, you mentioned Sandy Williams.
Sandy Williams. To me, now, he was the closest to Jimmy Harrison, --
Uh-huh.
-- to play Jimmy Harrison's style.
Uh-huh. How was that style -- How would you describe that style?

It was a swinging style. They had a lot of swing to it, a lot of little lip trill things, you know, in spots. But it was like you could take a melody and swing it. And Bennie Morton had that knack of taking the melody and swinging, just take the melody and swing it and add just enough little things in there so that you still would know it
was the melody. Yet and still he would improvise, you see.
Right.
But not getting too far away from the melody, which is an art within itself.
Uh-huh.
Today that's a lost art, I think, of playing the melody.
You're right.
And Sandy was with Fletcher's band for a while, too, Fletcher Henderson. He really fitted in the band. He was in -- In fact, him and J. C. Higgenbotham was in there together.
Sandy and J. C. were there together?
That's right.
Well, what about Snub?
Snub Moseley was with Alphonso Trent. He played a thing and still does today called a slide saxophone. I think it's the only one in existence. I've never heard of anyone else having it.
Uh-huh.
He was a very exciting trombone player. He played a lot of exciting things and he was quite a salesman. He has a little band around now, right today. Snub Moseley.
And the slide saxophone, it looked like, almost like
a soprano only it had a slide on it. It had the mouthpiece and the reed and everything.

Quent, that's -- Now, we've mentioned, Butter, we've mentioned here -- naturally, being a trombonist, you will join [ ] J, Vic Dickerson, Teagarden, Big Green, J. C. Higgenbotham, Claude Jones, Jimmy Harrison, Keg Johnson, Tyree Glenn, DePriest Wheeler, Lawrence Brown, Trummy Young. We just got through with Sandy Williams and Snub Moseley.

Now, if you -- just personally, who do you think was the most impressive in that whole thing? Which ones of these, if you can just offhand right off the top of your head, impressed you mostly as really -- We mentioned Dickie Wells -- all had different styles -- Dickie Wells and all these different -- Ed Durham, J. J. Johnson, Urkle Herbie Green, Bill Watrous, Carl Fontana. Basically, which ones really sort of influenced you and in what way?
Well, you know I've always been a trombone player. I've always been funny about saying who I thought --
Yeah.
-- was the best.
Now, you know, I got so much from each one of them individually that when you go to say, 'Now, who influenced you the most,' -- Of course, Claude Jones was really the cause of

me playing the horn. But after I left home I heard all these different trombone players and I got something from each one of them, you see. If a guy come up and ask you and said, "Who do you think is the greatest?" it's hard to say who is the greatest because you like so many of them, you know, for different things that they do because each one had something different than the other trombone players, and you've got something good from quite a few of them, you see.
Yeah, of course, yeah.
You see?
But I didn't mean it in the sense of who is the greatest,because --
