Butter, we're starting tape four here and we're still on the trombone players and we've discussed them, and you said you might want to have a little something to say about the influence, not who was the greatest, but influence. So what do you want to say?
Well, Claude Jones really influenced me.
Yeah.

He talked me into, really talked me into playing trombone. I didn't have no idea of ever playing a trombone before, and if you listen to Claude Jones anyway, Claude Jones could talk you into anything, if you knew Claude, --
Right.

-- see? And Claude really -- he got me interested. He got me interested in the trombone. And listening to him play with McKinney Cottonpickers, I thought there was nobody in the world but Claude Jones.

I had heard Dickie Wells play with Lloyd Scott at home around that same time, you know, during the same time, 1926 and '27 and '28. But Dickie's style was so complicated to me that it didn't impress me like Claude did. It was interesting to listen to him but Claude, you see, Claude could play melodies and his jazz playing was sensible. It was intricate, too, at the same time. If you listen to early
McKinney Cottonpicker records that was made in 1928, back in there, and '29, you would hear this.
Then, after that, when Lawrence Brown came to New York in '32, Lawrence Brown started to influence a lot of trombone players and he influenced me too, you see.
Right.
And he had everybody trying to play his solo on the 'Sheik.'
Right.
That's the record he made with Duke, you know, and 'Ducky-Wucky' and all those things.
I see.
So, really, my inspiration really was Claude Jones from the beginning.
Right.

Well, in looking back at this in retrospect, and you know the era we came up in and the social situation in America -- we were talking in the beginning before black and white players played together, but in this big auditory world of music where we don't see each other but we hear each other and we respect each other for how we sound -- you've explained to me some of your thoughts over how you felt about Tommy Dorsey and you named some other great white trombone players, Jack Jenney and Miff Mole and these, what do you think -- what is your impression of how white trombone players thought about
They respected them, the great ones did.
Sure.
Tommy respected great black trombone players. Tommy was even crazy about Tricky Sam, Joe Nanton.
Yeah, which we haven't mentioned too much about.
Oh, I was waiting for that later.
Sure, okay.
And Peewee Hunt always noticed black trombone players. So did Jack Teagarden. Jack Teagarden used to come up and hang out in Harlem.
Of course, I know that.
He used to ask Fletcher Henderson to let him sit in when he came to New York, you know, when he was with Ben Pollack, you see.

I remember that, I know that. That's the reason I wanted to just have it for the record because having known and seen these great white musicians that came around to respect us. Even though we couldn't play together, we were socializing, we would come to hear each other.
Uh-huh.
Even the black musicians could come

backstage and listen to white musicians when you couldn't come through the front door. And certainly white musicians always came to where black musicians played to listen to them and they were always very friendly and we always respected each other --
Oh, sure.
-- for our individual talent.
That's right.

But I wanted it for a matter of record so that young people would know that in this great world of auditory art, sound, that sound was love to us, and whatever one could do and whatever one could contribute to -- contributed to sound was respected by other great sound players.

Oh, definitely. And, you know, a lot of them used to come up to Harlem back in the early thirties, you know, when a lot of white musicians and white people used to come up to Harlem to hang out. There was no muggings. Nobody bothered anybody in those days. And Harlem was a beautiful place. A lot of night clubs there and it was patronized mostly by whites. The Cotton Club. Connie's Inn. Small's Paradise, some colored used to go there. And the Saratoga Club, you see. But mostly the patronage was white.
Yeah, the clientele that had the money to spend.
Exactly.
: Yes.

And there used to be a lot of after-hour joints, you know, up there from 133rd Street on up to 140th Street. Between Seventh and Lenox there was a lot of afterhour joints up there that had piano players. Guys used to go in and jam. There was a 101 Club there near Lenox Avenue, I think at 141st Street, that white musicians used to come up and jam and, you know, that way and play.

Then, you see, Milt, I can tell you something else, too. I remember being with Don Redmon's band when musicians used to sit, they'd come uptown and they'd have their tuxedo on with a stiff collar and cuffs and they would make a staff on their cuff and you'd play a riff and they'd write that down, you see.
: Sure.
A lot of things went downtown that way, too.
: They would copy the creativity -- notate, rather, --
That's right.
: -- the creativity of jazz musicians, black jazz musicians.
Uh-huh, but the records helped a lot, too.
: Right, of course.

And I give the white musicians a lot of credit because the white musicians really studied. He knew he had to study. He practiced a lot, he practiced a lot, where we used to go and just play. We had so much joy playing and we had so much originality and so much feeling that we didn't really, a lot of us, until later years we didn't take lessons, to practice like the white musicians did, you see.
Sure.

And that's the reason I tell kids today, please study your instrument and learn all the technicalities of playing your instrument so that whatever you want to do and whichever feeling you want to play with, you have got it under your fingers, you've got your instrument under your fingers to do anything that you want to. You don't have to practice every day to think that you'll become stiff. That's not it. You practice on your instrument and take lessons so that you have control over your instrument at all times so that you can do what you want to and play with any feeling you feel like, if you have your instrument under your fingers.
Amen, Butter, I agree to that so much.
I just want to digress again because in this thing we just have to keep digressing --
Uh-huh, I know.

-- about different guys. I'd just like to mention a couple of things. We mentioned -- We didn't mention in the saxophone section, we were talking -- we sort of skipped guys like Pete Brown. You remember Pete Brown? What a swinging person.
Pete Brown was an individualist, too.
Yes.
He was a swinging alto player. He come up in the 52nd Street days, too.
Right.
And he used to play in the Village quite a bit, too, just like the trumpet player I was speaking about, Frankie Newton, played in the Village for years. But Pete Brown was a fixture.
Alto sax?
Yes, yes, yes.
Can you describe him?
He was a little fat guy and was jolly as he could be. I don't think he ever said a bad word or did anything to hurt anybody, and he loved to play, loved to play anytime, anywhere, you know.
Right.
And he had just a -- he was just a swinging saxophone player. I don't know anybody else who really could outswing him because swing --
That's right. Rhythm was his business.
Exactly, exactly, exactly. Quite a few good alto players -- you know, I have to mention my friend from home, too, Earle Warren.
Right.
Earle Warren is an underrated alto player. I say he's underrated.
Right.
He played first saxophone with Basie for years and he was right there playing first alto. He played very little solos but right today he is very much in demand.
Right.
He's another alto player I wanted to mention, being from my hometown.
So we'll stick that in. Students of jazz, refer this back, please, to the saxophone department that we've mentioned.
Also, just to digress a little bit back to the trombone to -- what about Charlie Holmes?
Charlie Holmes? Charlie Holmes was the nearest saxophone player -- he had the nearest style to Johnny Hodges.
Uh-huh.
And, you see, by that he didn't try to

get but so far because every time he'd turn around people would say he sounded like Johnny. So Charlie Holmes got so he didn't play but so much, but a great saxophone player. He could have took Johnny's chair anytime playing. In fact Duke tried to get him once when Johnny left the band, but he would never play, he wouldn't leave town.

I don't think Johnny -- Charlie, rather, wanted to travel too much. Charlie Holmes didn't want to travel too much either. He had his roots here in New York and he was a very quiet guy. You never saw him. He stayed in a lot, you know. But a wonderful person.
I knew him when he was with Luis Russell. He was the first saxophone player with Lu Russell when I first came to New York.
And we forgot about -- we forgot to mention another great saxophone player out of St. Louis, Tab Smith.
Oh, gee. He was another influence on a lot of alto players. I knew Tab when he first came with Lucky Millinder in the thirties. He was a great influence. He made a lot of good records.

Now, his sound, if you listen to him, he kind of came up like in Johnny Hodges' feel, I'll put it that way, feel of Johnny Hodges like that. He made a lot of good records and he had his own band for a long time but he got sick and died too

early, like a lot of the good musicians did. And he played with Basie too. He played with Basie in the forties. In fact Basie had him and Earle Warren there together. What more alto do you want than that, you know?
Right.

I'd like to ask you this. We're still in the saxophone section. It seems as if, from my observation, that New England, in the New England states or out here in the East produced a great deal, a great many stellar saxophone players almost from one particular part of the country. Like New England, there's Connecticut and Providence, Rhode Island. There's Hilton Jefferson.
Definitely.
There's Toots Mondello, --
That's right.
-- the great saxophone player, played first with Benny Goodman for many years. And Johnny Hodges. He's from --
He's from Cambridge.
Yeah, Cambridge. And New England seemed to produce these great, great players, all of which, in my --
Harry Carney.
Harry Carney -- which, in my estimation, having known them and knowing their great love and
Oh, there's always been that closeness, you know.
Yes.
It's always -- New England, the people that they know you up there and they like you, they'll feel close to you and they'll stick together.

You know, I remember -- I have to say this, all due respects to Russell Procope, I remember when Calloway disbanded. When I went to Ellington's band, Ellington tried his best to get Hilton Jefferson because Johnny Hodges and Harry Carney wanted Jeff in there with them, you see. But Calloway kept Jeff with the small band and that stopped that right there, --
Right.
-- you see, because they wouldn't take nobody from each other because they was out of the same office.
Right.
But Johnny and Harry still, they wanted Hilton Jefferson in there in Hardwick's place.
I can remember when Toots Mondello was for many years at CBS and every time we spoke he always had such great regards for Hilton Jefferson and for Johnny Hodges --
Oh, sure.
-- because they were all great
lyrical players.
Yes, yes.
It should be noted that from one section of the country came these great lyrical first alto men, these academic saxophone players that --
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
-- knew their craft.
Oh, definitely, every one of them.
I thank you for bringing that in.
That was just getting to revert back to some of the saxophones that I thought we shouldn't go right on without even mentioning.
Uh-huh.
We'll never be able to get to all of the guys, but we just --
No, not trombone players either we won't be able --
No, no, no, we won't be able to get to them. But the ones that stuck in our minds and in our hearts most prominently, black and white, we would like to remember.
There's so many that were great, you know.
Okay, shall we go on to some of your -- I just want to get into some of the great drummers and some of the drummers that were very influential and contributed to
this great jazz era.
Now we'll start with Big Sid -- We'll start with Cuba because that goes back to --
Cuba Austin, Cuba Austin.
-- that goes back to McKinney's.

You know, Cuba Austin came from a carnival. McKinney got him out of a carnival, and he used to be a dancer, he used to clown, he knew how to do funny things with the sticks, and he was, oh, he was very colorful. A very colorful drummer. He used to do a little -- things on the stage, like we used to do a number called 'School Days' and he used to put on a hat and go out front with his little books and sing 'School Days' out in front. And he would spell at the end of 'School Days', a little thing he would do, he would spell o-n-e d-o-g, one hot dog.
Isn't that something?
You know, Mantan Moreland was his cousin.
Oh, I didn't know that.
That great comedian that used to make the Charlie Chan pictures?
Right.

And Cuba taught him all the dances that he used to do. Cuba used to do them when he was on the carnival. So McKinney got him from a carnival to play with the band, the same way he did Nesbitt. He came from a carnival.
Uh-huh.

But Cuba Austin was the first one. Of course, Lloyd Scott, I can't forget him. He was a good drummer. He was a very good drummer, a good salesman. Arnold Bolden was a good drummer and a good salesman. He came in behind Lloyd Scott with Cecil Scott's orchestra, a very good drummer.
Arnold who? Boldman?
Bolden, yeah.
Uh-huh.
And now, Big Sid, Big Sid Catlett, when I first worked with him was with McKinney's band, and he come in and took Cuba's place and, gee whiz, he almost made us forget about Cuba, --
Wow.
-- because he could do anything Cuba could do, only he did it with more finesse, --
Uh-huh.
-- you see. And just as a kid Big Sid was a fantastic drummer. And he -- Of course, when I left McKinney's band after --
You mentioned that he came in one time and played in --
In Cuba's place. When we played a dance up in Milwaukee, Cuba got sick in Chicago and, of course,
you know Big Sidney Catlett was from Chicago.
Right.
Well, we picked him up to take us up to the Eagle Ballroom in Milwaukee to play.
About what year was that about?
That was 1931.
Uh-huh.
1931. That was before Don left McKinney's band to get his own band.
That's about the first time you heard Big Sid?
First time I heard him and I never forgot him after that and nobody in the band did either.
Right.
And that was even before that he had left with -- the next time I heard of him, well, he was with Sam Wooding. You see, that was the next time I heard of Big Sid.
When was the first time you heard Zutty?
Zutty?
Just hold it for a second. There's a phone. [PAUSE]

Well, we've got the phone all straight.
We were talking about Zutty Singleton.
Yeah. The first time I heard Zutty was on record. I heard him with Louis Armstrong when he did 'West End Blues'.
Wow.

Those things, I heard that record before I even left Springfield. The only trumpet player I heard, a first trumpet player I heard copy it and really play 'West End Blues' exactly as Louis did it was Buddy Lee.
Uh-huh.

He could play it exactly like Louis. Now, I didn't hear Zutty in person. The first time I heard Zutty in person was when he was with Roy Eldridge at the Three Deuces in Chicago. You see, I was with Don Redman at that time.
That must have been around 1937, '36 or '37, right?
Yes, yes, that's right.
Because I had been to the Three Deuces in '35 myself and left to go with Cab, so that's --
That's right.
-- quite relative, it sort of leads us into that.
Yeah. You know, I was with Don Redman and Reynald Jones, he was Roy's cousin, and we used to get off from the Regal Theater and we used to go down there and jam at

the Three Deuces and then we would leave the Three Deuces and there was another little club over on the west side called Tony's, I think it was. We used to -- the whole band used to go over there and jam. That was before the union put down the law, no jamming anymore, you know, because they would advertise you when you would go to a place to jam and they'd say, "If we knew you was coming," they'd have a big crowd and you wouldn't be getting paid a quarter for it but they would collect, you know, advertise it.
Right. That's the reason the union had to really put that law down.
That's right.
It's unfortunate for us because we got the chance to play with each other, --
Sure.
-- but the owners of the clubs were taking advantage of that.
Exactly.
Right.
Did you know Kaiser Marshall or hear of him?
Oh, sure, sure. I knew Kaiser when he was with Fletcher.
Uh-huh.
In fact, the first time I heard Fletcher before I left home Kaiser Marshall was the drummer.
But I got to know Kaiser after I came to New York. He had left Fletcher but I still got to know him around New York because he still --
He was a nice quiet man, wasn't he?
Very, very.
From Texas, I believe.
Uh-huh. You know, he was one of the first ones to use the high-hat cymbal, --
Right, right.
-- Kaiser Marshall.
Right.
He and Ben Pollack.
Oh, Ben Pollack also, huh?
Oh, yes. Ben Pollack was a very good swing drummer.
Oh, that's great. Uh-huh.

But Kaiser Marshall was the first New York drummer to have a high hat cymbal, you know, on the stand. The rest of them had their cymbal like Cuba had. They had a cymbal, you take two cymbals and you take a great big rat trap and you take that rat trap and put a board on each end of the rat trap or the spring and then you put the cymbal on that board or cymbal on each one, and you take the spring, you use the spring of the rat trap and you put a strap across it to hold your foot in there, and that was your foot cymbal.
Oh, yeah. Then there was one on the side of the bass drum, too, you see.
Yeah, but that wasn't a foot cymbal. No, no. That was on the side of the bass drum, too, that went along with the beater, --
Right.
-- with your bass drum beater, you know?
Uh-huh.
But, then, you had this on here with your foot on the side. Cuba had one.
Uh-huh.
Cuba Austin had one and that's where I first saw --
(Unintelligible.)
Yeah, --
That's really an invention.
-- and make a foot cymbal out of it, you know. And then I didn't see the high hat till I came to New York, you know, and then I saw the high hat then.
Uh-huh.
Kaiser Marshall was the first one to have it. Then, of course, Walter Johnson.
Yeah.
Walter Johnson to me was the smoothest
drummer that I have ever heard.
Uh-huh.
And speaking of drummers, there was --
What was he like? Tell me --

A very quiet guy. Here was a guy that could play a gig all night long, play a four hour gig, it'd be hot in the place, and he would get through that night playing the drums and no wilted collar, no nothing. He looked just like he did when he came to work.
He always dressed impeccably, didn't he? Very --
Very neat, very neat, and the --
Very handsome man.
-- height of fashion, --
Right.

-- you know, and to this day if you see him -- he's an old man now and he still looks the same. He hasn't changed and he's in his seventies, and Walter Johnson looked just like he did back in the thirties.
Beautiful.
That's right.
And, then, there's one drummer that I have to talk about I'll never forget and no other drummer, I think, in this world will ever forget him, and that is Chick Webb.
Uh-huh.

Chick Webb set a style for a lot of different drummers. A lot of different drummers used to go to the Savoy and watch Chick. They used to watch him. I could name you several drummers. I don't like to call names because a lot of guys don't like to be associated with playing [with] somebody else's style which in turn helped make them great, you see.

But there's so many good drummers that watched Chick Webb that they stole from Chick, really. Chick was one of the most expressive drummers and didn't read a note, but he could hear an arrangement once and know every note. He'd tell you every note in that arrangement, everybody's solos. He would -- If there was any crescendos or decrescendos in the arrangement, he knew just where to make them, you know.
He could take a mallet on a cymbal, one mallet, and roll that mallet on the cymbal and make a crescendo on that cymbal and you wouldn't hear the beats of the mallet but you'd hear the crescendo.
Wow.
Describe Chick [to --]
Chick was a little, short hunchbacked guy, a lovable guy. He never did anything to hurt anybody in this world. He loved music.
From Baltimore, right?
Yes, and he used to take all the money
he made with the band and buy music with it. He never had any money because he'd buy all his money up in music.
Right.
You know? That's how much he loved music and he loved his band.
He just talked about his band incessantly all the time.
Oh, definitely.
His whole life was talking about -- singing and humming arrangements to all the people on the corner.
That's right. All the solos. He knew everybody's solo, you know.
Right.
And his band was impeccable when it came to playing.
He loved his musicians, loved them.
A very good band he had. He had a beautiful band when he had Dick Vance and Bobby Stark and he had Taft Jordan.
That's the three trumpets you mentioned?
That's right.
Uh-huh, and who was in the reed section?
Hilton Jefferson was in there for a
while and -- The saxophone player from --
-- Clark, Pete Clark. Waymond Carver was in there. Elmer Williams. That was the four saxophones he had.
Let's see. Hilton Jefferson alto, Waymond Carver played flute and what?
He played flute and alto.
Alto. And --
Elmer Williams was the tenor player.
That's three.
Yeah.
That's three.
And -- oh, what was the fourth baritone player's name? Yeah, well, Pete Clark used to double on baritone, too.
Pete Clark. That's the --
Sure, yeah.
Well, what about Papa Joe?
Joe Jones?
Yeah.
Joe Jones, let me tell you, Joe Jones was the first drummer I ever heard drop -- what they used to call drop bombs.
Right. That's with your foot pedal.
That's right.
Boom.
That's right, where you accent different places and make fill-ins.
Right.
If he caught an opening in there, Joe had it, you know.
An amazing man.
Oh, amazing, right to this day.
Very regal, huh?
Oh, there's not another one.
No, there won't be another --

He set a lot of styles, too, that guy don't even -- they don't think about it. But a lot of drummers that came up around Joe's era copied after him, too. They got a lot of things from him. You know, you have to get a beginning some place.
Right. He was the first one I ever saw turn the beat around and bring it back.
Oh, yes.
Ting ti-ti-ting ti-ti-ting ti-ti ti-ti ti ti-ti-ti ti-ti ti-ti ti, back to the --
That's right.
On this high hat cymbal and the sock cymbal. He was truly a master.
Yeah. Basie had a fantastic rhythm section back in those days when he had him and had Walter Page and the metronome, Freddie Green.
Freddie Green. That's supposed to be the all-American rhythm section.
That's right.
All-American rhythm section. Count Basie, Freddie Green, Walter Page, Joe Jones.
That's it, yeah.
They're the first ones who won an award in any kind of a poll as a rhythm section.
I know they did, yeah. Well, they had to. They deserved it.
Absolutely. Yeah, well, let's have some -- Cozy Cole. There's a name that --
Cozy Cole was one of the most rhythmic drummers I ever heard when I first heard him. I first heard him with Blanche Calloway. Then I heard him with Willie Bryant, you know?
Uh-huh.
Then after Willie Bryant, then he started going with small band things. He was with Stuff Smith.
Right.
Stuff Smith had a great little
entertaining band, you know.
Right.
But Cozy could swing, back in those days Cozy [swinging] and Cozy studied a lot. He started to studying a lot.
Great student.
Oh. When we was with Calloway, after -- between, rather, after every show and between shows, he would have that practice pad and his pipe and those big sticks.
Right, a rubber pad.
Yes, between every show --
Absolutely.
-- he would practice his rudiments.
I was there so you know I remember it with you.
Oh, was you. Was you. Do you know, that was a good rhythm section, too, you know.
Yeah, we had a good rhythm section. We didn't have too much jazz to play but it was a good steady strong rhythm section.
Exactly. That's what I mean when I say it was a good rhythm section. Anything that's steady and strong is good.
Right.
Togetherness. You can't beat it at
anything.
Right.
I remember when I came in Cab's band there was a drummer there named Leroy Maxey. Did you ever know him?
Oh, sure I knew him.
A great show drummer. He was the Cotton Club drummer.

That's right. He was a very good drummer, a very good drummer. To this day I don't know what happened between him and Calloway. I don't know to this day why he come out of the band. Because to me he was a very, very good drummer. I worked with him in Don's band later.
Right.
And he was a very good drummer to me.
He was a good drummer but -- the only thing, I was there when he came out of the band.
Oh, yeah.
And this is a story which should go in my department.
Hang on just a second. We have to double-check something.
I wanted to explain to you since you asked the question, although this should go in my category, what -- you didn't know what happened about Maxey.
Well, Maxey was a great show drummer. He'd been with

Cab through all of the Cotton Club, and every time a chorus girl kicked her legs up he had that cymbal right there. He emphasized every anticipation that a dancer could do. But in so doing he had never -- before Gene Krupa there were no drum solos. There was just play for the band. So Maxey, that's all he knew was play -- the chorus girls loved him. Every person in show business loved Maxey because he was such a great show drummer.
Uh-huh.

And then came along Gene Krupa with the drum solos, and Cab, who had Benny Goodman and Lionel Hampton and all and Gene Krupa, and he said, "Maxey, play drum solos." Well, he hadn't been able to play -- he hadn't played any, so when he gave him 16 bars he really didn't know what to do with it. And, naturally, Cab, I believe, wanted to go along with the times.
Uh-huh.

Whereas Cozy was out there playing drum solos with Stuff Smith and with Blanche Calloway and all these bands -- he was a great soloist -- so Cab, to keep up with the times of what Benny was doing, he got Cozy to come in the band because Cozy was a great soloist. That's why. We have explained that.
Now, I want you to go ahead on with your story.
Uh-huh, uh-huh, uh-huh. Yes, I
wondered --
Yeah, that's what happened.
Yeah.
Now, we've got to remember there's another one. Jimmie Lunceford had a great drummer named Joe Marshall -- I mean Jimmy Crawford, first.
Jimmy Crawford.
Jimmy Crawford.
Jimmy Crawford was a great all-around drummer. Jimmy Crawford could do anything and I've never heard anybody in a rhythm section play two beats like Jimmy Crawford played.
Oh, he made Sy Oliver's arrangements great with --
Did he? Did he? Oh. Him and Mose on the bass.
Mose Allen, the bassist.
Yeah, yeah.
Right. And Wilcox' on piano.
That's right.
That was a great rhythm section.
That's right, and the guitar player.
I don't think he ever --
Was his name Truehart?
No, no, no.
No, not --
He never played with another band after Jimmie.
Let's see, I can't recall his name.
He still lives here in New York.
Right.
His daughter was a singer for a while. I can't think of his name.
Uh-huh.
But, anyway, that was a good rhythm section. That rhythm section would carry you right over --
It's unfortunate that we can't remember the guitar player's name but I'm sure everybody knows because --
No, because --
-- it's a matter of record --
Yeah.
-- who the guitar player was.
Uh-huh, yeah.
And I think Joe Marshall followed --
He followed Crawford.
-- Crawford in that band.
That's right.
Joe was a Chicago drummer. I went to high school with him.
Oh, yeah. Joe Marshall was a great show drummer, too.
Yes, yes, he was.
Uh-huh, I know.
He went on to Arthur Godfrey --
That's right.
-- and did all of those early things with Arthur Godfrey in the radio.
And he went to Broadway, too, you know. He did --
He went to Broadway.
-- Funny Girl and --
Yes. So did Jimmy Crawford go to Broadway.
Well, Jimmy Crawford lived on Broadway.
He sure did. He was Mr. Broadway.
He did most of the big hits.
Right.
He did so many hits. Jimmy Crawford, I don't think he ever played a show that wasn't a hit.
That's right.
That's right. He just lived on Broadway and he got into that idiom and -- of course, he did a lot of recording, too. He was in demand for recording, you know.
Yes, very much. I did -- in fact, I
did all of the Jackie Gleason Music for Lovers Only with Jimmy Crawford.
Uh-huh, uh-huh, uh-huh.
He was greatly in demand.
Yeah.
And whatever other drummers you can name, you bring them on up to me.
All right.
Now, J. C. Heard.
J. C.
I got to talk about him, too.
He followed from Leroy Maxey --
Cozy.
-- to Cozy Cole in Cab Calloway's band to --
That's right, to J. C.
-- J. C. Heard.
That's right.
Now, J. C. Heard, you know, speaking of Joe Jones, now that was J. C.'s idol, --
Right.
-- you see. J. C., sometimes I used to watch him drum and he used to make little movements almost like Papa Joe, --
Right, right.
-- you know. He loved Joe Jones.
Well, it shows how we come -- from whence we came --
Exactly.
-- when the guys from -- one of the Young came through and followed through and added his own personality to it and became great.
Uh-huh, that's right.
J. C. Heard was a good show drummer and he was a good swing drummer and he could play good solos and he had a good personality.
He sang a little bit, too, didn't he?
Oh, sure, and could dance. You know, there's very few drummers that I know that couldn't dance? Every one of them could dance? Big Sidney could dance.
I remember one day seeing Buddy --
Buddy Rich?
-- Buddy Rich, Cozy Cole, J. C. Heard, and some other drummer all standing on the corner on Broadway dancing --
Sure.
-- because they were all former dancers.
That's right, that's right, that's right.
Because that's where they got that rhythm from.
Yeah. That's right. That's where it came from, really, and all the good drummers were good dancers. And, coming on down with the drummers, the drummers that I liked, --
Uh-huh.
-- down through the years, J. C. was one of them and I'll tell you another one that I will name him. My man -- I called him Dimps, with them big dimples. Panama.
Panama Francis.
Yeah. I called him Dimps.
Right.
He was with us with Calloway.
Right.
He was a very good show drummer.
There's a guy, Oliver something, Oliver -- and Kansas Fields. Do you remember Kansas Fields?
Oh, sure. Kansas Field went to Europe and stayed so long, you know.
Right.
A lot of guys went over there and stayed and you almost forgot about them, you know. They stayed over there so long.
And the great drummer, that stayed
[Hines']
Europe, that was with High's band?
Oh, just talked to his wife a little while ago.
Yeah.
Walter Bishop.
Walter Bishop.
Yeah. He was just through here not long ago, you know.
Is that so?
Yeah.
I wished I had seen him.
Yeah, because I talked to [Chick] and then she told me.
(Earl Hines')
Yeah. He played with High's band.
That's right.
And then we get on up to the modern times.
And Oliver.
Ah, --
The drummer used to play with Earl after him.
From Chicago?
Uh-huh.
Oh, yeah, Oliver Coleman.
Yeah.
Oliver Coleman.
He was a good drummer.
A very academic drummer.
Yes.
Bob Rosengarden mentions that when he was a kid he studied with Oliver Coleman.
Uh-huh, that's right. Yeah. Oh, there was so many good drummers, so many good drummers.
Of course, before -- Let's see, there was Tubby Hall and those guys --
Oh, yes. Oh, yes.
-- around Chicago, a lot of great drummers.
That's right.
And getting on to your time, Mel Lewis and Grady and those guys. You played with Mel Lewis, Mel Lewis, Thad Jones, band, and then Grady Tate. You played with them.
Yes.
These are all drummers that have been very impressive.
Especially Grady.
Yeah, especially Grady which is also a singer and a dancer, --
That's right.
-- and a performer, a performer.
To me, today -- To me he's today's drummer.
Right.
To me Grady is -- there's no question about it. He's today's drummer.
And we can't forget the drummer that was part of the New York rhythm section which Barry Galbraith, Hank Jones, and I were so much a part of --
Oh, oh.
-- doing a recording, Osie Johnson.
Osie Johnson, to me, was one of the greatest all-around drummers in the business.
Right.
There was nothing he couldn't do. He was a percussionist.
A complete musician.
That's right. A lot of guys are percussionists but they can't swing worth a dime. But Osie could do all of it, all of it, and that's the reason he was in demand, I think.
Another great dancer, singer, --
That's right.
-- arranger.
That's right. That's right, he could do anything. I loved him myself.
I spent a great deal of happiness in my life with Osie. But this is your story. I wanted you to talk about these things.

Yes. Now, going back to drummers that I worked with, too, I think Sonny Greer was the most colorful. Sonny Greer wasn't a swing drummer, actually, but colorful. He could paint pictures. He could create feelings.
Right.
He was very expressive, very expressive. He knew exactly what to do with Duke's arrangements.
Right.
And he didn't have to read. It's just that there was never a drum book in that band.

So come the next drummer in his place, Louis Bellson. Louis Bellson was an arranger, so Louis Bellson arrangements, especially the suites, Louis Bellson would take a first trumpet part, a first trombone part, first saxophone part, and take it home with him and make a drum part.
Beautiful.
That's right.
And who followed Louis Bellson in there?
Louis Bellson?
In Duke's band?

A little kid called Dave Black. He -- Louis Bellson used to do clinics in Philadelphia at a drum school and he heard Dave and Dave played two bass drums. You know, Duke didn't want you in there after Louis unless you played two bass drums, because to him Louis Bellson --
He got accustomed to it?
Yes.
Then Dave stayed for a while and after Dave left then is when Sam Woodyard come in.
Uh-huh.
To me Sam Woodyard was the greatest drummer that Duke has ever had.
I agree.

He had everything Greer had plus the swing and a memory. He could paint pictures. He knew exactly how to taste Ellington's arrangements without Duke telling him anything. Sam knew exactly what to do, and he would lay down a rhythm behind you, a beat behind you, forget it. Forget it.
I remember the rhythm section used to say, 'He's a good hawker. He'd just hawk you right to death.'
That's right, he would. He would. If you don't believe it, listen to Newport '56. He hawked poor Paul to death all the way through them 27 choruses.
We didn't -- Did we mention -- Well, we do want to mention Paul --
Yeah, later.
-- when we get into the Duke Ellington era.
Later, yes.
Let's leave the drummers for a while and get into some of the great bass players that you've been associated with, and start with -- oh, the man, the gentleman in --
I can start with the gentleman in Zack White's band --
Right.
-- that nobody knew much about.
Right.
He used to take a tuba, an upright tuba and stand up with it and hold it like this and bounce and play. He could swing you to death. His name was Montgomery Morrison.
Beautiful.
With Zack White.
Right.
He never would leave Cincinnati, but one of the greatest tuba players that I have ever known. He played an E-flat upright tuba but, oh, my goodness, he could
play solos and everything. But nobody could get him out of Cincinnati. He was the first great bass player that I worked with.
Right.

The next one was Billy Taylor. Billy Taylor -- Escudero was a good bass player, but Billy Taylor, he came in McKinney's band and he had a tone on the tuba, and he could attack a tuba and play rhythmically with the tuba just like you would pick a string on a bass fiddle.
Right.
That was --
Give you the percussive sound but then give you the nice rhythmic sound.

That's right. And had a very good embouchure for tuba. And he played a nice bass fiddle too. Legitimately he wasn't too much of a bassist. He played the bass all wrong legitimately but he got out of it what you would want, you know.
Right.
And he was the next great bass player I played with.
Now, after him, when I went to Don's band, Bob Ysaguirre was there. Bob was a good, just a foundation bass player. No solos, no nothing, but you knew he was there. That's how he could stay.
Then, -- I was with him all that time in Don's band, and the next great bass player I got to was you.
Oh, please.
That was the next great bass player, was Milton John Hinton.
Thank you.
That was it, beautiful eight and a half years that I learned a whole lot about the instrument from you. I used to listen to you and watch you. I used to watch every move you made, little do you know.

Yeah, thank you, Butter. Thank you. I can also remember that -- I don't know whether we mentioned it or not -- but at one time Franz Jackson wrote a thing for two basses in the band and we were on location and I happened to have two basses, and every time a local bass player or traveling bass player would come around, I would hand him the part and say, 'Check this out and see how it goes.' And they weren't as academic as they should have been, the stature in which they were, and they couldn't make it. And I remember one day you said to me, 'Hey, let me look at that thing --'
Yeah.
-- and you looked at the part and said, 'Hand me the bass.' And you played it right off because of your versatility and from then on every time we were on
location and we had two basses, you played the bass with me on it, which I thought was just miraculous considering name bass players, which will remain nameless, --
Yeah, I know, I know.
-- they tried and they really couldn't make the part --
Yeah, I know, you told me.
-- because it wasn't easy. It wasn't easy.
But that happened in the Strand Theater.
Right.

But, you see, I tell you, Milt, I started to fooling with the bass when Billy Taylor first brought the bass fiddle to McKinney's band. I used to take his bass and I used to fool with it and I learned a little bit about it, a little more, a little more. In Don's band Squirrel's I fooled with Bob Tsagary's bass and learned a little more, a little more, and a little more. And I played a little tuba, too, you know. So when I got to you and I watched you and watched different things, you know, you have to be observing. I watched you and listened to you and I used to watch different positions and the way you fingered your bass and everything, you know.
So when it come time and I would -- you know, a lot

of times when you was downstairs jamming with Dizzy, I used to be up -- you didn't know, but I was watching everything you did. So when it come time to do these things, then, -- you know, and your ear helps a lot, too, you see, --
Sure.
-- and by knowing from fooling with the bass like I had down through the years, in a way it wasn't that hard, in a way, you know. But, then, that bass you had, too, man, I used to love --
A great instrument.
-- love that instrument, you know. You can play it and it just spoke for you, you know?
It sure did.
That's right.
I've always said that bass played itself.
It did. It did.
Really.
I can tell you that,
It's just a great instrument.

But this is one reason why you are considered of all the players really and truly a super sideman, because I can't know of anybody that had the ears to listen and the concern with the entire orchestra to listen to everybody's part and to remember it and memorize it. So they've been people -- If

somebody was late or somebody couldn't show up, you could play it on your individual instrument. You could play the other guy's part, which was absolutely amazing. I know of no other musician in all the annals of jazz -- and I don't know anything too much about the other, the classical end of it -- but I don't know of anybody I ever heard of, any musician, classical or otherwise speak of anybody that knew everybody's part. I'm sure there must be others, maybe, in other worlds but certainly not in jazz.

Well, you see, that wasn't -- to me, I don't know. I used to argue with guys about this ear thing. You know, I figure if you hear an A tomorrow, today, or you hear a B-flat or C or you hear a D and you hear the note, why, tomorrow, when you hear that note, you don't know what it is? Now, I will argue that to my dying day, because to me that's so simple. It's so simple, you know. Why you can't -- Why you don't know what these notes are when you play them every day and you hear them?
It's simple because you're super.
Oh.
Because you're truly (Unintelligible) super.

You know, in Duke's band I heard these arrangements, right? I heard everybody's part. I used to listen to the saxophone section and I knew their parts by listening to it because I was -- you know, I'd get so wrapped up
in these things and it was phenomenal. And even in Duke's band I played bass. When Wendell would be out, I could play in his place.
Yeah, tell us a little bit about Wendell Marshall. He was Jimmy Blanton's cousin, wasn't he?
Exactly.

Wendell was a very good bass player but he's lived in Jimmy's shadow because it was his cousin. Blanton was -- I mean, Wendell wasn't what you would call a real heavy bass player but you could feel him. You would know he was there and he did the best, he tried to do the best he could and he improved a whole lot after he left the band.
He did. I enjoyed him. He made many record dates, many jazz record dates.
Oh, sure. Uh-huh, and he got in the show field, too.
Yes, in the Broadway shows. He was always concerned deeply about his health --
I know.
-- because Jimmy had died at 22 and they were cousins and I think he figured --

That's right. Well, he used to keep a quart of milk with him in the bus every day. He'd keep the quart of milk and his juices and he would drink that every day; while we was riding in the bus, he would be drinking this milk.
He was that concerned about his health, you see, -- I see.
-- that he wanted to stay healthy like that, you know?
Uh-huh.
And he played -- he got on the Broadway scene later and he played with a lot of good shows, --
Great shows.
-- good shows. The show that he left was the biggest hit on Broadway.
That's right. What was the name of it?
Ah, --
" Fiddler on the Roof.
-- " Fiddler on the Roof. " That's right.
" Fiddler on the Roof. " He did three or four years with the show.
That's right. And he left it to -- from what I understand, he wanted to be a minister.
Oh, yeah, he did?
Yeah.
He left it to join the ministry?
That's what I heard.
And one of the nicest men I ever knew.
Oh, wasn't he? He was a gentleman. He was a gentleman. He was really what you would call a perfect
gentleman. Yes, he was. He liked the ladies a little bit, you know, but he was very quiet about it and there was nothing boisterous about him. He didn't drink or smoke or anything, you know.
Right. Neither did Jimmy Blanton which we didn't mention. Maybe -- I don't know whether you knew much about Jimmy.
Well, I heard from guys in the band that Jimmy never drank or smoked either, --
Not at all.

-- but he drank -- once in a while Ben would get him to take a little sip of wine. He didn't drink a lot. You know, he didn't drink a lot of the wine, but he would just maybe take a little sip when he would be hanging out with Ben.
Just to socialize with Ben?
Yeah, 'cause he loved Ben, and Ben loved him. Ben never got over him.
Ben named him "Bear," didn't he?
Yeah, uh-huh.
Of which Duke wrote the song, "Jack the Bear," about?
Yes, yes. That's right.
Uh-huh.
How about Kirby? Did you ever know little Kirby,
John Kirby?

Yes, I knew John Kirby. John Kirby, why, I first saw him with Fletcher's band in 1930 down in Cincinnati, he had his tuba and his bass fiddle. Now, he was the first tuba player I heard play a lip vibrato on the tuba, and it was pretty. It was pretty, although he didn't play tuba too much after Fletcher's band. I don't know -- when he went with Lucky Millinder, he left Fletcher and went with Lucky, I don't know whether he played too much tuba then.
Well, the tuba was beginning to fade out.
It was.
It was beginning to get into the bass fiddle era.
That's right.
In the thirties the tuba faded out and the bass began to --
Now, I want to take you back to bass players, if you don't mind.
Do you know who was the first bass player to really play a string bass in a jazz band?
No, not really.
Pop Foster.
Is that so?
Yes, yes. He came to New York with it,
and he was the first one.
Wow.
Pops Foster, that played with Lu Russell. He was playing with Lu Russell when Red Allen and Higginbotham and all those guys were in the band then.
Uh-huh.
Well, we had a man from New Orleans in Chicago named Bill Johnson, which was of the same vintage and perhaps a little older than Pops, --
Ah, ha.
-- that we heard out there at about the same time.
Uh-huh.
Of course, Pops Foster came to New York and Bill Johnson came to Chicago.
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
Beautiful.
Yeah.

Now, John Kirby was a beautiful -- to me he was one of the best bass players, to me, in that era. Of course, he wasn't a soloist. He wasn't a soloist as some of the guys were, but he would play it the way you wanted it and you would get it that way all the time.
Now there's a bass player I want to mention. I saved him for the last, in a way, that I'll never forget as
long as I live and no one else will, and that's Oscar Pettiford.
Hey, hello. O.P., we called him.
That's right. Do you remember before he left Milwaukee and he used to come back stage and hang out with you every time you played the theater?

Absolutely, right. And Cab wanted to fire me and hire him because I brought him back stage. I remember it so very well because I almost cut my own throat by bringing this talented bass player and said, "Cab, I want you to hear him." And Cab heard him and says, "You ain't got no job."
(Laughter.)
Right. I remember O.P.
Now, after Blanton -- to me he was the most phenomenal soloist, you know, that I heard.
I think most bass players today remember him as being the most creative jazz soloist bass player --
That's right, that's right.
-- of all of us.

I worked with him in Ellington's band and when I worked with him there I'll never forget him. He just worked there a little while while I was there. He come in, you know, in Wendell's place. When Wendell left the band, he come in and worked in there a little while and he didn't want to travel too much. He came back to New York. And Duke thought
that he was the greatest bass player ever lived.
I agree, I agree.
You know?

What did they say in Duke's band after you came in the band? What was that -- I know you didn't play with Wellman Braud but he was the first bass player. But how was he referred to? I always -- He was my mentor -- because I'm older -- and he was the one that was in the band when I came in.
Did you hear any talk in the band about him?
Not too much.
I see.
Greer talked about him a lot.
Who?
Greer.
Sonny Greer, yeah.

Oh, yeah, because they was there together and Freddie Guy, you know. They would talk about him but you never heard too much -- Duke would mention his name now and then -- but you never heard too much about him, because after Billy Taylor came in his place they forgot about him.
Right.
And I can understand that, --
Of course.
-- you see.
Well, he was a New Orleans man that just -- he's like Pops Foster -- that just played string bass and --
That's right.
-- had a solid foundation.
That's right.
And a very dignified gentleman but not --
Exactly.
-- what we would call a forceful, progressive bass player.

Yeah, and Billy Taylor came in after him and Billy Taylor was really a good bass fiddle player for the band, you know. He made all those good records up until Blanton came. And, of course, Duke had two basses for a while when he had Hayes Alvis and Billy Taylor.
Hayes Alvers and Billy Taylor.
Yes.
I remember that because I was with Cab Calloway then.
Yeah.

Then Hayes left, and so when Duke got Blanton and he stood up there and played and Billy Taylor said, 'You don't need me no more. So I'm going home.' And that's when Billy Taylor quit, which you can't much blame him.
Well, okay -- That's true? That's when
Yes. Yes, he quit.
But what about -- he had another bass player that came through there that was pretty good, too, I think, who came in with that band. Well, we had Jimmy Woods.
Well, Jimmy Woods came -- I tell you, that was a thing of circumstance.
I see.
Now, well, Duke took Junior Raglin back for a while, you see, after Oscar.
Do you remember -- Say something about Junior, because he was one of the most lovable cat in the world.
Yeah, but he held give his heart away, --
Right.
-- and he loved whiskey and he loved to drink.
Yeah, he would --
And he would get juiced. But a good foundation bass player and could play solos. He was a good bass player.
Yes.
But --
He was a guitar player, too, was he not?
But -- First. He was a guitar player first.
Do you remember where he was from?
He was from out there in St. Louis.
And Omaha, cut been around that way.
Around that way, yeah.
Yeah.
Because, you see, Blanton and them -- he and Blanton played together before Duke got him when he was playing guitar and Blanton was playing bass. --
I see.
-- around St. Louis, you see. And that's when they knew about him then, you see.
Yeah.

But we was in Boston and Duke, you know, he couldn't keep him no longer, and so that's when Jimmy Woody got the job. We was playing Storyville. And Jimmy had, Jimmy Woody -- I mean, Duke had Jimmy Woody to come by and try out. So he kept Jimmy, you know.

And I taught him a few things that I knew. I taught him a lot of introductions and things, just like I did to other bass players that came in, like 'Satin Doll' all them introductions and things like that they didn't know and I used to teach them. I used to show them.
Because you knew every part.
Oh, sure, yeah, yeah. Uh-huh.
Beautiful.
Mingus played with the band for a little while and I showed him too. Mingus never forgot me, you know. Right to this day he would say I was the only one that showed him anything, you know.
Courtesy. (Inaudible.)

Sure, well, you do these things. You know, I love people, you know, and I don't mind showing anybody anything. I don't mind showing anybody anything if they want to know. If I can show it to them, I'll show it to them, you know, because I'm the guy that wakes up every day with a smile because --
Hello.
-- I have always treated somebody nice the day before or said something kind to somebody. I made somebody smile and made them feel good in some kind of way.
Right.

And whatever I could pass to the young musicians, the same way. If they would listen, I would pass it to them, you know, because there's so much that they don't know, that they are not taught, too, that I think -- I attribute that -- I shouldn't say this, maybe, but a lot of the teachers today are so busy teaching that they'll teach a kid and keep him coming back and coming back and coming back and he hasn't learned anything yet.
Just for This is the financial end of it.
Yes.
That's quite true, quite true, --
Yes.
-- which is unfortunate.
Which I couldn't do that. And I have talked about this before and I've been put down. But if I would teach, I'd have that guy playing and it wouldn't be too long before he could really be playing.
That's true. That's the reason I don't teach to this very day.
No, that's right.
Not unless I can help.
Yes.
If I could see that you have potentials, then I don't need -- I don't want it just for the money.

Sure. I've had kids to come to my house, and like I would see something wrong with the way they was doing and I would correct them. And the guy says, 'Gee whiz, I've been going to this teacher for five years and he never told me that,' you know.
Yes.
And 'Why don't you give me lessons?' Well, I just can't yet, you know.
But that's how Jimmy Woods got in Duke's band.
Well, now, there was another guy that we

haven't mentioned I'm sure you know and I know because we were together, from out in the west. I met him out in St. Paul, Minnesota, a little bit after I met Oscar Pettiford, and he almost blew my gig.
Oh, ho, ho, ho.
His name was Adolphus Allbrook's.
Who would ever forget him? This is one of the brilliant men, --
Absolutely.
-- one of the most brilliant men. He could do anything, I don't care what it was.
That's right.
He was going to the University of Minnesota and he used to astound the teachers out there. He used to tell them things, you know.
Absolutely.
He would -- It's a shame but a lot of times he made the teachers look bad because he knew more than they did, you know.
That's right.
And a wonderful bass player.
A great bass player,
The last time I saw him --
great arranger?
Yeah. -- The last time I saw him was
in Seattle, and he had this sleeping sickness. He usually would go to sleep at a minute's notice, you know.
Yeah.
But, oh, what a mind he has.
That man was a true genius.
Oh, definitely.
He played anything. He played harp.
That's right.
He played bass.
That's right.
Adolphus Allbrookson.
These are unsung people that never got into the mainstream of jazz but influenced all of us with their great talent --
That's right.
-- and with their great things.
That's right.
Did he play cello?
He played cello.
That's what I thought.
He was a Golden Glove boxer, a big strong man.
That's right.
That's how I first met him when he was a Golden Glove boxer in Chicago.

He could take a bow and make a bow play so -- he could take a bow just like, to me, the greatest guy I know today -- all due respects to you because you know I love you -- but, to me, I can listen to Richard Davis take a bow --
An unbelievable man.
-- and make a bass fiddle sound like a cello.
Absolutely.
I don't mean up in the upper range of the cello but the bass fiddle itself, its intonation, and his tone is so clear, you know.
Absolutely.
To me he's another fantastic bass player.
Absolutely. Richard Davis.
You can almost say -- It's a shame to say this, Milt, but he almost plays too much.
Yeah, well, he's super.
Yes.
He's absolutely super.
That's right. Yes, yes.
There's no question. If a word could be applied properly, appropriately, you could say Richard Davis is super.
Oh, yeah. But, oh, gee whiz, how would you mention Adolphus? Oh, wow.
Adolphus Allbrooks, a fantastic bass player.
Yeah and, you know, he played with Basie for a while, I think.
Yeah.
I think he did.
I think he played a couple of dates with Duke but he didn't really want to stay with anybody.
No, he didn't. No.
He eventually wound up writing for -- what's that guy that's got the television show for years? -- Lawrence Welk.
Oh, yeah.
He eventually wound up writing music for Lawrence Welk.
Lawrence Welk.
He's one of my most unforgettable characters.
Oh, sure. Who could forget him? We could talk about so many guys, gee whiz, that are characters. Jimmy Woody was a character.
Right.
He was. I'll never forget the time --

I have to talk about this. I have to tell this story.
We was playing Birdland with Duke and Jimmy Woodye, he liked to -- he was very good friends of Hazel Scott, and he wanted to sit down with Hazel Scott and let everybody see Jimmy Woodye sitting out in the audience with Hazel Scott and he asked Oscar to come up and play in his place.
What a mistake.

When Duke saw Oscar standing there Duke called 'Jack the Bear' and all the things there that had solos in them and, my God, -- Oscar knew every introduction. You know, he was with the band for about three or four years. So, let me tell you, Duke lit into 'Jack the Bear' and he said, 'Clang, clang.' And Oscar said, 'Do-do-do-do do-do do-do do-do.'
(Laughter.)

I said, 'Oh, my goodness.' So we come off the band-stand after the set. Jimmy Woodye come around the back. So Duke told him, he said, 'Say, Jamie,' he said, 'you know it's nice for you to sit out and enjoy the music.' He said, 'I know the band sounded good to you and it's nice for you to be able to sit out with the customers and enjoy the music.' He said, 'You know this is your job, though, and if I was you, I wouldn't embarrass myself like this,' and walked away.
(Laughter.)
What a diplomatic man.
Oh.
What a diplomatic man, I'm telling you. It's unbelievable. Let's digress a little. We didn't mention a guy, a bass player, and then we'll get away from the bass players.
Good.
Elmer James.
Elmer James was another very good bass player, a very --
He played with Chick Webb, didn't he?

Yes, he played with Chick Webb. -- a very good bass player and a very good foundation bass player. And, also, the bass player that followed him, to me, was a very good bass player. And right today he is playing at the Carlisle with --
Oh, yeah, Bobby Short.
-- Bobby Short. Beverly Peer.
Beverly Peer.
Beverly Peer was with Chick.
That's right. That's right.
Boston, from Boston.
That's right, from Boston.
Yeah, another good musician from Boston. A gentleman, --
Absolutely.
-- just like all the rest of them from up there that we know.
That's right.
Beverly Peer, yes, sir, he's right there right now. I don't know how long -- How long's he been with Bobby Short?
Oh, years now. They've --
That's right.
Years. I wouldn't care to mention the years. And they're mainstays they are the darlings of the social world in New York.
That's right.
Absolutely.
Yeah.

Well, so much for bass players, and if we think of anyone else, we'll just throw them in later. But we'll get on to some piano players, excluding Duke, we'll get on to-- You want to check your list just to see -- You want to take a breather for a second?
Yeah, I was trying to think --
Just check your -- Hold it. Let's just let you take a little breather.
All right. [PAUSE]
Yeah, we went out for a little repast
here now. We were supposed to go to pianists.
Uh-huh.

But before we go to pianists, just to make some little interjections here, as we were having dinner, you mentioned a couple of dear friends of yours, trumpet players, that you didn't mention, and that's Erskine Hawkins. Do you remember that? You said you --
Oh, definitely.

Erskine Hawkins was a high note trumpet player. He was one of these trumpet players that he was a very quiet guy and until you heard him play you wouldn't even know what he was going to say or what he was going to do until he got in front of the bandstand. He was a very quiet bandleader, too. The band came from Bama State Teachers College in Montgomery, and they came to New York. It was a college band, actually. They had three bands down there, a number one band, a number two band, and a number three band. And Erskine Hawkins and that band, the Bama State Collegians, was the number one band that they came to New York with.

And, of course, they came to New York to play the Savoy. They had a manager with them from the school. They came up here in a school bus. In fact, I was standing in front of the Woodside Hotel when they drove up from Alabama State to play in New York.
So Moe Gale heard them, from the Savoy.
Who was Moe Gale?

Moe Gale was the manager of the Savoy Ballroom. Also, he managed Chick Webb. He managed Teddy Hill. All the bands that played in the Savoy Moe Gale managed. In fact, when the Missourians was there, Moe Gale had Callaway signed up before he got to the Cotton Club.
That's Cab Calloway?
That's right.
Uh-huh.

He was the owner of the Savoy Ballroom. So he liked the band and he seen how Erskine was a high note trumpet player and he was a feature man in the band, so he put him in front of the band when he signed the band up, and he started calling Erskine Hawkins the Gabes, you see.
And that was his nemesis from then on, right?
That's right. But there was another good trumpet player in the band that played a lot of the beautiful solos and that was Dud Bascomb.
Now, there is no original recording of 'Tuxedo Junction'. The beautiful solo on there that really everybody listened to was the one that Dud played.
Ah, ha.
That was really what made 'Tuxedo Junction,' I thought, was Dud Bascomb's solo. Of course, Erskine came in in the last chorus, you know, to play his high --
(End of Proceedings as recorded.)
