PROCEEDINGS
Butter, I'm not sure I got everything about Dud Bascomb on that other tape.
Uh-huh.

This is tape five.

I just wanted it mentioned about -- you were mentioning about Erskine Hawkins and the great trumpet player he had in his band, Dud Bascomb. What did you say about him? He made that great solo?

He made the great solo on Tuxedo Junction. I think it was one of the most beautiful solos. But like a lot of times, you know, the leader gets the credit. But Erskine played a solo on the last part of the record. You could see the difference, because Dud has a much broader sound than Erskine.
Right.
Erskine -- A lot of high note trumpet players, Erskine was like a lot of them. You know, their tones are not as big --
Right.
-- as the regular trumpet players that play down in the horn, you see.
Well, I hear they have the mouthpieces programmed for high notes but not shallow enough to get a broad sound. Is that so?
Exactly, because they sacrifice it for the range, you see.
I see.

Well, I just wanted to mention that, which I don't know whether we had on here, was that Dud Bascomb's son now is one of the greatest bass players, one of the finest bass players in New York City now.
Oh, yes, I have worked with him.
Yeah.
Yeah, I've worked with him and he's something else with that Fender bass, gee whiz.
He sure is. He's really out of sight.
He's really got it under his fingers.
That's right.
Because he can play it as fast as a guitar player.
That's right.
Yeah.
Yeah, he's a fantastic kid. He plays so beautifully on that Fender bass and he's an excellent musician.
Oh, yes.
A very mild-mannered gentleman, a credit to the whole music business.
But, you see, like father, like son.
Right, I'm so happy --
That's where that is. You see, he was raised that way.
That's right.
And his surroundings that he came up in as a kid made him like that, you see.
Now we can go on to get to some piano players that you've known.
Oh, my goodness.
You just go ahead and mention some piano players, Butter. You talk for a while.

Well, one of the first pianists -- this will surprise a lot of people -- that I really heard that kind of made me listen -- I didn't hear him but once and then later on I heard him on a record -- was Earl Hines. He was playing with an orchestra out of Pittsburgh -- a singer named Louis Dippo. A lot of people never heard of him. But he was in the show Great Day in New York. He had the most powerful baritone voice I have ever heard. He used to -- Louis Dippo, Louis Dippo.
Louis Dippo, Louis Dippo.

That's right. But his name, Louis; they said Louie, you know. But that's who I first heard that impressed me was Earl "Fatha" Hines. He was playing a style of piano then that was way ahead, way ahead of his time. And I didn't hear him no more until I heard him on the records with
Louie. He made records with Louie. But I heard him then and he was with this orchestra out of Pittsburgh.

Then, the next pianist that impressed me -- of course, he impressed me on the organ more than anything else. I had the first recording that Fats Waller made in 1926 on the Victor organ, the big pipe organ that Victor had. One side was Lenox Avenue Blues on one side and "St. Louis Blues" on the other. And he was the first to play jazz organ. Also, he was a good pianist, a good rhythmic pianist.
Uh-huh.
Then next I heard the master and that was Art Tatum. Art Tatum was playing in a little place in Toledo called Charlie's Chicken Shack.
About what year was that, Butter?
That was 1931, 1931. I was with McKinney Cotton Pickers. And when we played Toledo with the band, he used to always come around and Don would have him sit in.
Wow.
And he would sit in and play then, and I had never heard nothing like that in my life.
Uh-huh.
So he came to New York with Adelaide Hall, and I think we spoke of the rhythm club before, and he come to the rhythm club -- somebody brought him by -- and I

was there -- I happened to be there in town at the same time. And he sat down to the piano in the rhythm club and played. And Fats was there and Fats Waller went and got every piano player that he could find. He went and got the Lion.
Willie the Lion Smith, that is?
That's right, and he went and got James P. Johnson. He got all the pianists around there to come and listen to Art. And do you know not a one of them sat down and played behind Art Tatum.
I don't blame them.
And from then Fats took him and took him around New York 'cause you know Art was blind and Fats just kept him with him. And from then on they was boys.
And if you listen to any of Art's piano solos, even if for one measure, he's going to stick a measure of Fats Waller's style in there somewhere, --
Beautiful.
-- you see? Because that was his friend.
Now, he, to me, -- after you talk about Art Tatum, it's hard to talk about other pianists. I worked with a very good pianist in Zack Whyte's band, too. His name was Herman Chittison Chitizen.
Oh, yes, a very --
And when I first --
"Casey" photographer.
"Crime photographer."
He did crime on TV -- radio.
Yeah, a crime photographer. He was the incidental pianist on "crime photographer" for years.
Just before you get off of Art Tatum, you say he came here with Adelaide Hall.
That's right.
Do you remember, was it a duo? Did they have two piano players?
No.
Well, there was one piano player named Joe Turner that played with her. That was they were supposedly have gotten him the job with her and at one time they played together. Do you remember that?
No, I don't. You see, Art Tatum went to Europe with her but Art Tatum came back.
Right.
And then Joe went to Europe, you see.
But Joe was with her first, wasn't that --
Yeah. I think Joe was with her first and then he left her, you see, because at that time when I came to New York and Connie's Inn in '32 I met Joe Turner then. That's when he wrote --
Joe Turner, the pianist?
Yeah. That's when he wrote Walking Through Heaven and a couple of --
Is that his tune?
Oh, yes, oh, yes.
Yeah, "I'm walking through heaven with you."
That's right, yeah.
Oh, well, Don's -- Whose band did that?
Jimmie Lunceford.
Jimmie Lunceford's band did that?
That's right, when Henry Wells was singing with the band and before [Paul] -- I mean, before -- oh, what's the singer? -- Grissom. Before Dan Grissom.
Dan Grissom.
Yeah.
Yeah, we didn't mention the vocalists, like Dan Grissom.
Well, Henry Wells was a reasonable vocalist on that, you see. And --
Well, go ahead on with Tatum.
And so --
What's this other piano player that you met after Tatum?
I worked with Herman Crittison.
Yes.

Herman Chittison was a wonderful pianist. He worked with Zack Whyte. He didn't stay with the band long after I was there because he had a radio program over in Newport News over there in Kentucky -- not Newport News but just Newport, Kentucky.
He got to be on the radio over there and he stayed on that station for quite a while, quite a long time. That was before he came to New York.
Uh-huh.
And I think behind playing in radio there I think he got the break in New York, too.
I see.
You see? And he was -- he had the longest fingers, and he was a little guy and he had long, very slender fingers and he could reach tenths.
That's Chittison?
Yeah, Herman Chittison.
Yeah.
I'm still talking about Herman. And a real quiet guy. And he came to New York and he just made it.
He played -- What did he play mostly, in clubs and then --
That's right.
-- swank restaurants?
That's right. He was that type of piano -- just like you heard him play on 'Crime Photographer.'
Yes, society piano player.
Exactly. He could sit down and relax you, you know.
Like the old master before him, Luckey Roberts.
Oh, well. Luckey Roberts, he was really the epitome of society pianists. He got the best jobs of any pianist in New York.
That's right.
He played all the big society jobs. There was another one, too, called Ford Dabney.
Uh-huh.
He was another one back there, pianist, that got all the society jobs.
Uh-huh. Luckey Roberts was quite a writer, too, wasn't he?
Oh, yes, uh-huh.
Do you remember any particular thing he wrote?
No, not particular.
How does that thing go? (Humming.)
(Humming.) Glenn Miller played that.
Yeah, he had a very famous hit song. I
can't remember the name of it right now.
'Twilight Time.' x
I think that -- I think he wrote that.
Uh-huh, yeah.
It was something like one of those famous songs like that.
Yes, he did, yes.
Yeah, Luckey.
Uh-huh.
And Ford Dabney, you say he was --
He was just a -- he never played nothing but society gigs and society parties. Rich people used to have him come to their house and just play for their entertainment.
Uh-huh.
Maybe if he wanted to bring a drummer with him or a guitar player or something like that, okay.
In other words, back in this day, this era black pianists had the same kind of jobs that Lester Lanin and all of those guys had then? They were --
Oh, definitely. And we had a black band in New York that played those jobs, too, way back.
What was the name of that band?
Leroy Smith.
Leroy Smith, a society band.
'Moonlight Cocktail'; not Twilight Time.
That's right. We called him the white Guy Lombardo, in a way.
A black Guy Lombardo.
I mean the black Guy Lombardo. I didn't mean the white. Oh, my goodness, what am I saying? (Laughter.) But he was the black Guy Lombardo.
Describe Leroy Smith.
Leroy Smith was a little guy, kind of hunchbacked, and he played violin.
Right.
A perfect gentleman. He was from Detroit.
He wasn't a hunchback but he was bowed over?
Well, yeah. Uh-huh, like that, yeah. And he held his head, you know, --
Yeah.
-- like that.
He had a curve in his back.
Yes, uh-huh. He had a very, very good band and the saxophone players all doubled. They doubled on all the instruments.
They were out of Buffalo somewhere?
Well, they started out in Detroit. He
came from Detroit, but he got his band in New York.
I see.
Yeah.
Now, Wilbur de Paris was the trombone player with that band. You know I spoke of him a good while back.
Yes, yes.
He was the trombone player with that band. But I never got to meet any of the other guys because they never came around.
Yeah, they --

They weren't guys that hung out, you know. They were above hanging out, you know. You know, they were so society conscious themselves, you know. Very clean-cut guys, perfect gentlemen, every one of them, and if you saw them, they was impeccably neat.
Cool dudes.
Oh, yes, oh, yes. That's what we would call them now.
Yes.
Well, you mentioned Fats. We didn't really elaborate --
Oh. Fats was a fantastic, he was one of the most fantastic entertainers. I think if Fats would have lived to the TV era, he would have been a big star on TV. I always have believed this.
No question.
Because he had such a personality and could play. He was very entertaining. He knew just what to give the people.
He was only 38 years old when he died? Is that right?

Yeah, 38, 39. You remember he died when we was on the way to California and he was on the way back. We was on our way, on the way to do our part in 'Stormy Weather.' He had played his part and he was on the way back.
That's right.
And died on the train in Kansas City.
You and I were with Cab Calloway.
That's right.
What year was that, Butter?
1943, April.
Man, you're amazing. Your ability with dates is just phenomenal.
That's right, I'll never forget it.
Well, what about -- anything else about Fats? You know, he did a lot of those piano rolls, didn't he?
Oh, sure, he did a lot of them and so did James P. Johnson.
And who else?
And I think Eubie Blake did some, too,
if I'm not mistaken.
Earl Hines, perhaps?
I don't know about Earl, but I do know about Fats and I know about James P. Johnson doing piano rolls way back there, you know.

And Fats, I have to talk about Fats because one of the great things he did, he revolutionized playing swing organ. He was the first one to ever play swing organ when it was a pipe organ before they even thought about a Hammond. He was playing swing organ then. He used to come in the theater, the Lafayette Theater, and he wasn't working there, he'd just come in between -- he and his buddies would follow him down the aisle and he'd go down in between the picture, or between the stage show and he'd get to swinging and have them people patting their foot and the show couldn't go on.
Yeah.
And then when I came to Connie's Inn, Connie had put an organ for him, a miniature Estey organ in there for Fats to play in between dance sets and the show.
Connie Immerman?
Connie Immerman.
And Connie's Inn?
Yeah, Connie's Inn.
On Seventh Avenue and --
131st Street in the basement.
I see.
And he had an [Estey], a miniature pipe organ, built in there for Fats to play.

Then Fats got so he didn't want to stay on that job. He didn't want to sit down there and play. And sometimes, you know, Fats liked to drink. He liked to swing. He was -- Well, he was a swinger, he was a baller. He liked his friends. He liked to be around his buddies, you know? And he had a lot of buddies. Everybody loved him.
He sure did.
What are you going to do but love him?
Just a happy cat.
Yeah, and he always spread happiness everywhere he want.
Right.
Then when he couldn't make it, then that's when there was a lady, a black woman that was born in Bavaria, Germany, and Connie got her to play the organ in Fats' place.
Do you --
And her name was Leola Carter.
Wow.
That's right. If you know, she used to be a vocal coach for a while. She had a studio in the Columbia -- I mean in the CBS building there on the corner of
53rd and Broadway. She used to have a studio in that building.
Uh-huh.
And she was a vocal coach --
I see.
-- for years before she died.
She was educated in Germany, huh?
Oh, yes.
Leola Carter.
Uh-huh, yeah. She lived in the Alvin Hotel there when I lived there.
The Alvin Hotel was a downtown hotel on -- what's that? -- on 52nd and Broadway.
Yeah, it was.
What happened there?
Well, there was some musicians stayed in there but after a while a lot of the people moved out. The only musician that lived in there almost until he died was Zutty Singleton.
Right. I think Pres died in there, too, didn't he?
Pres died in there and Shorty Baker got sick and he died. He lived in the same room that Pres lived in.
Uh-huh.
506B. I'll never forget it.
Well, just while we're on this kind of thing, Butter, we might say that here we're in this basement here in St. Albans, Queens, --
Yes.
-- at 17305 113th Avenue.
Yes.
And this community 40 years ago was a white community --
Uh-huh.
-- and Fats Waller lived right down the street, one block down the street.
He did?
From history, from what my white neighbors told me, he was the first black man to ever move in this neighborhood. And ironically later Basie bought a nice big house right across the street from him.
Yeah.

And then in later years Lena Horne moved out here and Jackie Robinson and Campanella and Ella Fitzgerald and Earl Bostick. So this community moved -- Babe Ruth was in this neighborhood in the early days when it was a white community. Babe -- It was a sportsmen's community where Babe Ruth lived, the great baseball player, Earl Sande, the great jockey.
Uh-huh.

And there was a white gentleman that lived around here. He was a dear friend of mine until he died. He was the last white person in this community. His name was Mr. Ellison. He lived right across the street from me and he would sit on my lawn. We'd sit out there and talk and he told me about the great times and the great poker games that they had with Babe Ruth and Earl Sande, --
Uh-huh.

-- and Fats Waller was welcomed in there and was accepted; being a great drinker and a great sportsman, he was in the midst of these poker games. I'd just like to interject that into your -- since we're talking about -- where we're doing this taping now right in this same community in 1976.
Uh-huh, uh-huh. Well, I'm glad to know that.
Yes.
But, just like we said about Fats, Fats could mix in anywhere --
Any place.
-- with anybody and he would bring happiness wherever he went, you know.
What a person.
And I used to go hear him every chance I got. The last time I heard him was in the Apollo Theater.

Hammond had just given him an organ. In fact, Hammond built a three manual organ for him in his house, that he had in his house out here. The top manual had a novochord and solo-vox accompaniment on it back there in those days.
Wow.

But he had this new, I think it was a new B-3 organ that Hammond -- and he told me to come back stage, and, you know, I went up to his room; you know, Fats always kept wine up there. He never would give you a drink out of his bottle.
He drank gin, wasn't it? Wasn't he a gin --
No, he was drinking wine then. They had taken him off of gin.
Oh, I see.
He was drinking wine then and he never would give you a drink out of his bottle. He'd pass you a whole bottle for yourself.
(Laughter.)
That's right. He never would give you a drink out of his bottle. He would give you a bottle. And everybody in his band, when they opened up, there was a bottle in front of their stand, --
Wow.
-- on the bandstand. A bottle for each
guy in the band.
He was some kind of cat.
What a beautiful person he was.
Yes.
And he ate. He was a big eater. His wife used to bring his dinner in a clothes basket. You know, one of those old-fashioned clothes baskets?
Right.
And not a plate for him to eat, but the food would all be in serving dishes and he would eat out of the serving dishes.
I see.

You see. And he'd never ask you to have a taste. He never asked you to have any of his food. And he'd laugh and talk, he'd laugh. Talking about him, oh, he was such a lovable guy. And that's the last I saw him was in the Apollo Theater and he told me to come on the other side of the stage, he wanted me to hear this organ because he knew I liked the organ, you know.
Right, that's right, you played the organ, too.
Oh, yeah. You know, I used to go early in the morning -- at some theaters we played with Calloway, I used to get permission to go early in the morning. Danny Barker used to follow me sometimes.
Yeah, a great guitarist, Danny Barker.

Uh-huh, and I used to go and get permission to play the organ before the theater opened early in the morning. I used to get there at seven o'clock, eight o'clock in the morning. That's how I hurt this ankle.
Count Basie had a great love for the organ also.
Well, Fats taught him.
Is that so?

Fats taught him organ. Oh, yes, he'll tell you to this day that Fats started him out on the organ when he was in New York before he even went to Kansas City. You know, Basie and Elmer Williams come over here and hung out in New York together from over in Jersey.
Elmer Williams is a saxophone player?
That's right, that I told you was with Chick Webb.
Basie came over from Red Bank, I guess, huh?
That's right, and so did Elmer Williams.
Is that so?
Uh-huh, they used to come over and hang out together before they really got into the business.
Uh-huh. While we're on that, on the
question of Fats having a big appetite, you know, you were never known for having a small appetite either.
Oh, yes, but not like him.
Yeah, but tell me about some of the great appetites, some of the great -- Butter, I can remember you sitting down when you were young then and preparing a plate and really going at it pretty good.
Tell me about some of the guys you sat down and ate with?

Oh, Chu Berry, he was a monster with the plate. Tyree Glenn. They used to call each other -- Chu Berry used to call Tyree 'Beef Stew' Berry and -- I mean, Tyree would call Chu 'Beef Stew' Berry and then Chu Berry would call Tyree 'Glutton' Glenn.
(Laughter.)
Now, I've sat with some -- and Don Redman, he was another one that was a fantastic eater.
And he was only five feet tall.
And our former boss, you know, was no slouch, you know. Calloway could eat. I saw him eat.
What about Benny Carter?
Oh, Benny Carter was another one, but Benny Carter could cook, too.
Yeah, he was a great cook.
Yes.
I've eaten at his house.
Yeah, Benny Carter could eat, man, and just sit there and laugh and grin and talk to you to keep you from noticing how much he was eating.
Uh-huh.

And one of those kind of things, you know, one of those kind of guys, you know, that would just talk to you and keep you watching maybe, you know, like somebody watching you to see how much he wasn't eating -- how much he was eating. You know, you didn't have to pay any attention to him.

But, then, -- Let me see, did I mention Coleman Hawkins? Now, Coleman Hawkins used to come to Detroit and he would eat at the restaurant on the corner, Smith's, and there was a restaurant around a side street -- I forget the name of it offhand. But, anyway, he would order his chicken here in Smith's, then he'd go around to the other corner and order a steak dinner there, see? Now, by that time he'd come back and the chicken dinner would be ready. And after he'd finished the chicken dinner, he'd go around the corner and by that time that he finished the chicken dinner the steak dinner would be ready. And nobody would -- knew. You know, they wouldn't even know what he was doing. But, you know, I was always watching people.
Watching them. What town was that in?
Detroit.
I see.

Out at Forrest and St. Adwine out there. There was a lot of colored people lived around that district at that time, you know, and a lot of good restaurants out there, because I can tell you about the good restaurants.

I know you can.
Oh, by the way, since we're on this subject of food Butter, it's a very important subject, I think, concerning -- in this era which we're talking about. Before, in the thirties and the forties and the twenties, there was a lot of prejudice as far as black musicians were concerned, black people were concerned, and we didn't stay in white hotels. We had to get rooms in people's homes and we had to eat in the colored restaurants or have people cook for us.
Yes.

I think it was so relative with us, that we had such a relationship.
Can you name some of these places, that we used to eat in some of the towns that was great or had some great cooks? Remember Mom Sutton in --
In Atlanta.
Mom Sutton in Atlanta, Georgia.
That's right, yeah.
Tell us about her.
Mom Sutton, all the musicians used to come. She was another woman that had -- for a while there she would let you pitch till you win, --
Uh-huh.
-- because certain bands would come in and they abused her and she started putting, making complaints out for you, you see.
Yeah.
And there was Mom Charleston in Philadelphia.
Moms --
Charleston.
In Philadelphia?
Yeah, she was a big fat --
Havelow.
No, Mom Havelow too, but Mom Charleston was before her.
Oh, is that so?
Oh, yeah. Now, Mom Charleston used to be up the street around the corner from the Lincoln Theater --
I see.
-- when the Lincoln was at Broad and Lombard, you see.
I see.
And she was a big woman and she could
cook. She could cook like everything. We used to go over there and just -- Don Redman -- we used to go -- Don Redman was a eater too, you know.
He was a fantastic eater. And we used to go in Mom Charleston's and eat.
Mom [Havelow] was great, too.
She had a whole brownstone house and --
That's right.
-- you ate in the basement, right?
That's right.
On the first floor the bandleaders lived. There was an apartment there with a piano in it where Basie or Duke, whatever the bandleader, was in. Remember that?
Sure.
We don't know how many tunes -- God knows how many tunes that Duke wrote on that old piano in Mom [Havelow's] first floor.
Oh, yes.
All of the sidemen had to go way up-stairs to stay.
That's right, that's right.
Name another. Do you remember --
Then there was Pop Henry's in
Cincinnati.
Uncle Henry, yeah.
Yeah. That was a pitch till you win.
That was around the corner from the Sterling Hotel. That's where we all stayed.
That's right, uh-huh. It was around on Fifth Street -- No, Fifth or Third. Third Street? I think it was on Third Street because the Sterling Hotel was at Sixth and Mound.
Sixth and Mound.
Yeah, because I lived there when I first went there.
That's where all the black musicians -- that was a black hotel.
That's right.
You remember there was a rat there that everybody used to talk about?
Jerry.
Jerry.
Jerry was so old until the hair was off his back. He used to shed the hair off his back sliding in and out of them holes, we used to say all the time.
And everybody just knew Jerry, this great rat, he was so old.
Oh, sure, yeah.
Tell us about that.

And Jerry would -- they had these trash cans in the hall, you know. Everybody would put their garbage out there. Jerry would know and Jerry would walk down the hall besides you and didn't pay you no mind. He'd walk right on by you and go to his trash can and leap up there and try to get what he wanted out of there. And nobody paid Jerry any attention. Nobody was scared of him. He didn't bite nobody. He didn't bother nobody, you know.
It's hard to tell people that, but so many musicians of our era know that Jerry used to walk up and down those halls. This rat was big as any cat we ever saw.
That's right. But what was so beautiful that a lot of people don't know, do you know some of those ladies were the best cooks in the world?
Unbelievable.

You see, any -- I don't care. If we had went to the white restaurant, the food wouldn't have been as good. I know this today because it was all good, wholesome food. It stuck to the ribs, we used to say.
That's right.
And they didn't mind filling your plate up, --
That's right.
-- you know? They cooked for you like
Right.
-- you see. That's what made it so good.
Now, since you're on the subject about us not being able to eat in restaurants, do you remember when we was with Calloway when you guys had the kitchen --
Yeah.
-- that we used to have on the road?
Yeah, we used to carry a kitchen.
And we used to take turns about cooking?
Right.

And do you remember when we played the theater in Youngstown and the food was going out in the audience and the man come back and told us not to cook no more because the people were sitting out there drooling?
Yeah.
(Laughter.)
I think Feet and Lamar Wright put some cabbage on and had it cooking while the show was on, --
That's right.
-- and the aroma went all out in the theater.
It did, it did.
And the manager came back and said, 'Hey, fellows, everybody in the audience is starving to death.
That's right.
Please cool it over that cabbage back there."
(Laughter.)
That's right.
Oh, that's amusing.
We carried that stove around because it was necessary. We'd get into some towns where there was no restaurants --
True.
-- and we just -- we had to go a long ways to get some food.
Yeah.
So we just had us an automatic kitchen and we set up business and everybody would take turns and go to the store on your day --
That's right.
-- and cook.
That's right. Well, you know, in those days, you know, all the RKO theaters had kitchens in the back-stage.
Right.
They had kitchens. They had playrooms for the kids if you had kids with you.
Right.
Individual shower -- sunken tub and shower in each dressing room.
Right.
Adjustable lights. They had a chaise lounge, --
Really high class.
-- red carpet.
Right.
And each dressing room had -- was the name of a state.
Right.
And they was beautiful theaters all over the country, --
That's right.
-- and we played every one of them, you know.
We sure did.
But we had some good places to eat, though.
Do you remember Edwina's in Philadelphia?
Of Washington.
Was that Washington?
Yeah, Edwina's. Oh, yes. I stayed in
her house.
Washington, D.C. Yeah.
Across the street, up the street, from the Howard Theater.
Yeah. Every town had a lady that we relied on, black orchestras and black show people coming in, and they prepared food for us and it was really first class.
That's right, that's right.
And this was the way we survived, right?
Oh, definitely.
I was trying to think of the name of that restaurant in Cleveland that we used to go to across the Majestic Hotel.
Oh, yeah, and they got up the street -- they had the barbecue place across the street.
Oh, yes, oh, yes.
The best barbecue you will ever --
Oh, yes.
Well, you know, you can get good barbecue, but to me, of the middle western states there was no barbecue like Chicago. You could get some barbecue in Chicago.
That's my home town, man.
I know.
The only place that come close to Chicago barbecue was a place in Detroit, a guy called Magnus.
I see.
Magnus Clark.
Uh-huh.
He had wonderful barbecue. And there used to be a place in Evansville, too, Evansville, Indiana, --
Indiana.
-- where the guy used to cook it in the pit. He used to go right in there and take if right off the pit.
I remember that, yeah.
You remember that place?
Hot sauce.
Yeah.
Just beautiful.
You know, originally Evansville, Indiana, was Big Sid Catlett's home originally --
Oh, is that so?
-- before he came to Chicago. We used to -- I saw his father there and a lot of his people. But -- Louisville was another good place.
Oh, yeah. Louisville. There were a lot of nice places to eat there.
Oh, yes, some wonderful places.
I don't know how we got off on this food thing, but we were talking about piano players. Maybe pianos and food and you and I and food because we always enjoyed it.
Oh, yes.
It was a great thing.
Me, yes. You know, I love my food. That was my biggest -- I never was a real drinker -- I smoked a little bit -- but food was always my thing.
Yeah.
The guys would be going out hunting to drink, I would hunt something to eat.
(Laughter.)
For a good [nice] restaurant.
Sure.
You and Hilton Jefferson. Jeff was also a good eater.
Oh, yes, I know.
A gentleman. He --
Wasn't he a gentleman?

He should have been a surgeon. He wouldn't use -- he wouldn't pick up a piece of chicken with his hands. He would take -- I told him -- he would take that knife and cut the chicken and I'd say, 'Judge, you use it like a scalpel the way you slice -- '
Oh, wasn't he, wasn't he? And he could take a knife and fork and clean a bone --
That's right.
-- so beautifully. But, you know, he
come up in that New England area up there --
Right.
-- and everybody was so -- you know, everything had to -- so much class.
Everything was so sedately.
Yes, and his aunts raised him, you see, --
Right.
-- and they was very particular with him and you could tell it, you know.
Yes. Always a gentleman.
Oh, always a gentleman. He'd tip his hat and he'd take the lady by the arm when he took them -- I used to like to watch him when he would go out with a lady.
Yeah.
A perfect gentleman.
A perfect --
Etiquette? Perfect etiquette.
A southpaw gentleman.
Oh, yes.
He was left-handed. I used to look at him across from the table and I would be amazed how a left-handed man could so skillfully handle that knife and fork.
Oh, sure.
Beautiful.
(Laughter.)
One of my dearest, dearest friends, Hilton Jefferson.
That's right. Oh, man, I loved him. I loved him. Who didn't?
How about Billy Kyle, to get back to some piano players?
Billy Kyle?
Yeah.

Billy Kyle to me was a fantastic piano player. I first heard him with Lucky Millinder; that's when I first knew him. He was in that great band that Lucky had back there in the thirties when he had -- Andy Gibson was in the band, Sweets Edison was in the band, Charlie Shavers.
Whose band was this?
Lucky Millinder.
Wow.
That's right. Well, Billy Kyle was the pianist in there and John Kirby was the bass player in there, and I never paid much attention -- Oh, Tab Smith, I think, was one of the saxophones in that band.
Right, he was. I remember.
Yeah, Tab Smith. But I never paid much attention to the rest of the band.
Uh-huh.
But the brass section always astounded me. Oh, big George Matthews was one of the trombone players, I think, in there, too, for a while.
Yeah, which we haven't mentioned. George Matthews. Yeah, a very great trombone player.
Oh, yes, very melodic.
Right.
Very melodic. He was such a big guy, gee whiz, the trombone looked like a toy when he played.
Right.
But a very good trombone player and still very active today.
Is that so?
Yeah. He's quiet but he gets his little gigs and things.
I'm real happy to hear that.
I think last year was the last year he played. He was playing a circus every year, --
[Great.]
-- you know, and then he was in the Apollo band for years. He was in the Apollo band for years up there when Reuben Phillips had the Apollo band. You remember Reuben Phillips?
Sure.
He used to be with Ersk -- I mean, with
Andy Kirk.
That's right, a saxophone player.
Uh-huh, yeah. And --
Yeah.
What did you like mostly about Billy Kyle? What kind of piano player was he?
Billy to me was an exciting piano player and swing, too, and it was very commanding to me the way he would swing a piano. And he'd sit just as straight at the piano and play.
Yeah, and good looking, too.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, he was a very good-looking guy. The ladies liked him.
Yeah, very much.
Yeah.
And Buster Bailey was in that band, too, for a while, you know. He was with Lucky. So was Red Allen.
Red Allen, that's right. 'Ride, Red, --
That's right. 'Ride, Red, Ride.'
'Ride, Red, Ride --
That's right. Yeah.
Right. -- came out of that band.
That's right. But that's when I knew Billy Kyle, just before he went out with John Kirby.
We've mentioned Luckey Roberts and Fats
Waller, and Earl Hines we're mentioned. There's another piano player that was -- Do you remember the piano player that was with Erskine Hawkins, Avery Parrish?
Oh, yes, Avery. Oh, yes. Sure, Avery, yeah.
Yeah.
It was 'Across --'
What was that great blues that he was -- that he wrote? Tippin In?
He didn't write 'Tippin' In.' The band wrote 'Tippin' In.'
Oh.
The band wrote Tuxedo Junction, too.
Uh-huh. But Avery played --
There was about three different --
-- 'Tippin' In,' didn't he?
Oh, yeah, sure.
It was a piano solo.
Yeah.
(Humming.)
Now, what is that? Across -- No, 'Across the Track Blues' or something like that is what that blues thing was. (Humming.)
Yeah.
'Tippin' In' was (humming). That was
"Tippin' In."
Oh, I see.
Yeah.
Well, we've gone through a lot of musicians --
Now, we -- Oh, yeah, but we --
Go right ahead.
-- but there was another good pianist that was with Don Redman, was Donald Kirkpatrick.
Oh, yes.
A great pianist and a great arranger. You know, he was with Chick Webb way back.
Uh-huh.

He was with Chick Webb, one of the first pianists with Chick Webb. And Don got him from Chick, in fact. He made a lot of good arrangements for Don, a lot of beautiful arrangements. He was a quiet guy, and he could eat, too, Kirk could.
Uh-huh.
He was married to Johnny Hodges' sister.
Oh, is that so?
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
That's interesting to know.
Yeah.
Who's the other piano player that Pearl Bailey had for so many years with her that died just recently? He was a friend of Don Redman's.
I know, and he was a friend of Kirkpatrick. He and Kirkpatrick used to have a piano duo down in the Village.
Yeah. We'll recall his name in a few minutes because --
Yeah, I know.
-- he was a great pianist.
I know, and a very good accompanist.
Yes.
You know, there's a very few guys that to me are very good accompanists. I can name you a lot of them that are good accompanists today, you know?
Uh-huh.
Now, to me, one of the greatest accompanists for a singer back in those days was Benny Payne.
Uh-huh.
Benny Payne was a fabulous accompanist.
That's right.
But nobody, you know, -- I don't care -- and for a dancer, he would make a dancer go crazy out on the floor --
That's right.
-- the way he would play behind them. Bojangles tried to get him. Bojangles Robinson tried to get Benny Payne. Quite a few times he tried to get Benny away from Calloway.
That's right. That's right. He had a little guy with him. Bojangles had a little guy with him named --
Putney Dandridge.
-- Putney Dandridge.
Yeah.
Right, that just played for him.
Yeah.
But Benny also played all of the things in the Cotton Club behind --
That's right. That's right.
-- Bill Robinson.
That's right. Benny to me, boy, Benny Payne was something else. You know, I admire Benny, --
One of my dearest friends.

-- I admire Benny. The only thing I ever got mad at Benny about was that Benny should have been a great entertainer himself instead of going around and accompanying other people because he was just as great as some of the people he accompanied, you see?
Yeah, that's quite so, quite so.
But he always, I don't know, he liked to be in the background, it seemed as though.
Well, even he and Cab, he and Cab were dear friends when Cab was doing Broadway shows.
Uh-huh.
And they sort of had a handshake or something --
Yeah.
-- that they would always look out for each other.
Oh, yeah.
Which didn't quite work out that way because Cab got to be a leader and Benny was always there supporting him.
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
But Benny always -- even they used to sing some songs together on Cab's band, right?
I know.
What was the songs they used to sing, Butter?
Oh, I don't remember that.
Cotton, give me a hand, Brother Cotton. Is that one?
Oh, yeah, that was one of them, yeah.
That was one of them.

But, you see, -- How that happened, you see, Benny used to sing with the trio up at the Cotton Club before Calloway's band even went in there. He used to sing -- they had a trio, a men's trio that used to sing up there.
One of the guys that was in the trio did Uncle Remus, the picture. Jimmy --
Oh, Jimmy Basquette.
Jimmy Basquette.
Jimmy Basquette.
He was in the trio with Benny Payne.
Is that so?
And the other piano player -- I forget the man that played the piano in that trio.
Uh-huh.

Anyway, they used to sing in between dance sets and everything. They used to entertain, you see. And, of course, Benny before that, Benny used to accompany Mattie Hite, who was one of the greatest entertainers that ever hit New York. A cabaret singer and Benny was her accompanist. They used to make -- In those days they made $200 a night tips.
Wow.
In those days. I'm going back before 1930, around that time, because Calloway didn't get his band till '30, really.
I see.
And that's when he got his band. When Duke went to make Check and Doublecheck with Amos and Andy, the picture, Check and Doublecheck, --
That's right.

-- they didn't have nobody to come in the Cotton Club to take Duke Ellington's place. So Duke Ellington told Herman Stark and Owrey Madden to go over and hear this kid over at the Savoy Ballroom, "He's a good entertainer. He looks good. He's got a nice personality. And I think he could do something with it."
Who was this kid?
Duke Ellington -- Calloway.
Oh, Cab Calloway.
That's right.
Oh, that's amazing.
That's right, and I can tell it because I think all the people implicated are dead now anyway.
Yeah.
So, anyway, they went over and saw Calloway and they liked what they saw and they told Owrey Madden, "We want his contract. Now you give us his contract or else we'll blow up the Savoy Ballroom."
Oh, yeah. These were the real boys in those days and when they said something, you did it.
Oh. Owey Madden was as powerful in Harlem just like Al Capone was in the south side Chicago.
Right.
That's the way Al Capone -- I mean, that's the way Owey Madden was in Harlem, you see.
Yeah.

And Bo Gill tore up that contract and Herman Stark and Owey Madden took Calloway and put him in the Cotton Club. And the band was a cooperative band and they took the band away from the boys and give it to Calloway and said, 'This is your band.' And they got him signed up --
take the Missourians to Cab Calloway's band.
Exactly. Then, Irving Mills, naturally --
Uh-huh.

-- Irving Mills signed him because Irving Mills had every band in the Cotton Club. They signed Calloway up, put him on the air and made a little club -- I forget. If you could call in a name, you could get so many records. It was a real long name. I forget what it was right now. But he made --
Oh, yeah.
He made 'St. James Infirmary'. And they created -- for the Cotton Club show they created Minnie the
Moocher and 'Smoky Joe', you see?
Right.
And from then on, shew, Calloway was gone.
Cab Calloway was it.
That's right, and he, all the guys in the band, he started to firing different guys in the band from the Missourians -- he was always trying to improve his band. You have to give him that.
And keep --
You see?
Yeah. -- and keep control also.
Oh, definitely.
Because now there's no more cooperation.
Uh-uh, no.
Yeah.
So --
[Yeah], Butter, that's interesting.
So we was speaking, still speaking about pianists, wasn't we? I was thinking about Benny Payne.
Yeah.
What a great accompanist he was.
Uh-huh. And Hank Jones? What about --
Hank Jones to me -- there's nothing you can say about Hank too much. Hank is one of the most --
He's the epitome of pianists.

That's right, full-fledged pianist. Any kind of piano you want, any kind of piano you want, Hank Jones can play it. I don't care -- If you want him to even go back to 1915, he can play that. Up till now, if you want him to play a vant-gark, he can play that.
Whatever.
It doesn't make any difference. And I love his sound on the piano. There are certain guys that get a tone out of a piano. He gets a tone -- artistic
Which is really (inaudible)?
Yeah, Art got a tone out of the piano, to me.
Right.
And --
The piano, being a pluckless instrument where you just strike it, it takes quite some doing to --
Oscar Peterson to me is another pianist that -- oh, I can name you pianists that -- and Phineas Newborn.
Oh, yeah.

Phineas Newborn, of the young pianists, to me is the greatest, of the young pianists. Of course, he's younger than Oscar and the guys that came up in the Art Tatum era, you know. Of course, Oscar's a little later than Art

Tatum. But to me, I put Oscar right there, you know, in that category just about, you see. Not as great as Art because nobody to me would ever be as great as Art. But he's up in that category. And Phineas Newborn, too, to me is about up in that category.
Right. Where does he live now? In California someplace?
In California, yeah.
Yeah.
You know, he had problems.
He had a nervous breakdown or something.
Yes, he did, yeah. But I have records of his, of him at home.
Oh, yes.
Shew, beautiful.
I made some records with him.
Uh-huh.
What about the little kid, the little short kid from Pittsburgh, Erroll Garner?

Oh, well, let's don't even mention him. Do you know, when we used to play Pittsburgh's Stanley Theater, Danny and I used to get him and take him out with us. He wasn't but about 17 years old and we used to take him -- Of course, you know, back in those days, you went to every place you wanted to go. You know, there was a lot of
houses of ill repute --
Sure.

-- in Pittsburgh. And we used to go around there, not to be a purchaser, but we used to like to go hang around -- Danny used to like to go talk to the girls. And we used to take Erroll Garner around there to play for them. If his father knew that --
(Laughter.)

-- you know? And Danny told him -- Danny Barker used to tell him, he said, "You better come to New York because there's nobody in New York played like you, nobody." He said, "Why don't you get yourself together and come on to the big city so you can be somewhere and get someplace?" Danny Barker talked to him then about that.
That's amazing.
That's right.

So we come to New York and, I don't know, I think we was playing at the Park Central Hotel and we looked up and we went down 52nd Street and down to Tondelayo's and here's Erroll Garner sitting up there playing.
That's amazing.

That's right. And, of course, Art was in the street then, you know, and Art did him just like Fats did Art. Art Tatum took Erroll Garner in his hand. Erroll was scared to death. The guys used to laugh at him, and
Art told him, he said, "Don't pay them no attention. You go ahead and play your piano, boy, like you want to play it."
Which he did.
You know? Which he did.
Oh, that's amazing.
Yeah. But Art labeled him, though. Art labeled him. Art told him that he was a piano player like a piano player that plays in a house of ill repute, you know. I can't use the word, you know, --
Yeah, well, we know the word.
(Laughter.)
And Erroll never read a note of music and his brother studied -- his brother was a good pianist -- his brother studied like everything. His brother never could play like Erroll could.
Butter, do you remember what his name was?
Linton.
Linton?
Linton Garner.
Yeah.
Uh-huh, yeah.
That's amazing.
He was Timmy Rogers' accompanist for a long time -- the comedian, Timmy Rogers? --
Yes.
-- he was his accompanist for a long time, Linton was. And can arrange. Linton can arrange. He's a nice arranger.
Uh-huh.
But Erroll didn't study. He didn't read a note.
Lightning only struck once in his family.
There you go.
And then Hank Jones' family it struck three or four times.
Oh, my goodness.
There's Hank and Elvin and --
Thad.
-- Thad.
That's right.
Hey, let's go on to some of the bands, now, that you had played with. Your reputation of playing and supporting in making great bands sound good is longer than any other sideman that I know of.
So the last band we talked about that you had been in was what?
Was Calloway.
Calloway's band. And you left Calloway. Where'd you go? You went to Basie?
No.
Where'd you go?
When I left Calloway there was a long lull in between --
Uh-huh.

-- because Duke had talked to me and Duke told me not to take -- When he went to Europe that time, he left the band here, and he went to Europe, I think he figured some of the guys wouldn't be there when he got back or one or two of them that he didn't want to be there. And he told me not to take no regular job with anybody, you see, but to wait till he came back.
Uh-huh.

So I got a job with Lucky Millinder. Lucky Millinder had a very good band, a great band. However, I stayed there, I think it was three weeks and I got fired, the only time I ever was fired in my life. But Lucky told me I was a great trombone player, I was a gentleman, and he liked me very much, he said, but he was looking for something. And he said until he found it, he was going to still fire different guys, and he said, 'In the event that I realize that I have made a mistake in firing you, I will gladly take you back.'
That's beautiful.
You know? And he fired me and Gene Simon at the same time.
Who was Gene Simon? A saxophone player?
No, trombone player.
Oh, Gene Simon.
Yeah. We was in Don's band together.
I see.
See, Gene Simon took Claude Jones' place with Don Redman back in '33 when Claude left.
Claude left to go with Fletcher then, huh?
Went back to Fletcher.
I see.
And he played with Chick for a while, too.
We were talking about --

-- so, anyway, I went with Lucky and he fired me and he took Gene Simon back. He fired me and hired two white trombone players. Yeah, Freddie Zito -- and a dear friend of mine, too, Freddie is. We worked in the house band at the Waldorf together. And Porky Cohen was a very dear friend of mine. Porky Cohen was the only white trombone player I knew that could play the plunger. He played the plunger with Charlie Barnet when Charlie used to play Duke's arrangements, and Porky Cohen was the plunger. He played the plunger. He was a very good trombone player.
And the trumpets? He had -- Lucky had in the trumpets, he had Nottingham, he had Reynauld Jones, had Joe Wilder, and Frank Galbreath. That was the trumpets.
Yeah, trumpets.
And the trombones was Al Gray and myself and Gene Simon, you see? And I can't --
And the reeds?
The reeds? Heads Adams. He's from Buffalo, I think.
Yeah, Heads Adams. What a name.
Yeah. And the singer, the great vocalist at that time, Bullmoose Jackson.
Oh, yeah.

Bullmoose Jackson was in that saxophone section. Billy Mitchell was in that saxophone section. But I can't think of the rhythm section. I just can't think of them. There was two brothers, one a pianist and one a bass player. And the one that was a bass player turned out to be an organist around Detroit. And the drummer I forget. I've seen the drummer around now, every now and then, and I forget his name, too.

But it was a good band, a good band, and Lucky -- Bullmoose told me a lot of times Lucky fired so many guys that, he said, for the time he was there he had played with about a hundred different saxophone players. He said sometimes he
would come to work at night and he didn't know who was going to be sitting there.
But even after he fired me and Gene, he took Gene Simon back and had him as a road manager.
Uh-huh.
That's the kind of guy Lucky was.
So then I waited around New York and just waited around, and me and unemployment insurance made it.
Sure.

And when Duke came back from Europe, I called him and asked him did he want me in the band. And then he told me yes, he said, 'You're going to take Claude Jones' place.' And I said, 'Oh, gee, I didn't want to do that,' you know, because, gee whiz, I mean Claude, you know --
That's your buddy. (Inaudible.)

Oh, God. Then I got to thinking and I said -- Well, I knew Claude wasn't getting along over there. I knew that too, you know. There was a little jealous thing going on in there, you know, between him and Lawrence, I found out later, because he didn't want to play a valve trombone and Duke wanted him to play valve trombone because Tizol played valve and that's what he wanted in that particular chair, you see. And so Claude didn't really get to play solos like he wanted to, you know.
And so I said, 'Well,' and I went to meet the band in
the Duke Ellington club in Washington and I took Claude's place in the band, and I was playing --
What year was that, Butter, when you joined --
That was October 21, 1948.
Wow.
That's right. And Tyree had joined the band, oh, over a year here before I got there.
19? What year?
Uh-huh.
Uh-huh.
What town was that in?
Washington, D. C.
That's Duke's home town, huh?
That's right, and it was a club they tried to open called the Duke Ellington Club. It didn't last long because they couldn't get a liquor license.
Uh-huh.
But we played there. That was the most fantastic experience, to sit in that band.
Well, when you joined that band, who was in that band?
Well, the trumpets was Al Killian, Shelton Hemphill, Francis Williams, Shorty Baker, and Ray Nance.
We had five.
What happened to Shelton Hemphill? I don't remember him.
Shelton Hemphill got sick. He had a stroke and he got sick and died. We used to call him Scad Hemphill.
Uh-huh.
Scad played -- he used to play first trumpet with Lucky Millinder for a long time, too.
Uh-huh.
And he played with Louie Armstrong's bid band, too.
Uh-huh.
Yeah. A little chubby guy.
Uh-huh.
A quiet guy, very nice guy. I have a picture of him -- sometime I'll show you -- at home.
And the trombones was Tyree and Lawrence Brown and myself. And the saxophones was Procope and Johnny and Harry and Jimmy Hamilton, and Sears was still there.
Al Sears?
Yes.
On tenor saxophone?
Uh-huh. But Ben come in the same week that I joined the band. Ben come back in the band.
Oh, he rejoined -- he'd been in and --
He rejoined the band.
-- he rejoined?
That's right. So we had six saxophones for a while --
Wow.

-- until after the Clique Club. We got to the Clique Club in Philadelphia. The Clique Club was a club on Market Street. It had the longest bar I've ever seen, a big long bar. There wasn't many tables but a bar forever. And, like, when you'd get ready to come on, you'd get on the bandstand and they'd turn you around on a table.
Oh, a turn -- Yeah.
So whoever would -- when the band on the other side was finished, you know, he'd turn them around the back and you was out front.
Oh, I remember that place.
Yes.
What's the name of that?
The Clique Club.
Oh, yeah.
That's right.
I remember playing that with Cab Calloway.
Yeah, uh-huh, yeah.
Yeah.
That's right.

And so then Ben stayed and Sears left; he left the band and he started to staying around New York. I think he got into song publishing, and a lot of things he did, Sears did. Ben stayed in the band. We kept that same band, and in 1949 Duke let him go.

Butter, I'd just like to ask you this. There have been -- I see that Duke Ellington's band, like Benny Goodman's band, has had so many alumni, so many guys that come in, in and out of the band, and it's like a stamp of approval; if anyone has ever spent one hour in one of those bands, he's considered an all-time great because of these great leaders if they just accepted you for a week or two weeks.
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
I'd just like to, for the record's sake, ask you confidentially, what was Duke like to you and how do you feel about him and how did you feel about him? How do you feel about him?
Well, I feel about Duke Ellington -- Duke Ellington to me was one of the most amazing men that I have ever known in life. He was a great psychologist. He was a great diplomat.
How do you mean a psychologist?

He could -- anyway that you want -- he wanted you to play you would play that way without you thinking about it, because he knew his men to the extent that when he would make an arrangement, he would give certain guys certain parts or certain solos that he knew how they was going to treat it before that they even started to play it, because he used to hear before he would put it down.
I see.
He knew what it was going to sound like.
Uh-huh.

We had an arrangement in the book that -- I always played third because, like all the bands I've been in, everyone wanted to hear me play low notes. I had made a name around New York for playing low notes, "Get Butter to play third trombone," you know, --
Uh-huh.

-- or fourth. And I did it on a tenor trombone before a bass trombone. And I can make a bottom, I can make a good bottom with the tenor trombone. , So he made an arrangement -- I'm playing third -- and all at once for four measures I'm up on the first part. I said, "Now, something is the matter here." At the time John Sanders was doing the copying and I said, "Edward, didn't you make a mistake on my part?" I said, "Now, these four measures, I'm playing lead," and I said, "I have been playing third all the
time." So he said, you know, "Monsieur du Beurre," he said, "in those formations I heard you playing that top part."
What did he call you? Monsieur who?
De Beurre.
Who said that?
Duke.
Uh-huh.

Duke, when we went to Europe in '50, my nickname was Butter. Don Redman gave me that nickname when I first joined McKinney Cotton Pickers. I was young and tender and they said I looked like butter, so that stuck. So, anyway, --
Plump.
Yes, yes, I was round. My cheeks was round and smooth. In Cincinnati they called me "Baby Boy," before I got to Detroit and they called me "Butter."
Beautiful.
So, anyway, --
He said he heard you playing that first part.

Yeah. So he called me Monsieur du Beurre. Now, when we went to Paris in 1950, and Butter being my nickname, he found out that butter in French was Beurre, see. So after that he called me Monsieur du Beurre, you know, like Mr. Butter.
Like Mr. Butter.
And it stuck. A lot of guys, you know, that went to Europe with me, it stuck with them, you know.
Sure.

And I noticed how he would use different musicians in the band. He would take your sound and use it. He would give you certain notes and certain chords, like he would give me certain notes in a chord that he wouldn't give Lawrence or give Tyree or even Britt Woodman or John Sanders, and that's the way he wrote, you see? And that's the reason that he had a lot of different arrangements on one tune in a book. If there was a change in the personnel of the band, that arrangement wouldn't sound the same to him, so he would make a new one, you see.
To fit the guys?

That's right. And he knew how to use every one. He had two great clarinet players in the band. He had Jimmy Hamilton and Russell Procope. He knew just how to use them. He knew how to use Harry Carney on that baritone saxophone. I have watched different arrangements that sometimes Carney would be playing up above the tenor, even, and then all at once when he wanted a big drop he'd -- Bam -- he'd drop it right down and make that whole chord just fall down like a big rock hit the bottom of the ground, you know?
Yeah. So you'd call him a musical chemist, more or less, eh?
Oh, definitely.
He'd mix sounds like you mix --

That's right. It was his workshop. He could do with it what he wanted it to, and there was so many arrangements in that book that a lot of people didn't even get to hear, because he was always writing. We would be on the bus, he would be writing. We would be playing a job, and I'd look over there sometimes, and he would be writing on the bandstand.
That's Duke Ellington?

Yes, and then he'd get to his room in the hotel and he'd be writing. And the copyists used to catch, they used to catch the devil because every time they'd turn around he was bringing something else in, and we'd play it that night. He'd pass it out at the beginning of the job. And some of those things were so pretty, Milton. They were so beautiful and fantastic. No title on them or nothing, and he'd take it up. And if he liked it, then he'd add another chorus next night and maybe about three days later he'd add another chorus. You'd have three different pieces of music to one arrangement. No title on it or nothing. And a poor guy -- If we ever would have a sub come in, he wouldn't know what to do. He wouldn't know what to do.
I witnessed that myself. It was really
You did?
I had no idea.
Yeah, and sometimes I used to tell him, I said, "Edward," I said, "why don't you play this thing that we played in such and such a town?" He said, "Oh, that? What was that?"
Yeah. You called him Edward?
Oh, yes, sure, I always called him Edward, yeah.
2 nice relation,
That's beautiful. That's (inaudible)
Yeah, because, man, oh, I loved this guy.
Monsieur du Beurre and Edward.
Yes, uh-huh. Yes.
So tell me more about it. What was your relationship with him, Butter?

My relationship was beautiful with him. He loved trombones. He always loved trombones. And a lot of times he used to come and talk to me about quiet things. You know, things -- he asked my -- even -- I can't say he asked my advice. He would talk to me sometimes to see my reaction to different things, you know. The man was a brilliant man. He was a mental giant. You couldn't outtalk him. I tried to
quit the band twice. He kept me up in the Paramount Theater once for an hour after the show closed. And there's no way in the world he'd let me go and so I finally got a raise.
Oh, beautiful.
That's twice I got a raise that way, and both times Basie asked me to come with his band and that's what got me the raise both times. I can talk about that now, you know.
Sure, yeah. Well, years later.
Yeah.
Now, that band -- when I joined that band we had, like I told you, we had -- the personnel changed.
Uh-huh.
It changed. Al Killian left. Cat Anderson came back.
About what year was that?
That was 1950, the fall of '50. Al Killian -- I mean, Cat came back in the band. And we also had a trumpet player, Nelson Williams, that had been in the band in Francis Williams' place.
I see.
And --
(Unintelligible)
Well, one of the
fellows, Francis Williams. You haven't mentioned when he came in.
Francis Williams was there when I got
there.
Oh, he was?
Oh, definitely. Oh, sure, he was there when I got there. And when --
That's 1948?
Uh-huh, when Shelton Hemphill died and he left, well, when we got ready to go to Europe, Francis Williams didn't go. He got Nelson Williams to go.
Oh, yeah.

And Al Killian almost missed the boat, so -- Duke was kind of, you know, kind of [skimmish] about things like that -- he didn't know whether Al Killian was going to make it or not -- so he got Ernie Royal to come with us. So we had five trumpets on that trip in Europe.
Wow.
And you never heard high notes.
Oh, that must have -- that must have really given everybody a nosebleed, with Ernie Royal there.

Duke wasn't taking any chances, you see. He had been on that trip over there before and he wasn't taking no chances this time. So Sonny was getting -- he was drinking quite a bit at that time, so he got Butch Ballard as the extra drummer. And that whole trip Sonny hasn't got drunk yet 'cause he didn't want Butch up there playing his drums, you know, playing his gig, of overshadowing him. And it was

a beautiful trip.
That's when I started to playing the plunger. Tyree
didn't go either. So that's when I really starting to playing
the plunger and from then on I had Tricky Sam's chair.

And one time down there -- Oh, going back to that
trip, too, I must tell about this.
Yeah, go right ahead, Butter.

We had three trombones when we started
out. Ted Kelley was the other trombone, in Tyree's place. And
Ted Kelley got over there and we was there two weeks, and he
had promised this girl that he was going to marry her and he
came all the way back to the United States to marry this girl.
And after he got married he asked Duke if he could come back
and Duke told him no, there was no use in him coming back there
for just two more weeks, you know. So Ted never got back in
the band, so it left just Lawrence and myself.

And we get to Italy, Lawrence got sick -- he had
trouble with his back and he had to lay on a board all night --
that left me by myself. I was playing Lawrence's solos, play-
ing Tricky Sam's chair, and I would take different parts and
whatever part that I thought would fit in different spots, see?
I would play that part whether it was first, second, or third,
whatever I thought would fit. And I had to do that by myself
until we got back.
We got back to the United States and then Tyree come
back and made an album with us, the Masterpieces by Ellington, which is a beautiful album.
Where did Tyree go?
Tyree just stayed in New York.
Oh, I see.

He just stayed in New York and got to gigging around New York and everything and that was right before that he got the Ted Steele show, you see. And he was really doing -- he was doing all right for himself. He wasn't hurting at all.
I'm sure.
Tyree wouldn't, --
I'm sure.
-- you know.
So then he came back. What year was that he came back?
We came back in '50 and Tyree came back just to make the album and that's all. He wouldn't stay in the band.
What album was that, Butter? Do you remember?
Masterpieces by Ellington.
Wow.
A beautiful album. Three extended versions of Mood Indigo, of Sophisticated Lady, and -- Mood
Indigo, Sophisticated Lady, --
Oh, that's quite adequate for me, but if you want to name the rest of them.
Uh-huh. Anyway, --
Yeah.
-- we had the extended version and Billy Strayhorn played piano solos on there.
What were the guys like in the band? How did you get along?

I got along with them beautiful. I'll get along with anybody. You know, Milt, just like I said before, if you live with love in your heart, it -- you know, people will know. I never had a minute's trouble with nobody.
Well, how was the band in general amongst one another?
Oh, that was a fun -- that was a weird scene.
