So, Butter, what were you saying? It was a weird scene?

Yeah, it was a weird scene because sometimes the guys would sit on the bandstand and they wouldn't say nothing to each other, especially in the saxophone section. They didn't hang out together or anything. The trombones were always close. The trumpets were -- Ray always, he was a loner.
Ray Nance, that is?
Yes. And Al Killian was a loner, by himself. Shorty used to hang out with anybody that was available that wanted to hang out. That's where Shorty Baker was at, you know?
Uh-huh.
He just liked everybody. And Lawrence was a very quiet type of guy.
Sophisticated.
Oh, definitely, definitely. Here was a guy that used to shave with two razors so his face would be really clean --
Really?
-- because he had a heavy beard. He would --
How did he do that?
Well, he would shave with a safety
razor and then he would finish it off with a straight razor.
Wow.

Yeah. A very neat guy. I think Lawrence used to let the cuffs down his pants and dust them out at night even, you know. He was very immaculate, very immaculate. A very clean guy. He -- But he wasn't a guy that you could kid with or nothing, either. Of course, sometimes Tyree used to get to him.
Tyree could get to anybody.

Sure, and Ben. Ben could get to him because, you know, Ben nicknamed him Sweety Brown because of him being so nice and always so neat and everything, and he kept this sponge in his pocket, Lawrence did, to wipe his face off all the time, you know, so that there would be no shine on his face. And Ben Webster nicknamed him Sweety Brown.
Oh.
(Laughter.)
Yeah.
Hey, just for the record, again, Butter, Quentin, would you just name the band, this particular band you're talking about, the members of that band? What year was this about?
Well, this is -- Well, when Ben came back in the band, it was 1949, and I gave you the personnel then.
Oh, did you?
Yeah. But, of course, when he first nicknamed him Sweety Brown that was back in the early forties, --
You're right.
-- the '41 band when Wallace Jones was in there and Rex Stewart was in there and Cootie and --
You weren't in that band, were you?
Oh, no, no. Whoever thought that you would ever get in that trombone section?
Well, I was there. You're right.
With Lawrence Brown and Juan Tizol and Tricky Sam? No way.
Yeah, that was a no-no.

That's right. No trombone player. I used to go up there to the Hurricane so I could even just sit in. When we played the Strand Theater I used to go out there after the last show so I could sit in Tizol's seat.
That was a fantastic band, wasn't it?
Oh, my goodness.
Name that band, Butter. What year was that that you're talking about? 19 -- ?
Oh, about 1942, '43, when they played the Hurricane. It was before we went in the Zanzibar across the street.
That was a giant Duke Ellington band.
Well, Otto Hardwick was there. He hadn't left yet. And, of course, Harry was there.
Harry Carney.
And, of course, Ben had left then.
Ben Webster?
He had left then. In '43 he had left. But Albert Sears was there.
Al Sears. Tenor sax?
Jimmy Hamilton hadn't left. Chauncey Horton was in Jimmy Hamilton -- the chair that Jimmy Hamilton later took. Chauncey Horton came in when Barney left, Barney Bigard, you see.

And, of course, the trumpets was Rex -- Taft Jordan had come in the band. Taft was there, Rex Stewart; Ray Nance was there and Shorty. Shorty had come in the band. He had come out of the Army and was in the band then. And at that time Lawrence was on vacation so Sandy Williams was playing in Lawrence's chair, you see.
Uh-huh.

And that's when I first got a chance to work with Sandy, and, really, you know what Sandy -- Tricky used to tell me all the time, you know, -- Tricky had a real high voice -- he said, 'Gee whiz, when are you going to give me a break? When are you going to sit in my chair, man? You
sit over there in Tizol's chair all the time." I told him, I said, "It'll never happen. I'll never try to play -- I'll never be able to grab that plunger. No, no." And where did I wind up?
Right, and you're --
With the plunger.
-- the only one that ever really replaced him.
Yeah. Well, I tried, you know, because I had all the records, you see. It wasn't that hard because I heard every note he played. I knew all his solos, in fact.
Uh-huh.

So when I joined the band and I started to playing the plunger, all I did was take Tricky Sam's style, actually, and relax it, you know, and try to bring it up to, you know, make it a little, you know, more relaxed.
Except you got closer to the "ya-ya" than anybody did.
Well, that was the sound, that was the sound that you wanted.
I know, but Tyree was in there and he played the plunger his own way which was great and sounded marvelous, but it wasn't a "ya-ya." It was "wa."
Well, I know, I know. Well, you see,
I heard Tricky make "ya-ya."
Yeah.
So naturally I'm going to try to duplicate that sound because it was the nearest thing to what I thought Ellington would want.
Yeah.

Then, you see, when I first came in the band, Duke told me, when I started to playing, he said, you know, he said, "Let's not play this too pretty." He said, "Tyree played a little bit too pretty." He said, "Let's not play this too pretty." He said, you know, "This is folklore."
Oh, beautiful.
You see?
Yeah.
And I knew what he meant.
Right.
It was all -- every piece of music he wrote, you know, was black music.
Right.
It described the black man, whether it was a pretty black man or whether it was a sad black man or whether it was a happy black man. His music described it.
Or a beautiful black woman or a sad black woman?
Oh, definitely, uh-huh. And then, you
know, he liked colors. He was a frustrated artist, you know, and 'Black, Brown, and Beige.' And he wrote 'Transbluency.' He wrote 'Mood Indigo.' Those were all colors, you see.
Colors.

And he wrote 'Turquoise Cloud' for Kay Davis to sing, you know. But anything the man wrote, I'm sorry, there's nothing you can say about it. He was in a class all by himself. The man could take blues and make a symphony out of it, because there was more 12-bar choruses in that book, but when you heard it it really didn't altogether sound exactly blues. There was composition -- descriptive music. Everything in there it described somebody's life or described a happening. It was all descriptive music, you see.
And he would know just which man to pick to give him the solo to play that he knew they would describe it like he wanted it described. That's what kind of a creative mind he had, you see.
Right, right.
And that's what made the band so fantastic. It was just -- any, any -- every band while I was there, even when they changed men -- you know, in 1951, we went through a big change in the band.
Uh-huh. What was the change?
Well, Johnny Hodges left to get his own band. We was playing the Thunderbird out in Vegas at the

time and I noticed that Juan Tizol, I see him come back stage and talk to Duke, you know, because he had been with Duke from 1929 up until about '44. He left the band in '44 to go to Harry James. So I knew they was very good friends because he used to do all the Duke's copying and everything and, you know, Tizol wrote a lot of tunes in that book, too, you know. Tizol had quite a few tunes in there. He was the co-writer of 'Caravan'. He wrote Pyramid. He wrote 'Conga Brava'. He wrote 'Fiesta in Blue' and 'Perdido'. So he and Duke was very close.

So I saw him come back stage and I said, 'Now, something is funny here because Johnny's leaving,' and Sonny Greer was gone with Johnny and Lawrence left to go with Johnny. So they didn't send all the way back to New York for a trombone player, they sent to Los Angeles because it was close to Frisco and got Britt Woodman. And at that time Claude Jones had came back. He had came back to the band, but Jones was juicing again -- and we went to go out to the microphone to play 'Mood Indigo' and Jones knocked over a whole stand of music and everything going to the microphone, you know.

So we went on to the Oasis, the club in Frisco -- and, by the way, when Johnny left we sent to Kansas City and got one of the Douglas brothers. They were saxophone players in Kansas City, good saxophone players, but it wasn't really what Duke wanted.
And we had Charlie Smith come out to play drums.
Well, Charlie Smith was a nervous wreck, and Duke's band liked to have run him crazy because he didn't know what to do.
Charlie Smith from New York?
Yeah, yeah, yeah. The little lefthand drummer.
Yes.
And he started to getting juicy -- the band liked to have run him crazy and he never was right after that, I don't think.

So we played the Oasis and we went across the country till we got to Omaha and played a theater concert. I looked up and here is Louie Bellson, and Charlie Smith is telling us goodbye and the Douglas brother, they sent him back to Kansas City, and here's Willie Smith and here is Tizol and they sent Jones back home.
Wow.
Phew. Wow.
Louie Bellson brought a couple of his arrangements and he brought the Hawk Talks with him, --
Right.
-- and he brought the drum number with him, you know.
Yeah.
And -- a couple of little things he wrote, you know. And that band started to tightening up, and

when we got back to New York we went to Birdland, the first time we ever played Birdland. Procope went down and told everybody down there, he said, "All right," he said, "you've been listening to this jive you all playing here, this be-bop, whatever you call it. Come down here tomorrow night and get a lesson." You know how Procope --
Yeah.

You know, Symphony Sid never played any of Duke Ellington's records, you know, at that time. He never played Louie Armstrong. He didn't play Duke Ellington. He would play Bird Byrd. He would play Diz, Sarah Vaughan, and people like that.
So Birdland was packed and jammed that night. We opened up in Birdland and the people went crazy down there.
What year was that, Butter?
That was 1951.
Uh-huh.
We opened up down there -- we had finished the Biggest Show of '51. No, it was 1952. What am I saying? It was '52, because we had did the Biggest Show of '51 and we had come off of that. It was 1952.

And we -- the people -- when Duke let us play what we wanted to play, and we didn't do nothing but swing all night long. That band was fantastic. And the band had tightened up just like that by the time we got back to New York and played

the one-nighters. Willie was tight in there and, of course, Tizol knew the band anyway. And Louie Bellson was cooking, he was cooking. He had taken a lot of the arrangements that he didn't know or he figured he didn't know, he would take a first trumpet part, the first trombone part, and the first saxophone part and take that music home and make a drum part so he could play it right, and he did play it right.
That's beautiful.

And that night in Birdland he went into that double-drum thing of his -- and some of the other fellows, you know, our brother drummers, they got mad because they figured he shouldn't be with Duke, you know, and he was making them look bad, in a way, which he was, to be truthful. I have to tell the truth.

Then we lit into Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue, and that was the first time that Duke told Paul to go out and play some choruses. People were standing up screaming in Birdland. And Symphony Sid got red as a beet, dirty dog, 'cause, you know, it was all against his,--
Yeah.
-- you know.

And the next day you could hear it all the way out to Long Island. People was talking about that opening in Birdland. And we -- the band was something else. The guy just stood there and just looked at us when we come off the
bandstand and he said, 'Well, I can't say the word,' he said, 'Well, I'm a so-and-so.'
Yeah.

He looked at us, you know. And from that night on that was it. The band cooked. But it changed the style a little bit when Louie Bellson came in to play drums and Willie Smith came in and Duke let him make a few arrangements, you see, --
Sure.
-- because he is a very good musician, you know.
He's excellent, and the nicest human being in the world.
A beautiful person.
The nicest human being.
A beautiful person. Everybody loved him, all over, you know. So he stayed with the band quite a while until he met Pearl -- Louie Bellson, he met Pearl. Tizol introduced them in Washington.
Is that so?
That's right. Because Pearl used to live at Tizol's house when she would be in California.
Uh-huh.
But Louie used to stay at Tizol's house, too, but they never met. They never run into one another.
Right here in Washington where Pearl is from?
That's right. And that's where they met. So we got back to New York and we was playing the Paramount Theater and I looked up and Louie was getting ready to go to London to meet Pearl to marry her.
That's beautiful.

That's right. That's when he left the band. We sent and got Dave Black. But we lost Willie Smith out in California. He left the band. He went to join Billy May. And that's when we got -- for a while we had Porter Kilbert for a while and got Hilton Jefferson.
Oh, yes, that's right.
Hilton Jefferson came in, and that's all they wanted. They really wanted Jeff in there.
Right.
And, you know, Procope liked Jeff, too, because he and Jeff played together in Fletcher's band for a little while, you see.
Yeah, they're all New Englanders and Easterners.
That's right. Yeah.
And Jeff's wife was sick and Jeff didn't want to stay away on the road.
I know, and then Jeff hurt his leg, you
know; he fell off of a bar stool. His foot was hooked around the bar stool and he kind of broke his ankle a little bit, and so he had to come home, too.
Oh, boy.
And his wife would fake these heart attacks, --
Right.
-- fake these heart attacks so that he would come home.
Right.
You know, he'd get scared to death and he'd say, "Well, I have to go home."
That's right.
You know?
Then Bill Graham. He was in there for a while. But Bill Graham, he had everybody drinking his wine, so Duke thought he'd better get rid of him.
(Laughter.)

He'd have everybody drinking Thunderbird. They had a word around, you know, "What's the word? Thunderbird. What's the price? Thirty twice. Where do you cop? At the liquor shop." They had a whole verse to it.
So then, after Bill Graham left, then he got Rick Henderson out of Washington.
Uh-huh. What did Rick play?
Rick played alto. He come in that year.
Let's hold it up for a second just to take a breather, then we'll talk in just a minute.
Oh, wow, we have to stop now?
Okay, Butter, go right on. What were you saying?

So we got Rick Henderson to play alto, come in the band to play alto. He was a good saxophone player but he was influenced by Charlie Parker. So when he came in the band, Procope took quite a lot of the lead over.

Rick made a couple of good arrangements, and it was a funny thing, you know. Rick Henderson played one way but he wrote another. Now, he played be-bop saxophone to me but his writing was rather on the commercial side, you know, and to me it was an oddity. But he made good arrangements, but I don't care who would make arrangements in that band, Duke would take it and tear it apart, you know, --
To get the sound.

-- which he would like to -- which he did, rather -- not like to, he did with his own arrangements a lot of times. You would start out with letter A and you're liable to jump over to D, maybe to F and then back to B and down here to G and back up to A, you know, and finish you out like that.

So I asked him one day, I said, "Gee whiz, Edward," I said, "why do you want to cut up an arrangement like that? It sound good the way we played it the first time down?" He said, "Well, I didn't like the continuity."
Ah.
So that's the reason he would change it, you know, because I would ask. If I wanted to know, you know, I'm very inquisitive, I'll ask, you know.
That's the reason you had such advancement.

Yeah, just like I asked Billy Strayhorn once about -- I heard the saxophone section play a thing and he had Harry Carney playing up above the tenor for a few bars and then, all at once, he dropped him below the tenor, you know, back down on the bottom. I said, "Sweet Pea," I said, "I heard what you did then." He said, "Now," he said, "now, Butter," he said, "now," he said, "let's not do this," you know.
(Laughter.)
What was --
Because I was copying to him, you know, because --
Sure.
-- Sweet Pea, he was such a phenomenal writer, too, you know.
Yeah, tell me about him, just so that
we can right. How did you feel?
Billy Strayhorn and Duke Ellington to me was the greatest musical marriage that has ever come about.
Uh-huh.
There are times -- you know, the only way that you could tell the difference between their writings was that Billy Strayhorn had more tenderness than Duke, you see.
Uh-huh.
He was a very tender little cat. He was quiet.
He was a delicate, small man.
That's right.
Hold it. There's the telephone. Excuse me.
[PAUSE]
So tell us about --
I was speaking about Billy Strayhorn --
Billy Strayhorn.

-- and Duke. Sometimes, you know, the arrangements in that book that sometimes Duke would start it out and he'd write a chorus or a half maybe, a few more bars, and he'd give it to Strayhorn and tell him to write something over it. And then Strayhorn would write it and he'd get tired and he'd give it back to Duke to make the last chorus. And somebody would say, 'Well, gee, who made that arrangement,' you
know. How are you going to say who made it?
You couldn't tell by the continuity?

But it all fit in, you see. Only the guys in the band would know, you see, that would know, guys that played the arrangements every day. And when Duke got Billy Strayhorn, I think that was one of the greatest things that ever happened to him, --
Uh-huh.
-- that time because --
How did he get Strayhorn? Were you there when he got Strayhorn?
Oh, no, no. He got Strayhorn in '39.
Uh-huh.

He got Strayhorn in Pittsburgh. Strayhorn wanted to write for the band and he brought some things to Duke and Duke liked it. He liked it and he kept Strayhorn with him and Strayhorn was a big help to him later on. Strayhorn arranged a lot of hits. He wrote a lot of hit tunes in that band: 'Chelsea Bridge,' the 'Passion Flower' for Johnny Hodges. I think he wrote Daydream. A lot of pretty things. I think he did write --
Was there another thing of his (humming)?
Oh, yeah. Oh, there was so many things in there that he wrote, so many pretty things. I named Chelsea Bridge, didn't I?
Yeah.
And, of course, the theme song, 'Take the A Train', was his.
Yeah, and that hard --
'Lush Life'.
'Lush Life.' That's what -- the one I was thinking about.
'Lush Life.' 'Lush Life' was a very controversial piece of music, --
Like what?
-- a very misunderstood piece of music.
For example, how?
Well, if you listen to the lyric and it tells you about living the lush life in some small town, you know, and about going to the gay spots?
I see. Well, it might have been controversial for that time but in these days -- that was so much ahead, I mean, the --
Exactly.
-- gay life is a normal life now. I mean, everybody's entitled to -- Of course, in Strayhorn's day it perhaps was being very daring to speak of that sort of life.
It was, it was, it was.
Even though Strayhorn could probably perhaps be associated with that, --
Exactly.
-- and he was expressing his opinion that there shouldn't be any -- I can see what you mean by controversial.
Yes.
But in this world today where we're seeking freedom for everyone, everybody should be entitled to be whatever you want to be.
Exactly, and do what he wants to. I think -- I've always --
It's amazing that you say that because I never -- Being a bass player, I don't think I've really ever heard those lyrics.
Who wrote the lyrics?
He did.
Oh, no wonder.
Oh, yes, yes.
And Duke was daring enough and broad-minded enough in that time to do that. Isn't that amazing how far ahead this great man was?
Oh, so far ahead. And, of course, I can tell you too, there was some titles on some of the music in that book that you better not put on a record.
Uh-huh.
But we knew. We used to laugh, you
know.
Sure.
But later on they would put the title on a record that, you know.

I wonder if the people in the gay -- the gay people that are so well recognized and respected now, do they know about how this fantastic man, Strayhorn, felt about his life and how daring he was to write this magnificent piece of music and still name it.
Well, I think, to me, he was so far ahead of the average person, gay or not gay, intellectually, till they just -- I don't think they really realized or picked up on it really.
Well, maybe in years to come when people will begin to research Duke and his associates that they will become aware of this pioneer --
Yeah.
-- of freedom.
Because Strayhorn never made himself obvious at all.
Never.
Never. He was the perfect gentleman and he always was around the ladies. The ladies loved him.
And the gentlemen loved him. I know I loved him dearly.
Oh, sure, sure.
I loved him dearly.
That's right.
He was just a very delicate, sensitive man, a magnificent artist.
I think Ben Webster nicknamed him, too, Sweet Pea.
Sweet Pea.
Yeah. He was so little, you know. I think Ben nicknamed him, you know. Well, what are you going to do? I loved him. I used to hug him every time I saw him, you know, because --
And this great album that Duke wrote called "And His Mother Named Him Bill."
Oh.
I have that album.
Well, you know, I A and R'd that date.
Is that so?
Yeah, he had me come to A and R the date because I knew all the -- you know, I knew all the music.
Sure.

I knew where the saxophones was supposed to be brought up, I knew where the solos were. So he told me, he called me and said, you know, because at that time I wasn't playing, and he said, "I want you to come and A and R
this date." Of course, -- That's beautiful.
-- they didn't put my name on the record, you know.
But that's beautiful.
And the last tune that he ever wrote was on that record. Johnny Hodges played it.
That Strayhorn ever wrote?
It was the last tune that he wrote.
What was it?
He was in the hospital at the time and he wrote a tune that Johnny performed on that record called 'Blood Count'.
I have the album.
Play 'Blood Count' and listen to that. That was the last thing he ever wrote. Remember that.
Wow, I surely shall.

Yes. And I had a ball that day and that's when Duke asked me why didn't I go play the fender bass, because he knew I played bass. He said, 'Why don't you get a fender bass? You can't play the trombone now.' He said, 'Why don't you get a fender bass and come with me?' I said, 'I don't have one.'
Oh, I see.
What a beautiful man, you know, at
that time when I --
What a beautiful relationship.

Oh, beautiful. And I used to just -- you played that music and you became so engrossed in that music, you became very engrossed in that music. That's the reason I memorized like I did. I never had to open my book. I never did. Once the valet left my book in a town and Duke said, "Can you play [ ]?" I said, "Go ahead and play." I remembered every arrangement in there.
Butter, what year did you get sick in the band and what was the occasion? What happened?
When I got sick?
Yeah. Were you with Duke or you had left?
Oh, no, uh-uh. I was here in New York.
Oh, I see. Who were you --

I had been playing the Americana all the time, the Copa. I had done two Broadway shows. By then I had done Fade Out, Fade In. I had done Gigi Jeanmaire when she was over here from Europe. It was a fantastic show. And I was playing bass at [ ]. I was playing behind different vocalists. And I was recording (2 left.) I was doing the rock and roll scene too, you know.
And I had this growth on my neck and I said, "Well, I'd better have it taken" -- she, my wife discovered it -- I'd
better have it taken off, she told me. I went to New York Hospital and they took a biopsy and everything and I had to have an operation.
Uh-huh.
So I went --
It was nonmalignant?
Oh, no, it wasn't malignant at all. No. So I went to Atlantic City and played with Melba Liston. She had a band up there, for Kim Weston.
A trombonist, trombonist.
Yeah, a great trombonist, too.
Right, and arranger.

Yes. And Kim Weston, she -- so Melba had the band for Kim Weston. I went up there. So when I came back the doctor I thought would be in town, I would have this operation. Instead, he was out of town. I didn't know when he was coming back and I was supposed to go in the Americana Hotel for four weeks and I turned it down, you know. I could have made the four weeks.
Wow.
I was supposed to go in there with Tony Martin and a girl singer -- oh, gee --
Which shall remain nameless.
Yeah.
Carry on with your story.
Yeah, so I was supposed to go in there for those four weeks and so I went on and had the operation and then I wasn't able to play anymore --
Uh-huh.
-- because it made my face like someone with cerebral palsy -- not cerebral palsy. I mean, oh, gee, Bell's Palsy.
Uh-huh.
Yeah. It made my face like that, so I wasn't able to play until 1969. That was 1966.
Do you think it was a mistake, an accident of the surgeon or it's just an unfortunate thing?
I think it was an unfortunate thing. I don't think it was an accident of the surgeon because I've talked to different doctors since then and they said not to blame him.
I see.
I talked to doctors up at St. Vincent Hospital, the surgeons, and they told me that I shouldn't blame him because that type of operation was very tedious where you have to go through the nerves.
Uh-huh.
Now, he went through all the nerves in my face and he tried to knit them all back together.
And he missed one, huh?
Well, no. I think he missed more than one, you see. But, thank God, I'm able to play again.
Because of your -- what do you call it? Rehabilitation and your strong will to want to --
Oh, no, no one would stop me. No one could take my music.
You're absolutely indestructible, Butter.
Well, I have to play. I have to. I've been playing since I can remember. I'm not going to stop playing music. Kid Ory played when he was 80. Who's he?
That's right.
You know?
And I saw you in the condition with your face all turned around and we had just such great sympathy and fighting for you and to see you overcome this great thing.
Yeah.

And when you -- we couldn't really believe it. It was like a miracle and knowing the strength of a man like you. Here we called you a super sideman because of your strength and your great ability to play, to play all of these orchestras. But to see you physically super like this, I can't tell you how much inspiration you have given to the rest of the musicians.
Uh-huh. Well, I had to, you know.

There was times that I was working at an anti-poverty program up in Harlem with the kids up there called Harlem Backstreet Youth. And there was times I'd come home and I would catch my wife, Jackie, I would catch her out and I'd sneak the horn out and I would hold my finger on this side so that the air wouldn't escape when I was blowing. I would blow --
from the right-hand side of your mouth?
-- and hold my horn down in g to make position so I could blow because with it closed like that, I could blow, you know.
Yes.
And I'd set the horn back in the case. I didn't let her know, you know, that I was doing this because I didn't want her to see --
Yeah.
-- to see me, so Benny Powell was a very dear friend of mine. We was in Basie's band together.
A trombone player?
Oh, yes.
Right.

Yes. And Benny Powell come by my house one night and he said, 'I know you haven't had your horn out of the case.' He said, 'Let me play your horn.' So a friend of mine, Dickie [Cohen], was playing the piano. So I went on and instead of handing the horn to Benny Powell, I went

on and played the tune. And Benny's mouth dropped open, my wife, Jackie, shed a few tears, you know. And I went on and played the horn like that. So Benny told me he was playing with a piano player, Duke Pearson, over at the Vanguard, so Benny told me, he said, "Look," he said, "I'm going to have a record date." He said, "You go over there and take your horn and just sit there and hold it. You don't have to play," you know, "if you don't want to or don't feel like it." He knew very well I wasn't going to sit there and not try to play a note.
So I went on and I played, did the best I could. So finally Benny had me do it, you know, a couple of times for him again, a couple of spots. And I called Tony Bennett, talked to Tony.
Oh, you knew Tony, huh?

Oh, definitely. I had worked the Town and Country with Tony, and I don't know how many times I worked the Copa. So Tony told his contractor, he said, "Call Quent to come on down here to the Waldorf." He said, "We know his condition, but I just want him here," you know.

And he called me and I went down to the Waldorf and I sat there -- it was kind of rough at first -- but -- Wayne Andre was there. I think Freddie Zito was there, and Bill, he just came in town to do that show.
Bill Ellerton?
Yeah, Bill Ellerton was sitting beside
me. A beautiful guy.
Isn't he an amazing man?

And all the trombones -- Tricorico Chicarice, Soldo tenor player, and all the guys in the band, Joe Salda, they told me, "We're with you." They said, "We know your condition," you know. They said, "You know we're with you." They said, "You just go ahead and play the best you -- as good as you can and we'll understand."
What an inspiration that is.
Was it? To have guys with you like that?
From the top to bottom, like a guy like Tony Bennett to give you that chance.
Oh.
When people tell you that there's not kindness and goodness in the world --
Tony to me is one of the most beautiful persons -- he's a very human person, --
Right.
-- you know?
The same to me.

And behind that, that December when the Waldorf closed for the winter, when it came back to February, the Charlie Terry combo called me to be in the house band. He said, "I want you to play in the house band," he

said, "because a lot of the guys don't want to play the dance music." And I said, "I don't mind. Sure I'll play." And I played in the house band then up until September '73 when the Charlie Terry combo went out. And he even let me off to go to Russia with Thad and Mel and I came back and still had my job.
That's beautiful.

You know. And it was a good thing for me to play that dance music because I knew all the tunes, and sometimes I didn't even use the trombone parts. I would make up a baritone part with the bass trombone.
Yeah.
And all the guys, they love that in the band because they didn't have nobody else before that to do these kinds of things.
That was qualified to do such a thing?

Yeah, yeah, and I used to always make up a fourth part and they'd turn around and grin and smile, you know. And the Charlie Terry combo told me that I had a job there as long as he had the band there.
Isn't that nice?
Uh-huh, uh-huh, yes.
That's amazing.
So from then I went on back to playing again, you know.
That's beautiful.

And Thad Jones got me to go back to the tenor trombone. I was playing bass trombone all the time, you know, during all the recording sessions and all that because there was no good colored bass trombone players around yet.
Uh-huh.

Jack Jeffers was just coming on the scene and Benny Powell was still with Basie. He hadn't come off the road with Basie yet, you know. And I was the only one, actually, playing bass trombone. And I had a ball with it. And I practically learned that myself, too, but Tommy Mitchell taught me a lot, Bart Varso (ng), I would ask him a million questions when I saw him about the horn, and Tony Studd was my greatest teacher.
Tony Studspinski. [Studspinski], yeah.
Is that his right name?
Yeah.
I never knew.
Tony [Studspinski].
Oh, he's great. I'd tell him today --
A very marvelous man.
Oh. [PAUSE]
So you were saying about these -- the goodness of musicians and especially trombone players and the great Tony Bennett and how he gave you an opportunity to sort
of revamp yourself and how everybody -- Joe Saito and Tony Studd and Wayne Andre and you recalled many others that --
Uh-huh. Well, do you know, to me there's two instruments in the band that they always seem to be close to one another. Trombone players have always been close to one another and so have bass players.
Always, bass players.
Those two. They are always close to one another.
Always close.
They always love each other, --
That's right.
-- you know, and Tony Studd taught me how to practice, how to form my lips so I would get a rounder sound, and told me how to attack and everything. Tony taught me all these things.
Is that right?
And I tell him all the time, 'I thank you today,' you know. And Tony Studd to me is one of the all-time great bass trombone players.
Right, he is, truly.
There's only about -- well, my favorite bass trombone player, actually, is George Roberts, you know.
Uh-huh. I don't know him, but if you say so.
You don't know him? He's the bass trombone player of California. He does all the recordings with everybody.
Oh. I've heard him. I've heard his sound.
Oh, isn't that beautiful?
Yeah, I've heard that. Lots of records and recordings.
That's right.
Yes, I've heard that.
Oh, yes, he's --
I just didn't know him by name.
I've met him. I've met him. He's a fantastic bass trombone player.
Yeah.
And they record him like he wants them to. He's not a blasty trombone player, so he makes them put the mike where he wants them to put it, they tell me, that he can demand this.
Well, I like the way you play, too, Butter.

Well, you know, I've always been a melodic trombone player to a great extent with the exception of when I get that plunger in my hand. Then my mind goes filthy. It gets soulful then because I like blues, too, and

if you played with Duke Ellington any length of time, you will know to play the blues. Of course, I've always liked the blues anyway; regardless of being a melodic trombone player, I liked to listen to anybody that played the blues if they could play the blues. To me Johnny Hodges was the greatest blues saxophone player. Outside of being a melodic saxophone player, he could get filthy too.
How did he get that name "Rabbit"?
His size. His size, like a little bunny rabbit.
Bunny.
Yeah, a little rabbit. I think Ben Webster, I think, nicknamed him that, too, I think.
Ben Webster had a quality of nicknaming people.
Oh, sure, he did.
He named Cab Calloway "Twist"? Do you remember that?
Yeah, uh-huh, uh-húh.
And these things sort of stick, you know?
And he called Basie "Groundhog." And I can understand that, too.
(Laughter.)
Being a dear friend of mine and one of the great men that I worshipped, I don't ever remember having,
him having any nickname for me, so he would always refer to me as 'Yo.' 'Yo,' just like hello.
Uh-huh.

"Yo." So maybe somewhere along the line, I'm not photogenic at all and perhaps he couldn't see any, nothing photogenic in me, so he just said, "Yo," like when he tapes -- we correspond by tape and he always starts his tape, "Yo."
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
But that's amazing.
Oh, yes.

Since you're speaking about that, you might speak something about Ben and this great creativeness of him. He almost started a whole new jazz language. Remember the things he used to say, jazz -- the way he spoke? If he asked you for a hundred dollars, you remember what he would ask for if he wanted to speak of a hundred dollars?
No, I never did.
He'd call it a cow.
Oh, yeah?
$50 was a calf. If it was $150, he would say, 'A cow and a calf.'
Oh, wow.
And a quarter was a [ ], --
Yeah, I know that. I remember that.
-- and 50 cents was a lion.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
And a dollar was lion two 2.
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
This creative man had all of these kind of way of nicknaming and setting up an entire new language --
Oh, definitely.
-- we could use.
Sure.
A girl was a "soft."
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
A white guy was a "gray."
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
But I want to get along with your story. I just wanted to --
Well, you know, back in McKinney's band we had a language similar to that --
Uh-huh.
-- that we called Synguadny.
Yeah, that's right.

Uh-huh, and ladies we used to call -- if a girl was an ugly chick, we called her a "bear," and if she was a nice-looking chick, we would call her a "tweed." And if she was a real beautiful chick, we would call her a "period," because that would be the end of the sentence. You know, you
couldn't no farther.
You can't get any further than that.
Yeah. And we used to call -- like we would talk about their legs? We used to call them "gams."
"Gams." Right.
You see. You know, later on the guys called them "reeds."
Yeah, gams, yeah.
And different things like that, you know. We won't go any farther.
(Laughter.)
[Daniel] was what you sit on.
Oh, definitely. Oh, yeah, that was your [Daniel], yeah.
What you sat on was your [Daniel].
That's right, and --
That's beautiful.

Oh, beautiful. We used to just -- and Basie's band, too, had a name, too. We called -- if we played a dance and played a colored dance, in Basie's band you would call, all the colored chicks you'd call "Jane," and the black cats you would call "John Thomas."
Janes and John Thomas?
That's right, yeah.
And a very square cat we'd call a
[done]
Oh, yeah, oh, yeah.
He was so unhip.
Oh, yeah.
That's so --
Oh, you had these things handed down, you know, from band to band. The kids today, you know, they have a language going, too, different things.
Uh-huh.
Well, now, you were in Duke's band for quite some time. Unless you want to speak some more about that Duke Ellington band, and we could go Oh endlessly about that.
Oh, yes, yes.

Now, the band stayed like that until we got to -- we played the water show in 1955. We played the water show out in Flushing Meadows. That's where they had the water show during the World's Fair both in the thirties and this last World's Fair. And we played a combination water show and ice show with Duke's band.
Now, Paul couldn't work that -- he couldn't work that water show.
That's Paul Gonsalves?
Gonsalves. He couldn't --
Why?
Because he was not a member of the New
York union at the time.
Oh, I see.

Britt Woodman couldn't work it because he wasn't a member of the New York union then. And they got -- for some reason or other they got Ray Nance to work it, you know. Shorty Baker couldn't work it because he wasn't a member of 802 yet. But -- so I had to play first trombone. Rick Bert Henderson couldn't make it because he wasn't 802, so they used a lot of guys that -- Ward Sillaway was the contractor out there and Ward used a lot of guys that had been formerly with the Waring band. He used Virgil Davis -- we used to call him Stinky Davis. He used Virgil Davis on the alto. Of course, Harry Carney couldn't make it and Russell Procope couldn't make it and Jimmy Hamilton couldn't make it. And he used a guy named Johnny Culp on the other tenor. Johnny Culp used to play in the band at the Stork Club and he was an insurance salesman on the side, see? And they used a violin -- they had a violin section. They had two harps. One of the harpists became a jazz harpist later on. Her name was Betty Glaymon.
Oh, yes. I know Betty very well.
That's right, yeah. Remember she played with Oscar for while when Oscar Pettiford had a little band?
Right.
And the other girl, I forget her name.

She passed on. And the drummer passed on also. Now, we played the water show for I forget how many weeks it was, maybe eight or ten weeks. I liked the job because if it rained you didn't have to -- you'd come out there and report and go on back home. You didn't have to work. So when we finished the water show that's when Johnny came back in the band. Johnny Hodges came back and we didn't have a drummer with us and that's when he got Sam Woodyard, you see. And, of course, Britt came back and all the regular guys came back in the band, you see.
That's beautiful.
Well, when did you leave the band?
I left the band -- Oh, there's more I want to talk about the band.
Good, go right ahead.

Because this band was so fantastic. I want to talk about the concert we did at Newport in '56 which to me was history. We had 10,000 people there and I never seen people go crazy. That was the night that we did "Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue and Paul Gonsalves went out there and played 27 choruses. By the time we got to the end the whole place was in mayhem, 10,000 people.
Oh, boy.
A chick got up and come out to the front and started to dancing right out of the audience, and
she started to dancing and Joe Jones was there that night and he was standing down in front of the bandstand beating with a newspaper, beating time on there and hollering at us.
Oh.
That's right. And after it was over --
What was that? The Newport --
The Newport Jazz Festival.
What year was that?
Uh-huh.

And four guys got cut, too, we heard, you know. And George Wein come up on the bandstand and he was white as a sheet, he was so scared, and he told Duke not to play anymore. You know, he wanted Duke to stop, but he should have never tell Duke not to do nothing. You don't tell Ellington 'never.' If you don't want him to do anything, don't tell him not to do it. Tell him to do it, see.
Right.
Duke wouldn't listen to him and he went into a drum number. Went into a drum number that night even after that.
And that was mass hysteria then.
That was -- Right. -- and that was beautiful. And the concerts we played in Europe after that,
every one of them was -- the people just would lord over this man.
Yeah. Now, that's the band in 19 --
From 1955 on, when Johnny came back.
Who's in the band now?
Willie Cook came in the band for a while and Clark Terry and Ray Nance and Cat Anderson.
Wow, what an addition.

And John Sanders and Britt Woodman and myself were the trombones, but the trombone section to me was impeccable. Clean. I don't care, anything we played it was clean. We don't care what the other band -- how good they played or how bad they played. We always played good --
You did your part.

-- because there was a lot of love there between Britt and John and I, you know. And our tones blended. The sound of our horns blended together. We used to play unison things and we'd be so together it would sound like one horn. You couldn't tell it was unison, That's how the intonation was.
The same breathing and everything.
But when Sam Woodyard came in that really lifted the band up again. We'd been sitting out there playing that water show and everything was -- you know.
Uh-huh.

And Sam Woodyard come in there to play drums, and Sam had every record that the band made. He didn't even have to think about playing the music. Now, we had the drum number in the book, 'Skin Deep,' that Louie Bellson wrote, and Duke asked Sam, he said, 'Woodyard,' he said, 'can you play 'Skin Deep?' He said, 'Why, sure,' and we went and lit into 'Skin Deep,' and breaks and everything, solo and everything, he ain't missed nothing.
Oh, that's beautiful.
That's right. And from then on that was it.
Who was the bass player then?
Jimmy Woody.
Jimmy Woody?

Yeah. Jimmy Woody was the bass player. And there was a couple of times that Oscar come back and played in Jimmy Woody's place, too, out there in Long Island. Now, what's that place out there, on the hill out there? I know you have played out there. Stony Brook.
Oh, yes.
Stony Brook. Oscar come out and played with us one night and that's the first time I heard a speaker on an upright bass that sounded like that.
Yeah.
I think Oscar said he paid $400 for
that speaker. He had it made. And he come in that night and played with the band and we played Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue and Johnny Hodges marked on his stand, "Paul played 36 choruses."
Wow.

And Oscar was walking in so -- him and Sam back there -- and when Paul finished, he just turned around and he looked at Oscar Pettiford and he just fell down on the stand and laughed. He just laughed.
(Laughter.)

And we came off the bandstand, Sam Woodyard looked at me and he pointed to Oscar Pettiford and said, "You see there?" He said, "He lays it right in your lap." He said, "He lays it in your lap." He said, "So what are you doing to do?" That's what Sam told me. That's how Oscar played with him so.
Yeah. That's beautiful.

There's some beautiful stories about that band, too. We played the Graystone with Stan Kenton and that band swung all night long. They took us out of the ballroom and put us in the garden and the people were screaming when we finished there. And Stan asked his band to leave and they wouldn't leave. We was playing the last set. And we swung all night long and we didn't play the greatest thing, "Diminuendo and Crescendo", till the very last tune. We didn't even need it.
Wow.

And I knew that the band was going to swing that night because when we was dressing out there in the bus to go in the ballroom, Sam Woodyard spoke up and said, "Look," he said, "fellows, we're going to put the pots on tonight." I said, "Oh, oh." I said, "Oh, oh." So we did. He put the pots on. Yes, he did. And when Stan was trying to get his band to leave the cats were looking at us with their mouth open. They wouldn't even leave to go out and get in their bus, they were so astounded, like everybody else in the Graystone was astounded. Anybody that would want to play against Duke Ellington's band would become astounded, because I've seen this band sometimes they would get lax, just like any other band, you know, --
Sure.
-- and wouldn't play, but don't push them. Don't push them. My dear.
The game's over then.

They would fire up like nothing you ever heard in your life. And Duke would sit there and whenever you could see him with that frown on his face and he would start to humming that one tone, the band was knocking him out then and he was very pleased.
I've seen him with his head like this.
Oh, yes, oh, yes, yes.
(Unintelligible.)
And he'd get to hitting that piano and hitting them chords all in the middle, all in between.
Yes.
One of the greatest -- to me one of the greatest accompanists, for a jazz soloist, and he would hit a chord to let you know exactly where you was or where he wanted you to be --
Right.
-- and you would play that change. He knew where you was at all times.
Do you ever think there will be another, anybody like him again?
No.
I doubt it --
There never has been and there never will be, not in this life, not today.

Now, we've got an arranger now to me that is -- as far as making arrangements to me is the greatest arranger today, as far as I'm concerned, in jazz music, that comes almost up to that, and that is Thad Jones.
Thad Jones. Right.
Thad Jones is to me one of the greatest arrangers today. But Thad will -- he doesn't believe in being a politician, so that's --
He (Unintelligible) stays up.
He stays -- Yeah.
Well, Duke wasn't really one, either. He just --
Well, he didn't have to be because he had his own band and his band was at a caliber and he had enough years behind him that he wouldn't have to do nothing but play his music.

Except when you look at the annals of America and commercialism, that in all the annals of Duke Ellington, all the songs he wrote, he never really had a television show and a guy like Lawrence Welk had one for 24 years, you know.
Well, there goes that thing again, you know, that keep you in your place still, regardless, you know.
Yes, that's what I'm saying.
And that's the American way.
It's unfortunate that --
It is unfortunate.
-- a man like this, even in his death, he's been honored with so many great honors and so many doctorates, but to the mass media -- I mean, we eulogize great people.
Oh, yes. Do you remember they wouldn't give him the Pulitzer Prize, and he deserved it if anybody did.
So he answered them beautifully. He said, you know, he said, "I don't think they want me to become too famous too young." And how old was he then?
Oh, man, I loved this man.
We can't forget him.

Oh, I'll never forget him as long as I live. And I tell you something else about the Duke Ellington band. That band, if you've ever been in it, is a disease. I don't care who you play with, who you have played -- or who you have played after, you'll never forget it.

I was playing with Basie and we did an album with Duke's band, called the First. And I was in Basie's band but I was paying more attention to Ellington's band, and Ellington's band didn't play as good as I wanted it to and I got mad as a sonofagun. And I was with Count Basie, you know.
Butter, you weren't at the Bandbox when we played with Duke, were you? I was with Basie then. 1953?
I was with Duke then.
You were with Duke? I was with Basie then.
Sure. That's right.
And we played at the Bandbox.
That's right, downstairs and Basie come up and told Duke, "Now, look, man, come on now," he said,
"I'm trying to have my band now. Don't shoot me down." He come over and told Duke, he said, "I'm trying to build my band now," you know.
Yeah, wasn't it great to hear these two great bands playing together in one place?
Oh, yes. Oh, yes.
And the crowd receiving and respecting each one of them for their individual talents?
Oh, yes, definitely, definitely. Well, you know, they were great friends of one another, you know.
There's no question.

Oh, yeah, you know, they were great friends of one another, Duke and Basie was. And Basie always spoke well of Duke, you know. They was telling Basie once on the air, they said how great his band was and how great he was and everything out there in Chicago, I remember, on television. And Basie spoke up and he said, "Well, what about the master?" And they asked him, "Who? What do you mean, the 'master'?" He said, "Duke Ellington. That's who."
That's right.

You know? That's where he was at and he was right. He was right. Do you know, after leaving that band and you go to any other band and you play their music, do you know that their music felt mediocre? It sounded mediocre
to you? After hearing different chord structures that Ellington wrote, it was so far ahead of the time, --
Right.

-- and different mixtures that he wrote, you know, using the valve trombone like he did with the saxophones for certain sounds. And like playing the plunger, he wrote the backgrounds behind me playing the plunger that I just couldn't have played like that with anyone else because it still gave me a certain feeling that made me play, that I had to play and would play. Because in the first place the inspiration of the music behind you was so beautiful and so fantastic and fit the scene of what you was trying to describe, so that you would describe it.
He could make somebody realize that even if he just walked in.
Exactly, exactly.
That's beautiful.

So when I left the band, I didn't leave the band on account of because I didn't like the band. I left the band because I was tired of traveling and I left the band in Europe to go with Quincy Jones because we had a show called Free and Easy and Sammy Davis was supposed to be the star of the show had we had our full run in Europe and come back to the United States. And I knew that if Sammy Davis was going to be the star of the show, I would be in New York for a year, two
years, you know, --
Right.
-- with any show that Sammy was with. But we stayed over in Europe.
What year was that, Butter?

That was 1959. I left him in October and Quincy came over in November. So Clark and I left at the same time. You know, Clark, he used to say all the time, 'I'm going to -- I'll bet I'll be here -- I bet I'll leave before you will.' I said, 'No, you won't.' So we wound up leaving together. And we stayed over in Europe until Quincy came and that's when I made a little record that --
[ ] recorded?
Uh-huh. And Clark worked in the Chat qui Peche Shocky Pairs. Clark worked in the Shocky Pairs until Quincy came.
What's the name of it?
Chat qui Peche Shocky Pairs.
Where is that?
A little club on Rue de la Houchette.
In Paris?
Yes.
Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Right around the corner off of Place St. Michel.
Uh-huh.
So we waited till Quincy came, and we knew when Quincy would get to Brussels. He came to Brussels because that's where we rehearsed the show.
Uh-huh.
Quincy had a very good band, a very good band.
Tell us something about it. I remember that band. Jerome Richardson, --
Well, the trumpets -- the trombones, rather, was Melba Liston, Jimmy Cleveland, and we picked up AAKE PERSSON Okie Pearson, a Swedish trombone player.
I see.

A very good trombone player. The saxophones was Shahib Shahib on baritone, Phil Woods on alto, and Porter Kilbert on the other alto, and Jerome Richardson on one tenor and flute, and Budd Johnson on the other tenor. And Joe Harris was on drums and Buddy Catlett was on bass.
Catlett, right.
We had a pianist. Patty Bown was the pianist. Les Penn was the guitar and he played flute, see.
Right.
And Lennie Johnson was one of the trumpets and Benny -- Benny used to be with Lionel Hampton.
Oh, a little short guy.
Very heavy-set like.
Oh, yeah?
He's in Europe still.
Oh, is that so?

He plays on radio in Geneva. And a trumpet player out of Seattle, he doubled on saxophone. So we always had four saxophones. At times we had three flutes because Shihab played flute, Jerome played flute, and Les Spann, you know. But it was such a good band. You know, we memorized the show?
Just two trombones? You and Melba Liston?
No, no, four. I told you Jimmy Cleveland and Ake Persson.
Oh, that's right. Oh, yeah.
Uh-huh. And Fred Standifer was the trumpet player that doubled on saxophone. Benny Bailey.
Right.

And we used a Swedish trumpet player. I can't think of his name right offhand. You know, that's been years ago and I haven't seen him since. We used him for the other trumpet, for the four trumpets. Now, we rehearsed in the World's Fair site in Brussels where the World's Fair was. We rehearsed in the

American theater. It had been the American theater at the World's Fair. We rehearsed the show there and each section used to go in the room and we used to take a sheet of music and we would rehearse it and memorize it. The trumpet section would go in a room and they would memorize and the saxophone section used to go in another room and they would go over the music and memorize. And we used to see who could memorize first. Then we'd all take it out and play it together. And we memorized the whole show that way. We didn't have no music stands anywhere on the stage. You should have heard that.

And the saxophones used to sit on one side of the stage, trombones would sit on the stairway on this side, the trumpets would be in the back, and the rhythm section would be almost by the trombone section. And people said it sounded like stereo out front.
That's amazing.

And Quincy was the only one -- the first one to do that and the band was onstage without no music and playing a whole Broadway show. It was a Broadway show. It was a takeoff from 'St. Louis Woman,' --
Right.
-- you see? It had all the Harold Arlen tunes, you know, 'Rain or Shine' and all those beautiful tunes.
Uh-huh.

And so the show closed when we got to Paris, so Quincy asked the guys in the band if they wanted to stay together. We said sure. So we stayed together. We toured all over Europe. We played the folk parks up in Sweden for the summer and when Nat Cole came over to Europe we did his tour with him. When the Platters came over, the singing group, we did the tour with them. And we just worked over in Paris until that September and we came back. We came back to New York, and when we came back to New York a certain booking agent was supposed to have work for us but that didn't happen. They didn't even know in New York that Quincy had a band, and it was a shame because it was such a good band, such a good band, good music. Quincy made the arrangements. Billy Byers made a lot of the arrangements. Benny Golson had some arrangements in the book. It was a good book.

Only thing that we found out about the band even though it was a good book and everything, there was not enough individual style for you to associate the band with having a style, you see. That was kind -- a little, kind of little bad, too, you see. A band has got to have a style.
Yeah, right.

And so then when I came back -- while we were still in the United States we did a picture for a Swedish film company called The Boy In the Tree and that was the last thing I did with the band. So I'm sitting in my room,
I had just been to the union to collect my check for that picture, and Snodgrass, he was the manager for Basie, come up to me and --
Henry Snodgrass.

Yeah, Henry Snodgrass. He was the road manager for Basie. Basie was getting ready to go over to play a job in Camp Kilmer. So he told me, he said, "You know, we've got to leave in about 15 minutes. Can you make it?" He said, "Al Gray said he's not going," you know. So he said, "You want to make it?" I said, "Yes." I said, "What can you wear?" And he said, "Well," he said, "we're going to wear -- if you've got anything brown, put it on." I had everything in blue, and you should see me undressing and changing clothes in 15 minutes to make the bus. I did. I made the bus.

And, of course, I had played in Al Gray's place before in Basie's band, you know, and played the plunger. So I went and played the job there in Camp Kilmer and I told Basie, I said, "Gee whiz," I said, "it's nice to play with you again," you know. He said, "I enjoyed it." I said, "I guess my man will be back tomorrow night," Al Gray, you know.
Uh-huh.
(End of Proceedings as recorded.)

I was telling you about how he --
you about Basie's band?
Yeah. So -- Are you ready to go now?
Yeah.

So I told Basie that 'Sure, I'd like to stay with the band.' And he wanted to know whether I wanted to join the band, and I told him 'Sure.' And we talked money and the price was right for me at that time, the price was right. So I said, 'Sure.' So I stayed.
I stayed in that band. That was the day before Kennedy's Inauguration Ball.
Wow. What year was that?
That was 1960 -- about 1961.
You're so sharp on years.
It was January 1961.
Wow.
Because I came back from Europe in September '60, you see?
We had stayed -- I had stayed over a year, actually, just about a year because I left Ellington over there in October of '59 and stayed over there with Quincy until September '60.
Uh-huh.
So, anyway, we went the next day and

played Kennedy's Inauguration Ball. I had to go get a tuxedo and everything and I rushed to get a tuxedo from Howard right down the street from the Albert Hotel, and went the next day and played at the Kennedy Inaugural Ball, you know. And I stayed in the band.
We went from there to the Latin Casino, you know.
Uh-huh.
In fact we went to -- Yeah, Latin Casino, that's right. And from there on I stayed with the band. And to me that was a very -- that was a phenomenal band. man.
Outside of the '43 Calloway band, which you know was one of my favorites, --
Sure.
-- Basie's band was the most consistent playing band I've ever played with, --
Uh-huh.
-- for every night they played. When you hit that bandstand, every living played.
(Inaudible.)
That's right. Of course, you know Basie is a tempo genius.
And he's a master.
Yeah.
People -- Elucidate on that. You know,

I was in the band for a short spell, a few weeks, but I never in my entire life knew of anybody that could set tempos. I don't think the public is aware with this low-key man that's just sitting at the keyboard what a master he is at setting tempos for dancing.
That's right, that's right.
Explain that, Butter.

You can't because this is such a natural thing there's no explanation to it. The man had such a natural feeling to play dance music and for swing and for tempo. He had such a natural feeling for tempo there's nothing that you can say about it because it's just a natural thing with him, which a very, very, very few bandleaders have. Very few.

You know what I found in the band when I played with Basie for the few moments I was there? That he seemed to be able to judge the audience, how they felt that night. He might not even play the same tune at the same tempo tomorrow night, but it will be just the right thing for that crowd that night.
Exactly.
And how can you account for a thing like that? This is almost impossible to explain, and I think very few people --
Feeling, feeling, feeling. Natural
feeling.
Natural feeling.
The man had natural feeling for people, too.
For people, the relationship.
He didn't get out and socialize much.
No.
He never did. And then he had a man there sitting with him --
Oh, Freddie Green,
Mr. Metronome.
That's right.
And whenever you --
Rhythm Willie.
Oh, my goodness. Oh, my goodness. He's beautiful.
Yeah, too much.
He is beautiful and he'll be there as long as there's a Basie band.
And I think [handwritten insertion] rightly so.
That's right.
Well, you see, Basie's band is the only one that really kept a guitar, and it's a funny thing. You know, to me a guitar adds something to a rhythm section if it's a good guitar.
It's the arteries of a rhythm section.
That's right.

You could say like the drummers are the heartbeat and you could say like the bass is the pulse and you can say like the guitar is the arteries. If you can take out the human anatomy and put the whole thing together, you know, -- and the piano's the veins that leads to the whole thing if you want to put it into the human anatomy.
Uh-huh.
But it's so necessary. It just solidifies and settles everything, a good rhythm section.
Uh-huh, uh-huh. Yeah, there's very few good, really, really good rhythm guitar players to me that's been in the business. When I say good rhythm guitar players, that sit down and chunk.
Yeah.
Holiday was the greatest that I've ever heard. Billie Holiday's father.
Billie Holiday's father, yeah.
He could hit -- but you could hear all six of those strings, though.
Yeah.
You could hear those strings when he -- and when he would, say, chung-chang, chung-chang, chung-chang, he'd lift you up out of your chair.
(Laughter.)
That's right, and he'd turn around and say, 'All right, let's go,' you know.
Beautiful.
And, of course, with Big Sid drumming you didn't need to really say it, you know, because that big shoulder of Big Sid would come up and down like that, you know.
Yeah.
But --
As big as he was, he could play so delicate and just everything in the right place.
Uh-huh.

Yes, and to me there's a white boy that is an unsung hero to me as far as playing rhythm guitar is concerned that people don't even talk about him, because he doesn't really play anymore anyway. He's got a copying service now. He's Sam Herman.
Sam Herman.
Sam Herman can play some rhythm guitar.
Right.
I remember when he was with Tommy Dorsey.
Right.
That was a very tight rhythm section --
Right.
-- for that type of thing.
Right.
And --
I also remember Barry Galbraith who was a fantastic --
Oh, yeah. He was another one. Oh, yes.
-- with Claude Thornhill. Oh, what a great rhythm section.
Oh, yes. Well, you know, Don loved him, you know. Don had Barry Galbraith --
I loved him, too. I'll love him forever.
-- on every record date he made. Every record date Don Redman had, if he could have Barry, he'd have Barry there.
That's right. I remember when a few years here in New York Hank Jones, Osie Johnson, and Barry Galbraith and yours truly was considered the New York rhythm section.
That's right.
What a magnificent player.
Oh, yes.
Like Sam a great man, too.
Oh, yes, uh-huh.
That's beautiful.
Yeah.
So Basie's band had the personnel. Now, I'd like to talk about the personnel in that band, too, --
Right, right.
-- because the trumpet section was so phenomenal.
Right.
Snookie Young to me is one of the unsung first trumpet players, lead trumpet players in the business.
Rightly so.
I think he's one of the greatest first trumpet players in the business. He's been doing the Tonight Show for how many years now? And he --
I don't remember. Doc Severinson is quite aware of it and loves him dearly.
Oh, definitely. Oh, sure. He's playing with Doc's regular band. He plays first trumpet with Doc's regular band now.
And we had -- Thad Jones was there.
Beautiful.
Sonny Cohn is a beautiful trumpet player from Chicago.
Right.

And we had Albert Aarons. He came in in Joe Newman's place. He stayed in California. What a beautiful trumpet player he is, too. A very nice guy. All of them were nice fellows, every one of them, in that band. And the trombones was Henry Coker --
Oh, yeah, we can't forget him.
-- and Benny Powell and myself. I think Henry Coker to this -- he's still with Ray Charles.
Is that so?
Uh-huh.
What a master. He's come through all of the things we've come through.
Yeah.
Henry Coker.
And the saxophone section, they were monsters. They were monsters. Had Marshall Royal to me is one of the greatest first alto players in the business.
He's a general.
Oh, definitely. And Frank Foster and Frank Wess. What are you going to do with that?
Right.
What are you going to say about those two players?
That's right.
And Frank Wess played alto and tenor
in the band where sometimes they had three tenors.
And a [raise].
Yes. And Charlie Faulkes was sitting on that end. He's an old standby, you know.
That's right.
He'll be there, and --
that baritone saxophone.
That's right. And when I joined the band Budd Johnson came in. Billy Mitchell was leaving and Budd Johnson came in.
Oh.
Forget it.
And Sonny Payne -- Mr. Personality -- he was the drummer then, and Big Ed.
Oh, Ed Jones on the bass.
Ed Jones. Yeah, he could pull some strings too, you know.
Oh, he's a powerful, powerful bass player.
That's right.
Cant miss him, every beat is just right there.
And I loved that band. I loved that band and I stayed with that band for a year and nine months, and the only reason I left that band was because I still
wanted to come off of the road.
That's right.
I just got tired of the road. That was the end of my 33rd year on the road. I left my home town in 1929 and this was 1962, September. I had been on the road 33 years and I thought that was enough.
Yeah. I can understand that.
And every band that I was with played one-nighters with the exception of Calloway. Six of the years with Calloway we didn't do one-nighters. I don't think we did over 30 out of a year.
That's right.
We did nothing but theaters and clubs, you see.
That's right.
So I think I had had enough and so I said I'm going to stay home. I'm going to stay in New York and I'm going to get into a recording thing, play some night clubs around and see how I can do.

And Clark Terry, the beautiful man that we spoke about a while ago, got me to come to Jim and Andy's. I didn't know who to talk to, who to go to, or nothing. He got me to come around to Jim and Andy's and meet some contractors.
Beautiful.
And he got me to go to Radio Registry.
Wow.
Clark was the cause of that. And I got to know Jim Kulavares
Oh, yeah.
He's a beautiful man, beautiful man.
What an Angel, the savior of musicians, an owner of a nightclub, of a bar called Jim and Andy's.
Uh-huh.
Jim Kulavares was the owner and Andy was the cat, captain
Yeah, I know. I know. That's right. It's true. And do you know, Jim at one time was a contractor, too.
Oh, yeah, sure.

He was a contractor and he still was. A lot of times people would call up there for musicians and say, 'We need a drummer,' and Jim would look over the crowd -- or 'We need a bass player' or 'We need a trombone player' -- Jim would look over the crowd to see who was there and call over to one of the trombone players or who he thought would make it and he would go ahead and make it.
Many times.
You know?
Let's see. How many musicians got gigs
Oh, gee, a gang of musicians. And it was a good -- like food, it was good food in there.
Yeah.
And Jim -- a lot of musicians owed Jim, too.
Oh, yeah.
A lot of them, you know, that --
He would let them have money to go away.
Yeah.
And most of them when they -- the honesty musician really showed himself. I know Jim, he had a heart attack right back of the bar, --
Uh-huh.
-- and a great deal of musicians came up to his wife later and said, 'I borrowed this amount of money from Jim,' because there was no record for it.
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
Then he'd say, 'I was paying him back $5 a week and I wanted you to know.' And if they hadn't said that, Mrs. Kulavares wouldn't have known what that money was.
Oh, definitely, because he never kept a count. No.
I remember Ben Webster left to go to Europe, to Copenhagen, on one of them -- and it took him a
couple of years, but Ben sent every dime. I can assure you that he sent every dime back to Jim Kulavares.
Well, I'll have you know that when I first started out in New York, and I didn't have no gigs around then, you know, because I didn't know what to do, he loaned me a hundred dollars.
Wasn't he beautiful?
Not only one time. But the minute I got it I went right back and gave it to him, you know.
It made it good (would) for all of us because who knows when we need the money, you know.
Oh, yes.
But I can the honesty of that. That goes back to like the people did the same thing for Mr. Collins back from Harlem on Seventh Avenue and 127th Street.
Oh, another good place to eat that we didn't mention.
Yes, right.
And Mom Baker, too,
That's right.
But musicians owed Mr. Collins when he died, though, because a lot of them had rooms. You know, Don Byas used to room up there.
Right. I used to room there. I had a room there one time.
Oh, you did?
Sure.
Ah.
We had no place else to go.
Uh-huh.
$6 a week and 50 cents for my food.
Gee whiz.
That's right.
At the Woodside I was paying eight and a quarter a week.
Yeah. Tell us about the Woodside. We haven't talked about the Woodside.
The Woodside was one --
That's where Basie and --
-- of the greatest hotels, one of the greatest hotels in the country.
In Harlem.
And nothing lived in there but musicians and pimps and prostitutes.
(Laughter.)
That's all that lived in the Woodside.
Right.
And the Woodside had -- when you come in, on each floor, you could go around one corner, there was a kitchen around there, and around the other corner in the
other part was a kitchen. It originally was an apartment house, --
Uh-huh.
-- but they made it into rooms, and everybody cooked. Nobody went hungry in there --
Right.
-- because you could come by and anybody would say, 'Gee whiz, have you eaten today?' you know.
Something's always smelling good in the hall.

Oh, yes. Basie's band came to New York. They was hungry. And the road manager, he was in California -- I can't recall his name right now, he always cooked beans. He could cook the best beans you ever ate in your life, you know. And I watched them. They went around there -- they scuffled for a good while when they first came to New York. But it's a funny thing, I never seen Erskine's band really look like they -- they might have been scuffling but you never saw it like you did Basie's band, you know.
Uh-huh.

But the Woodside -- and we had a place downstairs where everybody used to jam. The guys after they played the Savoy -- they don't do that anymore, you know -- after they played the Savoy and different clubs and things, after they'd get off in the morning at two or three o'clock --
there was a big room downstairs in the Woodside and you'd see 20-something musicians down there jamming.
Wow.

Drummers would come by, piano players, and, like, the music never stopped because if a drummer wanted to take over, he wanted to sit down, he'd just move over and the other drummer would just sit there, and go ahead and take over, and the piano player would slide down.
Slide over, yeah.

And it was courtesy among musicians. If he was in there and you wanted to blow, if you stomped your foot twice, whenever the guy was blowing then, whenever he finished, then you could go ahead and blow.
Yeah, just like changing partners while you dance. You tap a fellow on the shoulder.
Yeah, that's right.
Yeah.
Uh-huh.
Can you hold it for a minute? Let's let me get the dogs in.
All right. [PAUSE]
Yeah, changing musicians on the bandstand was like tapping somebody on the shoulder to change their dancing partners.
Oh, sure, and, you know, like, now,

Teddy Hill's band would be up the Savoy or Erskine Hawkins' band would be up there, Basie's band would be in town, Don Redman's band would be in town, and we'd all go down there and jam. And it was a courtesy among musicians then, --
Right.
-- you see? It was respect, you see. And still, back in those days, the music business was treated as a profession.
Right.
Guys never got paid for rehearsals or nothing like that. They rehearsed for the love of music and wanting to keep up on their instrument, you see, --
Right.
-- and wanting to know more. And when you played with a big band you did get to learn more because you had a lot more men there that you could listen to.
It was like a school, a regular school.
Exactly, exactly.
Young fellows came in and were associated with older professional guys and they learned this way.

Oh, sure. That's the way I learned when I came to McKinney Cotton Pickers. I listened to all the older guys. I listened to them talk and they took me under their wing and told me where I should go and where I shouldn't go, you know. And you associated with certain people and you
didn't -- and you always carried yourself in a dignified fashion because music was a profession and you treated it as a profession, --
Right.
-- you see? You dressed like a professional man even, you see.
Sure.
You stayed clean and you carried yourself as a gentleman because you was a professional man.
Sure.
And I don't know where that went.
I don't know where it went either, except --
I don't know where it went.

-- when big bands left, there was no place for apprentice young players to come in and be affiliated, because each band, if maybe one guy would go out this year, so a new young fellow could come in and be associated with older guys.
Yes, that's true.
And this would be -- the older guys would give him the stern look where you better take care of it and be cool.
Oh, yes.
And you had to do this.
Oh, sure.
And this is how you learned. This is the way I came into Cab Calloway's band.
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
And it was such a process, it was like a school, like going through apprenticeship, --
Uh-huh, it was.
-- and learning what it was like to be a professional musician from professionals.
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
I guess we don't have enough of those bands around for young people to break in like that.
No, we don't. We don't have enough of them. But from what I can see today there's a lot of kids today that they really want to know, younger kids that are coming up, the very younger kids.
I find that too.
Not the kids that came up in the rock and roll era, the kids that are coming up now. They want to know.
They want to know. They want to know how and why. Where did this come from? And why did it happen? And why it's not happening now.
This is why we're doing this now,

Butter, so that they can see what it was like and what you were like and how you overcame all the difficulties and all of the hard times to become a super sideman, somebody which has never been and may never walk the face of this earth again, a super musician that had the respect of every musician, every band leader that existed.
Well, I appreciate that. But to me, too, you know, when God gives you a talent, you use it. You use it. You do not waste it. And if you use it wisely, He will help you along your way, --
Absolutely.
-- you see? But you have got to use it.
Right.
You don't waste it. You use it when talent is given you and I was blessed with having a talent.
Beautiful.
And I was very lucky, too, with playing with nothing but good bands, you see.
Right.

I would just like to say, in summing up this whole thing, Butter, what advice would you have for young people, young music students that are studying, regardless of where they are or what color or what their desires are and, especially, what advice would you have for all young musicians, and
then, in summation, what advice would you have for those that are seeking to get into this truly great American art form of jazz? Take your time and just elucidate on this.

Well, the first thing that I would like to say to them is, the first thing is to learn the fine points of their instrument. You have to study. There's a lot of work involved to learn the technical part of your instrument so that there's nothing that you can't do with your instrument.

And learn, try to learn an individual style. Now, you can learn individual styles by listening to a lot of other players that have interesting styles that you could take something from. You can take something from anyone that you can listen to. But don't copy, don't copy after any one musician because when you copy after a musician, he gets the credit. You don't, because you'll sound like him, you see. So try to get yourself an individual style.

And study is the greatest thing, and be a good listener. Listen to a lot of sensible music, because by listening to sensible music you can go on further to what you might want to do if you wanted to go farther.
And to non-sensible music.
And to -- Well, yes, yes.
Or classical or whatever.
Exactly, exactly. You can always do

what you want to do.
And there's another thing that I always tell musicians. If they can, please learn the piano. Piano is the foundation of everything and it helped me to learn trombone. Because it can help you with chord structures if you want to write, it can help you writing-wise. You can get a lot of ideas from it. And it's a foundation. So I would advise any kid that has a piano around to sit down and play it and try to learn as much of it as you can.
Learn the keyboard, and to see the keyboard and see the relationship --
That's right.
-- of how a chord is formed.
That's right.
On this particular instrument, keyboard, you can see the structure.
Exactly.
It's so programmed and so laid out that you can see exactly what it's like.
Exactly.

And please have self-respect. Please learn the art of self-respect because by learning the self-respect and by becoming an artist, you will go a long way in this life, and I can tell you that from experience.
Thank you, Butter.
How would you advise them about practice regardless of what instrument? How do you begin practice?
How did I begin practice?
How should a musician begin practice regardless of instrument? What would you think?
I -- first thing, if he's a piano player, he should find correct fingerings. You have five finger exercises, which is a great help as far as the piano is concerned.

Now, trombone. Trombone, you practice whole notes soft. And by practicing whole notes and you practice soft, you can gain a lot of control with your lip because you can feel the notes against your lip, how they feel when you play certain notes on the trombone.
You can feel that vibration.

Exactly. You can feel the vibration. Practicing loud, you have no -- you don't even learn control -- you don't learn the sound of your instrument. Because when you practice soft then you really can listen to the tone of your instrument, you see.
And this goes -- young people or students of jazz or students of music, this goes for any instrument.
Oh, definitely.
One can't play loud and fast and one
can't be --
Uh-uh, uh-uh.
-- one has to sort of -- it should be whole tones. They should start with long whole tones.

Long whole tones, that's right. And then you develop from there. And then as you go along, you can play half steps as you go along. Then you start to playing thirds and then you practice fifths, you see.
Practice scales. Scales can mean a whole lot to you.
Scales and chromatics.
That's right, and practice them slow and then gradually you can speed them up as you go along, --
Right.
-- you see.
Someone said once if you can play the chromatic scale, --
Yeah.
-- you can play anything.
That's right. That's right. You can.
You get all 13 tones.
You can. You can.
