But don't start by trying to learn to play a solo first. Learn your instrument first. Learn the technicalities of your instrument and get your instrument under your fingers.
Then when you go to play a solo you'll find out how much easier it is, you see.

We've been speaking with Quentin Jackson, one of the finest gentlemen in all the band business. He has played for all of the greatest musicians in the world, with the greatest bands, with the greatest orchestras, beginning with -- What was the first, beginning, Butter? Who was the first band?
The first band that I -- the Buckeye Melodians at home to Wesley Helvey's Troubadours to Zack White, and my first big name band, McKinney Cotton Pickers.

McKinney Cotton Pickers, all the way consistently, consistently playing trombone and singing through all of this to right now, here today, the Mel Lewis-Thad Jones band. If you can tell me in this year of 1976 of anybody that can compare with this, I'm willing to listen. Butter, I want to thank you. Quentin Jackson, I want to thank you. I want to thank your lovely wife which we didn't get a chance to talk too much about but which has been such a strong influence and helping you in your life, --
Uh-huh.
-- and we wish you continued health and success. And we know you've been through a tremendous amount of things with health problems but, thanks to heaven,
you're cool again and playing.
Oh, yes, I'm always going to play.
Beautiful.
And I hope, if I can, I will help some kids along the best I can, you know. I'm always willing to help because someone helped me, --
That's the story. That's the my exact feelings
Butter.
-- you see, and it should be passed on.
It should be. That's my idea of what immortality is.
Uh-huh.
If I can pass on whatever I've learned in my way along this world to someone else, then that means that I'll never really be gone, --
Uh-huh.
-- because whatever I've learned I passed on.
Uh-huh.
And when they go if they will pass it on, this is my assurance of immortality.
That's right, that's right.
Hey, Butter, thank you. Believe me, we've done a great many tapes, and if you've got anything else
to say, we'll be glad to hear it. All right. I'm sorry that I didn't get through the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band.
Well, just talk about it. We've got time.
Well, you know, --
Because you've played in this great band. How did you get in the band? Who asked you? Let's get into it.

Well, you know, Thad and I was in Basie's band together. And Thad, he didn't really know -- because I started playing bass trombone, you see, and by me playing bass trombone everybody thought that I had quit playing tenor altogether, you see. So Thad said, 'I want you in my band.' Benny Powell was leaving the band, you know, because he was with Merv Griffin and they're going to California. The show moved to California, the Merv Griffin show.
Right.

So I said sure and he said, 'We've got a bass trombone here.' He said, 'Why don't you go back and play your tenor because people would like to hear you play the plunger again.' So I said, 'Well, okay.' So I went back and started to playing the tenor again and he started to writing some things for me to play with the plunger. And the
Oh, yeah.
And that is a very interesting orchestra. I think Thad Jones has got the greatest, one of the greatest bands today --
I believe it.
-- because it is modern. Yet and still, it is not overdone. It is sensible. And he is a great writer. He writes beautiful. He can write very pretty, and he has a lot of humor in his writing.
That's right.
You can listen to him, to his music, it will make you laugh, you know.
Right.
You can listen to it, it will make you cry. And you can listen to it and relax. And I think he's the greatest arranger today. I still think Thad Jones is the greatest arranger today.
I agree with you. I'm sure he's one of the greatest.
Yes.
He's so creative. How about his conducting which I always admired?
Oh, that is a picture, to watch him conduct, to bring different things out of the band that he
wants brought out. And you have to watch him, you know, because he'll cut you out any time. If he figures somebody's playing a good solo, he'll cut you out.
Yeah, he's quite a unique --
Yes. And then he'll put that hand up and do this. That means you come in; at the end of the next chorus you come back in. You know, when he puts that fist up there.
Sure.
But he can conduct. I love to watch him. I love to watch him conduct. He's a picture.
No question.
And he loves his music, you see. He loves his music very much, and can play.
Oh, he can play beautifully.
Can play. He has a style to me all his own.
Yeah.
Beautiful, beautiful. A beautiful trumpet player and to me he's a beautiful man, too.
The only reason that I'm not playing with that band right now, Milt, is because, like I told you before, I don't like traveling.
Uh-huh.
But anytime I can go sit in that band,
Uh-huh.
-- you see?
Thank you, Butter.
I tell you what. We should touch on -- we've got time.
Sure.
We should touch on your life and your marriages. We didn't get too much into that.
No, you didn't.
I happen to know -- I was there in Cab Calloway's band when you met a lovely lady in Memphis, Tennessee.
That's right. Odessa.
Odessa.
Well, my first marriage, I married a chorus girl --
Uh-huh.
-- out in California. I was young. I was dumb. I didn't know. And this girl was a real fast girl. She was way faster than I would ever think about being.
What year was this, Butter?
That was 1931.
Uh-huh.
And she was a beautiful girl, and I
Uh-huh.
And I was going with another girl at the time out there, too, a chorus girl. And her name was Johnnie Mae Johnson. She became a dancing -- a dancing team, Smiles and Smiles.
Uh-huh.
And so I liked Lucille, --
That was her name?
-- my first wife.
Uh-huh.
I liked her. Her name was Lucille Forby.
Uh-huh.
And Eddie Anderson, who later became Rochester, told me, he said, 'Quent, you don't want her. She's not the right kind of girl for you.'
How did you meet Eddie Anderson?

Eddie Anderson was working in Sebastian's Cotton Club, in the show. He and Johnny Taylor had a pantomime act together and it was funny. This was a funny thing, one of the funniest things you ever saw in your life, that they did. They used to fall all down the steps and slide way out on the floor, you know. But it was all pantomime.

And so Eddie Anderson told me, he said, "You --" -- you know, I told him to tend to his own business. And I went on like a fool. The girl -- it was like a thing where she said -- she took me home, you know, and we made love -- she said, "Let's get married." I said, "Okay." She said, "I bet you won't." I said, "I bet I will." And we went on and applied for the license, like fools.
Uh-huh.

And we had an afternoon wedding out to her house, had an Episcopalian minister and everything, and the pillows to kneel on. And the Chez Norman Grill was a wonderful restaurant at that time and we had an afternoon dinner at the Chez Norman Grill, --
Uh-huh.
-- you know, that the gang at the Cotton Club had given us, you know, and it was really beautiful.
But that marriage didn't last. She stayed in California and she met me, she came to meet me in Detroit and I found out then that this girl was a playgirl.
Uh-huh.
She wasn't for marriage. So, you know, so we stayed together and that was like in June she came -- let me see. September she came to me. And December we were separated.
Oh, boy.

That's right. And so I didn't get married anymore. So I started to hanging out with all the chicks that I could so I could find out about women. All kinds of women I hung out with and I asked a million questions. And I wasn't going to get tied down with anyone, you see? That was September '32 -- no, '31. I didn't see her no more until when I came to New York and joined Don Redman, and I looked at her and I told her, 'Uh-uh, no, no. Uh-uh.'
(Inaudible.)
But I was man enough -- she needed a coat, she didn't have no winter coat. I bought her a winter coat that winter.
Uh-huh.
And she was living with a guy. And so I gave her a bag so that she could go on back to Philadelphia. She was working in a club there, because she was a singer, too. And that was the end of that.
Uh-huh.
So I didn't get married no more until when we was with Calloway's band, I went down -- we played in Memphis, Tennessee --
Right.
-- and Danny Barker and I was staying at this roominghouse.
Danny Barker, the guitar player?

That's right. We was staying at this roominghouse and I saw this little girl. She had a beautiful shape and she looked very neat and nice, you know. Down there in Tennessee them women used to wear those house dresses that were starched.
She sure was pretty. I remember that.
Oh, my goodness. She still looks good.
Beautiful.
And so I sent for her to come to visit me. We was playing Milwaukee at that theater up there in Milwaukee. Remember the --
The Riverside, the Riverside.
The Riverside Theater. And remember we had -- they used to send us barrels of beer back there.
That's right, the brewers.
That's right, and Calloway, man, that was the time he got tore up and Rudolph used to stand in the wings with ammonia pods to put under his nose so he could get back out on the stage.
That's right.
And I sent for her to come there, and then she went on to Chicago with me, and she went back home and both of us stood there and cried like babies because I had to send her back home.
Uh-huh.

So we went and played all the way across the country, and we was in Washington -- I got in a blackjack game and I won $75. So I called up Memphis and told her to come to Boston. I sent her the $75 to catch a train to Boston.
(Laughter.)

So she come to Boston. I'll never forget it. So she told me she couldn't continue living with me, she said. She said, 'I'll have to go back home. I can't continue living with you.' I said, 'Well, I'm going to fix that.' So we got up the next morning and I said, 'C'mon, we're going downtown.' She said, 'What are we going down there for?' I said, 'We're going down to City Hall because I'm going to fix it so you don't leave me no more.'
That sounds like the last story.
That's right, that's right.
(Laughter.)
I said, 'I'll fix it so you don't leave me no more.' So we went down and applied for the license. And we was playing the Southland, the club the Southland, at the time.
Uh-huh.
We was staying at a hotel called the Regent Hotel, I think it was called.
Uh-huh.
All of us was staying there. Tyree was staying there. Chu Berry and a bunch of us. Dizzy and Lorraine, Dizzy Gillespie.

And we came back in town and I'm going to get the marriage license and I found out it was Decoration Day and the city building was closed. I said, 'Oh, Lord, what am I going to do?' So I went by the city building and I found out it was closed, and this man was an elevator man. I told him, 'Please,' I said, 'what am I going to do?' I said, 'You know, I got to marry this girl. I'm going to leave here tomorrow and I've got to marry her now.' I said, 'Please, I need some help. Is there any way you can help me?'
He said, 'Well, I'll go up and look to see if the marriage license is ready. If it is, why, I'll give it to you.' And I gave him $3 --
Wow.
-- to go up there. And the marriage license was ready because the five days was up. You know, there was a five day period.
Right.

And so he sent me -- I said, 'Where can I get married?' And he told me how to go out to this justice of the peace. And we had to take the El, that El up there in Boston, we had to take it out. And the justice of the peace, he was a white guy and he had a white lady there
visiting him, you see, and she was our witness.
Wow.
And he performed the ceremony and we got married right there.
That's beautiful.
That's right.

And Odessa -- Odessa was a wonderful woman. She was a wonderful woman, you know. I brought her from Tennessee and she was a very ambitious girl. She didn't go no further than the ninth grade down there in Memphis, and she started to living in Chicago. She liked to live in Chicago because she had relatives there, you see?
Uh-huh.

So I let her stay there and she went and finished high school there. She sent to Memphis and got her credits and she finished high school there and then she got to be a dentist's assistant, you know. And she worked at that and I used to send the money home just as regular even though I was never there.

And, really, the marriage didn't mean anything to her because I never was home and she didn't like to travel and she didn't like New York at all because she had no friends there, and the only friends that she had there was Tyree's wife and Dizzy's wife. Other than that she didn't know nobody. Her friends were all in Chicago.
Right.
And her family, her aunts and cousins and things. So I let her stay there. That was it. That's where she was at. So this went on like that clear till in the fifties, you know.

Uh-huh.
You were married when?
We was married Decoration Day in 1940.
Uh-huh.
That's right, on May the 30th.
Uh-huh.
And this went on like that until 1955, '56. And I went to her and I told her, 'Gee whiz. You're a good girl. I'm not doing justice to you. I'm not a husband to you. I'm never home,' you know?
Uh-huh.
And 'you should get somebody that's going to be around you all the time because you deserve this,' you know?
Uh-huh.
So 'you go get the divorce papers and I'll sign them,' which I did.
Uh-huh.
And I said, 'I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll pay the rent for you until you find you somebody.
I'll still pay the rent for the apartment." And I did.
That's beautiful.
Clear up to 1960 when I went to Europe.
Uh-huh. And I couldn't send the money any more.
When I come back, this girl has saved all that money and had a grocery.
Uh-huh.
I talked to her. She got a grocery in Chicago called Odessa's Grocery. A guy was going out of business and I think she got it from him for $1,200.
Wow.

And she got her a little grocery store and called it Odessa's Grocery, and she saved her money, because, you know, she could save a dollar. Oh, she could save a dollar. If Odessa was going to save money, she'd hide it and she'd put it away. Now, at times I had seen money that she had hid and I'd say, "Odessa," I said, "what is this? What's this money here?" She said that don't belong to me. Immediately she'd put it away. She doesn't have it anymore.
(Laughter.)
That's a good thought, there.
(Inaudible.)
And so later on the next thing I know she -- today she has a self-service market, you know. And we
adopted a kid --
And you adopted a -- Yeah.
-- and she calls it Michael's Grocery
now.
And you adopted a kid. When was that?
That's right. 195 -- about 1957. Michael was 19 this past March 1956. So 1955, just about, we adopted Michael.
Uh-huh.
And she raised him.
That's beautiful.
And put him through school. He was going to a Presbyterian school, I think.
Uh-huh. That's marvelous.
Yes.
And so from then on I didn't have nobody. I didn't want anybody. I didn't have no lady. I didn't even have a girl friend, actually.
Well, you were moving around so fast.
That's right.
But then you met this lovely lady which you have now, which is just unbelievably attractive.
Well, you know, it's a funny thing about her. She heard me when I was with Don Redman in 1933 and she wasn't but about nine years old.
That's amazing.

Her mother was working in the Bureau of Engraving in Washington and she was down there with her mother from Boston and she told me her mother brought her and said, 'I want to go hear this portly gentleman sing.'
(Laughter.)
And that was me.
That's beautiful.
Then I didn't see her no more until 1947. She had been in the Air Force and she was out and she was -- we was playing with Calloway --
Oh, she was a WAC. What do you call that? Is that a WAC?
She was in the Air Force.
What do you call that?
WAF.
WAF.
Uh-huh.
And the next time I saw her we was playing with Calloway. We was playing Boston.
Uh-huh.
And -- the Keith Boston Theater -- and she was a camera girl up at the Savoy.
Oh, that's where....
That's right. Earl Warren had the

band up there at the time. And I went by to see her and I said, 'Gee whiz,' I said, 'look at this pretty thing. Oh, she's fine,' I told Earle. Big pretty legs and everything, and a beautiful shape. I said, 'Wow.' I said, 'Earle, I'd ask you to meet her.' I said, 'No,' I said, ''cause I know she's got a cat man will kill a rock about her,' you know.
Uh-huh.
Did you know I found out later she didn't have nobody then?
Wow.
And I could have never moved in or nothing.
Then I saw her once up in Maine when we played. She knew Paul, you know, because Paul had played with Sabby Lewis around Boston.
Paul Gonsalves, that is?
Yeah, Paul Gonsalves. And she knew him and she come on the bus to talk to him. She was working up in Maine. She could sing too.
So then I didn't see her no more till New York. She come down to Birdland, and her and Osie C. was great friends at the time.
Right.
Great friends at the time and very close. And he brought her down to Birdland to see Basie's band,
you know, and she come around the back. You know, it used to be, when you go around the back there -- you know, where the band room was?
In the back room there, a little aisle back there.

That's right. Well, I was coming down those steps and she was coming around. She said she was ducking those guys because she had on this beautiful white suit and these guys were always wanting to pat on her when they saw her suit and she got mad. And she come around the back to duck the bar --
Crowd.

-- to come around -- Yeah. -- and she come around the side because some of Basie's wives out of the band was sitting over there and she saw them. But when she was coming around there I accidentally bumped into her and she said she was so mad but she said when she looked at me I have such an honest expression on my face she said she had to smile, you know. So I said, "Wow," I said, "I'd really like to know who she is." I said, "This is a woman." I looked at her and said, "Wow," to myself, "this is a woman." And I knew I had seen her before.
And I seen Thad talking to her so I told Thad, I said, "Look," I said, "introduce me to her." So Thad, "He-he-he," he laughed. He said, "I know. You saw them big legs."
(Laughter.)
And I found out that Thad used to go with her up in Boston way years ago when he was up there and they almost run off and got married once.
Wow.
And Thad introduced me to her. Today I tell him all the time, I said, 'You know, you're the starting of this.'
(Laughter.)
I said, 'You're the cause of this.' And he laughs. You know how he puts that big laugh on.
Right. It's a good cause because --

Uh-huh. And so we became friends. I used to see her and talk to her in front of Birdland. Every time I would meet her, it looked like I'd be standing in front of Birdland or something and she'd always come up and we always exchanged words and we always talked and she gave me her address to come up to her house. But I knew that she was married at the time and I didn't want to go up to her house because if I went up there and I'd look at her, I'd have to look at her funny and I knew maybe her husband wouldn't like it. That's the way I thought.
Sure.
I didn't know how her life was then, and at the same time her and Osie was close. So I would see

her and we would always look at each other. There was always a look. And O.-C., when O.-C. was with her, O.-C. used to catch us looking at each other silent, and O.-C. always used to take her and split.
That's O.-C. Johnson.
Yeah. He'd take her and split.
Get out of there immediately (laughter).
Yeah, that's right. He would.
And she always looked at me and I looked at her, and when she became pregnant I thought it was O.-C. And I got mad at O.-C.
(Inaudible.)
There was a slight animal interruption. My dogs decided to get into the conversation.
That's all right.
So go on.
So I saw her and every time I would see her -- Now, I had never touched this woman. Do you know I'd see her with O.-C. and I'd get jealous. I loved the woman then and didn't --
Yeah, you didn't really -- wasn't aware of it?
No, I wasn't aware of it. I loved her then. So she would -- she got to know O.-C.'s wife very well. And so she told me, she said, "Well," she said, "we're
-- O. G. and I, we're not going to hang out like we did," you know.
Uh-huh.
And so we had a record date up there in our studios and she come up there and she said, "I want to talk to you." Just like that. I said, "Okay." So we went over to Junior's. You remember Junior's?
Yeah.
So we went over to Junior's and I ordered dinner. In fact, I had two trombones because I was playing the bass trombone and a tenor trombone on the date. Osie O. G. was on the date.
Uh-huh.

Osie O. G. was so whipped that night. I think he had been hanging out, too. He went to sleep up there before the date. He laid down out there in the control room. And so then I said, "Okay." So we went to Junior's and she ordered my food for me and saw that my food was right. And so that night I took her to her pad where she lived and I didn't even kiss her goodnight or nothing because I didn't want her to think that I, you know, I wasn't trying to be forward or fresh or nothing. I had that much respect. I liked her that much.
Well, you're that kind of guy, Butter.
Yeah, and I didn't -- you know. So I

told her, you know -- and she'd come over and see me in Brooklyn. I was living over there by myself and I had this apartment that a buddy girl of mine left me with to take care of for her, you know. A beautiful apartment.

So she said, 'Okay, I'll come over and see you.' And it was snowing. It was snowing like everything. And so she took the subway over and I called her and she let me know what time she was going to be, so I met her at the subway. She said she hadn't had a guy meet her at the train since she was a little girl when they used to meet up there at the station up there in Boston. The guys would meet you there where the streetcars came all the time, you know.
And I was standing there and I met her and took her down to my house. I lived two blocks from the subway. And I took her down there and I had that house spic and span. She walked in there and --
Everything was in place.
Oh, yes.

So, you know, life is funny. So I knew she didn't want to go back home in that snow, so I told her I would let -- she could have my bed and I'd let the bed down in front so 'you could sleep in there,' and she said, she looked at me and looked at that bed, she said, 'Oh, no. No. Uh-uh. No, I ain't going to sleep in there by myself.'
And that was the beginning of the year.
So she got in the bed and she slept and everything, and I turned my back. I gave her a pair of pajamas and I slept and I never bothered her. I didn't touch her, you see.
So she didn't go home the next day. She stayed here, and what did she do that for?
Yeah.
That's when everything started. And we talked and so we come to the conclusion that neither one of us had any business being by ourselves.
That's beautiful.
And we've been together ever since, and that was February 15, 1964.
Uh-huh.
12 years we have been together and the most beautiful 12 years in my life.
Oh, I can see that because I never saw two people that seemed to be so concerned with each other.
Oh, yes.
I tell you, you two are truly an example of what a man and a wife should be like.
Uh-huh.
And especially musicians, which need -- art needs for someone to care for us.
Uh-huh. What you --
I can't tell you how much I appreciate seeing this, seeing your deep concern for her and seeing her anticipate your every needs.
Oh, yes. Oh, yes.
I just want to close with that, Butter, because --
Well, I don't want to --
-- unless you want to say something.

There's one more thing I've got to say, that the reason we're like this is because, you see, she is a musician, too. She played violin in a recreational symphony in Boston when she was 15 years old and so I can talk music with her.
This is Jackie. This is Jackie.

That's Jacqueline, yes. And, you see, we can talk music. We test each other's ear, you know, because she had been a violin player, and we test each other's ear. We say what key is it. We'll go to the piano, because we have a piano, and we'll go and test each other's ear sometimes.
Oh, that's nice.
So we have a ball with music and we understand music, you see, and that's the reason that I think that my marriage is like it is, because there's so much understanding.
It is a beautiful --
We're extremely close.
Oh, that's beautiful.
Yes.
Well, unless there's something else you want to tell me, I think we should wind this up.

I think you've done a marvelous job, and I can't thank you for sharing your life with me and the rest of the world that young people in the future might know what a real truly great musician is like and what kind of great obstacles you've overcome in these 40 or 50 years in which you've been in this business and still.

Well, you see, there's only one thing more I want to say, Milt, that there should -- everyone in this world, especially musicians, should learn more about love of their fellow man. And love will also help make you a good musician --
Right.
-- because you will portray this in your playing.
Music is love.
Oh, definitely it is.
Is love.
Definitely it is. And any young musician starting out now, please, learn to love because that will give you freedom of mind, freedom of thought, because
you have no time for any hatreds or any discrepancies of mind.
Yeah, it takes away from your talent, --
Exactly.
-- this time that you spend disliking someone you could be enjoying and playing and --
Exactly, exactly. You can enjoy the beauty of life.
Right.
And that's where it's at.

Well, thank you, and I hope that in time immemorial, in years to come, that your contribution to society, your contribution to music, you contribution to this great American art form, jazz, will be known and will be appreciated by all those who will listen to your oral history.
Thank you, Quentin Jackson.
Thank you, Milton, and thank you for ever being associated with me.
It's been my pleasure, Milt Hinton, all the way.
Good. Thank you so much.
(End of Proceedings as recorded.)

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: Copyright notice and opening of the Smithsonian interview
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright notices, the Smithsonian header, and Hinton's introduction praising Jackson as a complete sideman before asking where he was born.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: Born in Springfield, Ohio; parents and two sisters
segments.summary: Jackson gives his birth date, his parents' names and the names and birth years of his two sisters; he is the middle child.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: Early piano: mother's Etude, prodigy at four, disliked lessons
segments.summary: His mother played piano, he played in church at four, took lessons from several teachers but disliked exercises and learned by ear and school singing.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: Buying a violin and studying with Mark Snyder
segments.summary: At eleven or twelve he buys a violin with his lamp-lighting pay, gets lessons from a Cincinnati Symphony violinist and plays solos with the school orchestra.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: Hearing great concert artists as a child
segments.summary: His mother took him to hear Paderewski, Kreisler, Caruso and other concert artists at Memorial Hall.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: His mother's and father's family origins
segments.summary: His mother came from London, Ohio, daughter of a horse trader; his father came from Danville, Kentucky.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: McKinney's Synco Septet and Claude Jones's advice to take up trombone
segments.summary: He listened to McKinney's septet rehearse; Claude Jones, who married his sister, urged him to take up trombone because good Black trombonists were scarce.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: Learning trombone from the undertaker Elmer Burns
segments.summary: Working for an undertaker, he learns positions from Elmer Burns's trombone and works out his friends' trombone parts note by note.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: Buckeye Melodians and drummer Gerald Hobson
segments.summary: His first band was the Buckeye Melodians at home; later Earl Warren's father took it over, and Gerald Hobson encouraged him with stories of New York.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: Wesley Helvey's phone call and leaving Springfield
segments.summary: Helvey, hearing of him through Hobson, calls the undertaker's office and hires him; Jackson makes sure the Brick crowd sees him leave town.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: Helvey's band, a new Holton and learning from Floyd Brady
segments.summary: On the road to Buffalo he is told to buy a better horn, then learns from trombonist Floyd Brady (Little Stump) in Cincinnati until January 1930.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: Joining Zack White's band
segments.summary: He moves to Zack White's band, with Si Oliver as arranger, a good band but outplayed by Speed Webb.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: Speed Webb's band and its star personnel
segments.summary: Jackson lists Speed Webb's trumpets, trombones, saxophones and rhythm section, including Teddy Wilson, Roy Eldridge and Vic Dickinson, and says he has never played with a sad band.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
segments.title: Hearing every part: playing Tyree Glenn's plunger parts with Ellington
segments.summary: Hinton asks how he learned everyone's parts; Jackson says by listening, and tells how he covered Tyree Glenn's plunger book for Duke one night.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: How he got the name Butter in McKinney's band
segments.summary: Don Redman nicknamed him Butter because he looked tender and plump when he joined McKinney's Cotton Pickers on December 7, 1930.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: Origins of McKinney's band: the Synco Septet and its members
segments.summary: He joined to sing after George Thomas was killed; Jackson recalls the earlier septet's personnel and how McKinney, a drummer, became its manager.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: Jean Goldkette, Don Redman and how the Cotton Pickers got their name
segments.summary: Goldkette hired the band for the Graystone in Detroit and brought in Redman; Jackson praises Redman as an early dance-band arranger and explains the Cotton Pickers name and Victor contract.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: The Kiss Waltz audition and McKinney's offer
segments.summary: Singing a waltz with Zack White's band in Wheeling, he breaks up the dance and McKinney's pianist brings him to McKinney, who wants him to replace Fathead Thomas.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: Negotiating his salary with McKinney
segments.summary: He asks for $50 a week and McKinney offers $60 though the others earned much more.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: Dance hall prices, packed ballrooms and WJR broadcasts from the Graystone
segments.summary: Admission was 50 to 75 cents, McKinney's band packed every hall, and radio broadcasts from Detroit were the best publicity.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: Asking for a $100 advance and the first train trip to Boston
segments.summary: On Clarence Paige's advice he asks McKinney for $100 and gets it, rides a train for the first time, and recalls Zack White's rickety cars.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: First rehearsal in Boston and the band's personnel
segments.summary: He meets Don Redman, names the reed and trombone players then in the band, and plays the second trombone part, prompting Redman's remark that he could see.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: Advice to learn piano first
segments.summary: Jackson advises any young musician to study piano as the foundation for every instrument.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: Making up parts and learning from Redman and Edward Cuffy
segments.summary: With few second trombone parts he invents his own; Redman, who knew every instrument, taught him and Cuffy helped him practice.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: Singing on McKinney records without credit
segments.summary: He sang on three records, but his name was omitted from one 78 where the vocalist is listed as unknown; Benny Carter had replaced Redman.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: Who was in McKinney's band when he joined
segments.summary: He lists the trumpets, saxophones and rhythm section, and Billy Taylor replacing Escudero on bass.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: Learning bass and tuba fingering from Billy Taylor
segments.summary: Watching Billy Taylor, he finds bass fingers like violin and works out how tuba valves correspond to trombone positions.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: Leaving McKinney in 1932 and the personnel shuffle
segments.summary: He stayed until about May 1932; Redman left to form his own band, Carter took over, and Rex Stewart, Hilton Jefferson and others came and went.

segments.chapter: McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's offer versus Don Redman's band
segments.summary: Henderson wanted him on violin, trombone, vocals and piano for $100, but Redman persuaded him to join his own band, where Fred Robinson then resigned.

segments.chapter: Don Redman's band at Connie's Inn
segments.title: Subbing at the Cotton Club and declining Calloway's $90 offer
segments.summary: While Redman's band played, he subbed a week for DePriest Wheeler at the Lafayette and Cotton Club, turned down Calloway's $90, and took $66 at Connie's Inn.

segments.chapter: Don Redman's band at Connie's Inn
segments.title: Connie's Inn: network broadcasts and the club
segments.summary: Redman's band broadcast on CBS and WMCA; Jackson describes Connie's Inn, its floor show, owners and its location at 131st and Seventh Avenue.

segments.chapter: Don Redman's band at Connie's Inn
segments.title: Broadcast setup with the brass on the dance floor
segments.summary: For broadcasts the six brass stood in a semicircle on the dance floor around the old spider microphone.

segments.chapter: Don Redman's band at Connie's Inn
segments.title: First recording in the wooden-box microphone at Victor's church studio
segments.summary: His first recording with McKinney used a single tiny microphone in a wooden box in Victor's converted church; the date was December 18, 1930.

segments.chapter: Don Redman's band at Connie's Inn
segments.title: Redman's three-trombone section and learning lip vibrato
segments.summary: Redman had the first three-trombone section; Claude Jones and Benny Morton taught Jackson lip vibrato in section rehearsals, and he praises every trombone section he played in.

segments.chapter: Don Redman's band at Connie's Inn
segments.title: Why he left Redman: the Cleveland New Year's job and joining Calloway
segments.summary: Redman's band declined; after an unpaid New Year's Eve job in Cleveland he came back to New York, leading to Calloway's band in January 1940.

segments.chapter: Don Redman's band at Connie's Inn
segments.title: The Woodside Hotel and the arrival of Basie's and Hawkins's bands
segments.summary: Living at the Woodside Hotel, the Black musicians' hotel, he saw Basie's band check in from Kansas City around 1936 and Erskine Hawkins's soon after.

segments.chapter: Don Redman's band at Connie's Inn
segments.title: Erskine Hawkins's band and its head arrangements
segments.summary: Hawkins's band made up its tunes among themselves, such as Tippin' In and Tuxedo Junction, though credit was disputed.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Calloway's offer at the Adams Theater and the uniform tailor
segments.summary: Chu Berry tells him Calloway wants him; at the Adams Theater in Newark Calloway hires him, and the band's uniforms come free from the tailor Carnik.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Joining Calloway in Springfield, Massachusetts and the trombone seats
segments.summary: He joined on January 8, 1940, replacing DePriest Wheeler, with Tyree Glenn taking Claude Jones's place after Jones and Calloway quarreled.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: The Calloway trombone and reed sections he joined
segments.summary: The section was Keg Johnson, Tyree Glenn and Jackson; he lists the trumpets and saxophones, with Hilton Jefferson replacing Chauncey Houghton.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Lip vibrato versus hand vibrato in the trombone section
segments.summary: Hinton recalls the section persuading Tyree Glenn to use lip vibrato; Jackson explains Glenn could never play a dead tone, and that Ellington disliked brass vibrato outside solos.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: The Calloway rhythm section and Danny Barker
segments.summary: They name the rhythm section of Bennie Payne, Hinton, Cozy Cole and Danny Barker and talk about Barker's tune and later career in New Orleans.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Section rehearsals and Redman's rule to follow the first man
segments.summary: Calloway was not a technical musician, so the sidemen rehearsed sections themselves; Jackson recalls Redman's advice to phrase with the lead player.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: The Calloway saxophone section and good times with Dizzy
segments.summary: Jackson names the saxophone section and recalls how much fun the band had with Dizzy Gillespie.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Cooking in RKO theater dressing rooms because of segregated restaurants
segments.summary: Because the band could not eat in white restaurants, they cooked backstage in the well-equipped RKO theater kitchens and dressing rooms.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Calloway traveled first class: uniforms, shoes and discipline
segments.summary: Calloway paid for five sets of uniforms and shoes and required cleanliness; the gentlemanly discipline made weaker new men straighten up.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Calloway as a disciplined leader and Buster Harding's farm system
segments.summary: A band is no greater than its leader; Calloway demanded discipline and kept replacements ready through arranger Buster Harding.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Songs Jackson sang with Calloway and Bennie Payne
segments.summary: He sang popular ballads Calloway did not want to do, took over Bennie Payne's tunes after Payne left, and remembers Payne's friendship.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Franz Jackson's arrangement for two basses
segments.summary: Franz Jackson wrote a number for two basses and Jackson and Hinton played it together, Hinton on three-quarter bass and Jackson on the big bass.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Chu Berry's influence and the Benny Carter arrangements
segments.summary: Chu Berry influenced Calloway to bring fresh music into the band, including Benny Carter arrangements like Change Partners and Dance.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: The Chu Berry automobile accident near Youngstown
segments.summary: On the road to Toronto the bus came on Lamar Wright's overturned car; Chu Berry was injured with a skull fracture and was delirious.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Chu Berry's pipe and watch
segments.summary: Hinton produces the pipe and watch he picked up at the crash scene and recalls Chu's delirious words about his change.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: How the crash happened
segments.summary: Brown, unused to the fluid-drive car, braked into a skid and hit a bridge; Chu Berry was thrown clear and, delirious, hit a doctor at the hospital.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Chu Berry's death and the minute of silence in Montreal
segments.summary: Chu died days later; Calloway waited until after the dance in Montreal to announce it and hired a replacement.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Calloway as entertainer who could count the house
segments.summary: Jackson and Hinton credit Calloway's entertaining gift; he could feel a crowd and tell within ten how many were in the house.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Reel Two opening, trombone posture, and a turn to personalities
segments.summary: Reel Two begins with a remark about Reinhardt's seated posture for breath control, and Hinton proposes discussing personalities of their era.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton on the corner and his boogie-woogie story
segments.summary: Jackson listened to Jelly Roll Morton telling stories at 132nd and Seventh and recalls his claim that boogie-woogie was New Orleans race horse music.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson as a quiet leader
segments.summary: Henderson was a milquetoast leader whose men were habitually late and he said nothing.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Hearing Fletcher Henderson's band in Cincinnati in 1930
segments.summary: Jackson calls it the most fantastic band he had heard and lists its trumpets, trombones, saxophones and rhythm section with Kirby, Walter Johnson and Clarence Holiday.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Hearing Duke Ellington's Jungle Band in Cincinnati
segments.summary: Passing through from the Check and Double Check film, Ellington's small-sectioned band played all original tunes; Jackson lists the men and discusses the jungle sound.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Rhythm Club instrument nights and cutting out strangers
segments.summary: At the Rhythm Club, instrument nights drew players, and newcomers who boasted were put in their place by Carter, Hodges or others.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Art Tatum arrives at the Rhythm Club with Fats Waller
segments.summary: The blind Art Tatum came to the Rhythm Club with Adelaide Hall's group and Fats Waller gathered the pianists; Jackson had earlier heard him in Toledo.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: What the Rhythm Club was and where it stood
segments.summary: It was a place for Black musicians to eat, drink, play cards and pool, on 132nd Street in the same building as the Lafayette Theater.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Seventh Avenue as a boulevard
segments.summary: Seventh Avenue was a beautiful promenade, immaculately dressed and peaceful, while rougher people lived near Park Avenue.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Lenox Avenue clubs: the Savoy, the Cotton Club and the Saratoga Club
segments.summary: He names the clubs on Lenox Avenue, including the Saratoga Club tied to Jack Johnson.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Luis Russell's New Orleans band
segments.summary: Russell's band filled in at Connie's Inn; Jackson lists its New Orleans players and praises Charlie Holmes's Hodges-like alto.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Chick Webb's band as a source of musicians
segments.summary: Webb's eight-piece band gave Hodges and Cootie Williams to Duke and once had Jimmy Harrison.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Jimmy Harrison's swing trombone and those who copied him
segments.summary: Jackson calls Harrison the greatest swing trombonist he heard, with Sandy Williams and Jack Teagarden borrowing from him.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Chick Webb the drummer who could not read
segments.summary: Webb had more imagination than ten drummers, phrased arrangements perfectly without reading, and could hum any soloist's chorus.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Chick Webb trading arrangements and humming solos
segments.summary: Hinton recalls Webb on Broadway singing whole arrangements and trading charts; Jackson recalls him humming Taft Jordan's solo at the Savoy.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Russell Pop Smith: the trumpeter who could not read words
segments.summary: Russell Smith, from Ripley, Ohio, could not read or write yet was a great first trumpeter and a sergeant in the First World War orchestra.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: The Smith brothers Joe and Luke
segments.summary: Joe Smith was a lyrical plunger-muted melody player and Luke a legitimate pit trumpeter in Blackbirds and shows.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Pops Smith's long career and late-life Tenderly
segments.summary: Pops, the best of the brothers, played first trumpet with Fletcher for years, retired with Calloway at 66 and played beautifully into his eighties.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Pops Smith cheating at cards
segments.summary: Pops cheated at cards, hiding cards in the baggage rack, and took Hinton's money on the train.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Russell Smith's wife puts him out and the veterans' lawsuit
segments.summary: After he sent money home for years, his wife evicted him; veterans' lawyers won him half the house, a car and a condominium, and he married her daughter.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Pike Davis, first trumpet in Blackbirds
segments.summary: Davis was a legitimate first trumpeter with a standoffish personality who always worked in shows.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Rex Stewart's tricks, appetite and reading
segments.summary: Rex Stewart had many tricks and false fingerings, a big appetite and a good ear that covered slow reading; Jackson played with him in McKinney's band.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Bobby Stark and Chick Webb's trumpet section
segments.summary: Stark was neat, quiet and one of the cleanest trumpeters; Jackson praises Webb's trumpets of Dick Vance, Stark and Taft Jordan.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Other trumpeters who impressed him: Buck Clayton and Charlie Shavers
segments.summary: Buck Clayton impressed him in California, and he rates Charlie Shavers among the greatest all-around trumpet players.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: John Nesbitt and the pickup McKinney's recording dates
segments.summary: Nesbitt arranged for McKinney's; when the band could not reach New York Redman recorded under its name with New York players like Hawkins, Fats Waller and Truehart.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Truehart, Jimmy Blanton and musicians lost to tuberculosis
segments.summary: Truehart and Jimmy Blanton died of tuberculosis; Hinton visited Blanton in a California hospital in 1942.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Steve Dunn, and start of the April 25 session
segments.summary: Jackson names Steve Dunn as a lyrical trumpeter; the tape is paused and the interview resumes on April 25.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Turning down the offer to lead a Cotton Club band; the super sideman
segments.summary: About 1939 Freddie Jenkins proposed a relief band at the Cotton Club, but Jackson chose to remain a sideman.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Joining Don Redman in June 1932 and the band's lineup
segments.summary: He took Fred Robinson's place on June 6, 1932; Jackson lists the whole band including Horace Henderson, with CBS broadcasts from Connie's Inn.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Redman's road band and his feel for dance tempos
segments.summary: After Connie's Inn the band went on the road; Redman understood dance tempos, which also made McKinney's a great dance band.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: The 1933 road show with the Mills Brothers
segments.summary: Redman's band toured East Coast theaters with the Mills Brothers and a full revue until John Mills's illness folded it.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Theaters on the circuit: RKO houses and Philadelphia's Black theaters
segments.summary: He recalls theaters in Cleveland, Boston and Philadelphia, including Sam Steeple's Lincoln, Pearl and Nixon Grand.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: The Casino de Paris show with Redman and Ben Pollack
segments.summary: In 1933 Redman's band shared Billy Rose's Casino de Paris show with Ben Pollack's band, whose members included Spivak, Yank Lawson and Eddie Miller.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: The Casino de Paris as a theater restaurant
segments.summary: Jackson locates and describes the theater restaurant, its convertible stage, floor show with Cardini and Smith and Dale, and Max Baer replaced by Bojangles.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Redman's five saxophones and three trombones
segments.summary: Redman originated the five-saxophone and three-trombone sections; Jackson explains the voicings with Jerry Blake and Donald Kirkpatrick's arrangements, and lists the section.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Break for a bite and turning to the Savoy Ballroom
segments.summary: Hinton notes they are having a bite, and moves to the Savoy Ballroom, with Jackson asking to start before he came to New York.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: The Savoy Ballroom's early years: Fess Williams and Chick Webb
segments.summary: Fess Williams opened the Savoy in 1926; Chick Webb's eight-piece band followed with Hodges, Cootie Williams and Truehart.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Cecil Scott's band from Springfield, Ohio and Dickie Wells
segments.summary: Cecil Scott's trio became a big band with Bill Coleman, Frankie Newton and Dickie Wells, whose humorous trombone Jackson praises.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Record companies of the era
segments.summary: Jackson names Brunswick, Victor, Columbia and Vocalion as the main labels.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: The Savoy house bands, Basie, and the Savoy Sultans
segments.summary: Chick Webb was the main Savoy band, followed by Basie and the Alabama State Collegians; the Savoy Sultans, musically rough, outswung everyone for dancers.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Teddy Hill's band at the Savoy
segments.summary: Teddy Hill's band, second only to Webb's, had Dillard, Collins, Eldridge, Dickie Wells, Procope, Chu Berry and a high-playing brass section.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Don Redman's physique, sports, pool and ice cream
segments.summary: Redman was about five feet tall and powerfully built, left-handed, played every instrument, played shortstop, shot pool and ate ice cream with Jackson.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Benny Carter and the 1930 Henderson band; tuba and bass together
segments.summary: Hearing Henderson's band with Carter in 1930, Jackson names the whole lineup and says bands like Kirby's and McKinney's used both tuba and bass.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Benny Carter and Don Redman as multi-instrumentalists
segments.summary: Carter plays trombone, trumpet and piano beautifully and can pick up the alto after months and play perfectly; Redman also played several instruments.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Russell Procope and Edgar Sampson in Henderson's band
segments.summary: Jackson met Procope and violinist and composer Edgar Sampson in Henderson's band in 1932; Sampson wrote Stompin' at the Savoy and Blue Lou.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Waymon Carver, Chick Webb's jazz flutist
segments.summary: Webb's band had the first jazz flutist, Waymon Carver of Atlanta, who made a record with Pete Clarke on two flutes.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Why today's players lack the old musicians' versatility
segments.summary: Jackson blames disc jockeys, booking agents and a trend away from big bands, though young people now ask where the music came from.

segments.chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
segments.title: Teaching young musicians and the loss of togetherness
segments.summary: Hinton finds young players uninterested in clarinet or academic training; Jackson says rock money and individualism replaced section playing, and togetherness in music mirrors the world.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Reel Three opening
segments.summary: The Reel Three header and Hinton's recap of the previous session; Hinton moves on to other musicians of the 1933 era.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: McKinney's trumpeters: Buddy Lee, John Nesbitt, Doc Cheatham and Rex Stewart
segments.summary: Jackson recalls Hilton Jefferson and the trumpeters of McKinney's band, including Buddy Lee as swing first trumpet, Nesbitt as arranger, and Rex Stewart's false fingering.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: High-note trumpeters: Tommy Stevenson, Al Killian and Shad Collins
segments.summary: He praises Tommy Stevenson's altissimo with Lunceford, Al Killian's range in Redman's band, and underrated Shad Collins.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Shorty Baker learns to read in Redman's band
segments.summary: Redman found Harold Baker in St. Louis in 1936 and taught him to read; working with Redman was like school.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Joe Keyes, the schoolteacher trumpeter
segments.summary: Keyes played with Bennie Moten and McKinney's, read anything, played melody with the plunger and taught school in Missouri.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Bob Carroll and the musicians from Louisville and the Midwest
segments.summary: Bob Carroll, Dickie Wells, Frankie Newton, Bill Coleman, Jonah Jones and Buddy Lee came out of Louisville; Ohio, Indiana and Illinois had many territory bands.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Redman forms his band from Horace Henderson's men
segments.summary: Redman took Bob Carroll, Rupert Cole, Talcott Reeves and Manzie Johnson from Horace Henderson's band to form his own in 1931.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Territory bands and musicians flowing to New York
segments.summary: Hinton and Jackson say great musicians came from Louisville, Ohio, Kansas City, St. Louis and Atlanta to make New York the entertainment mecca.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: The Alabama State Collegians from Birmingham
segments.summary: Jackson names members of the Alabama State Collegians, including Haywood Henry, Bill Johnson, Sammy Lowe and Dud Bascomb.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Paul Webster, Lunceford's high-note trumpeter
segments.summary: Paul Webster replaced Tommy Stevenson in Lunceford's band and could play any high note; Hinton calls him the black Clark Gable.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Taft Jordan and Frankie Fairfax's Philadelphia band
segments.summary: Taft Jordan was an all-around trumpeter and clown with Chick Webb; Jackson thinks he and Dizzy played in Frankie Fairfax's Philadelphia band.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Charlie Gaines's band and Louis Jordan
segments.summary: Louis Jordan came out of Charlie Gaines's entertaining nine-piece Philadelphia band before going to Chick Webb.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Freddie Jenkins, Little Posey of the early Ellington band
segments.summary: Jenkins was a flashy dressing trumpeter with missing fingers who contracted TB too soon.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Horace Henderson's Collegians at Wilberforce
segments.summary: Horace Henderson's good band at Wilberforce included Freddie Jenkins, Rex Stewart and Benny Carter, and used so many of Fletcher's arrangements.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Prince Robinson and Ed Inge on clarinet
segments.summary: Prince Robinson played the clarinet solos on McKinney's early records; Ed Inge played a very modern clarinet, years ahead, and could arrange.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Rupert Cole, Bob Carroll and Elmer Williams
segments.summary: He briefly characterizes Cole and Carroll and calls Elmer Williams, long with Chick Webb, the most melodic tenor he heard.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Ben Webster, a class by himself
segments.summary: Webster was lovable and could make you cry on tenor.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Russell Procope and the John Kirby sextet
segments.summary: Procope read anything; the Kirby band, he says, was the greatest little band, swinging classics sensibly in the best hotels.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: The Kirby band's arrangers, Charlie Shavers and Billy Kyle
segments.summary: Shavers and Kyle made most of the Kirby arrangements, and Shavers wrote tunes like Undecided.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Don Byas, the all-around tenor
segments.summary: He first saw Byas with Eddie Mallory's band, rates him unequaled as a tenor, and recalls Byas staying in Europe after the 1946 Redman tour.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Why the interview names so many sidemen
segments.summary: Hinton explains the oral history aims to credit the many musicians who made the great bands great.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Ted Buckner of Detroit
segments.summary: Buckner's solos on Lunceford's Margie were mistaken for Willie Smith; Detroit had good bands, and Buckner played xylophone with four mallets.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Al Sears and Buffalo as a center for musicians
segments.summary: Al Sears came from Zanesville and played with Zack White in 1929; Buffalo hosted Alphonso Trent, Lunceford and Stuff Smith.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Willie Bryant's band and his dancing partner
segments.summary: Willie Bryant, an entertainer rather than a musician, led a band with Carter, Webster and Teddy Wilson; Jackson first saw him with the Whitman Sisters' show.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: TOBA and Toby time
segments.summary: Jackson and Hinton explain the Theater Owners' Booking Association circuit of segregated black shows and its nickname.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Blanche Calloway and Cab's showmanship
segments.summary: Jackson first saw Cab Calloway as a kid with Blanche Calloway's show on Toby time; her stage moves became Cab's.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Illinois Jacquet and Lionel Hampton's first band
segments.summary: After a break, Jackson first heard Jacquet in Hampton's 1941 band and lists its saxophones, trumpets, and rhythm section.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Elton Hill, Eddie Mallory and Hardy's Alabamans
segments.summary: They discuss arranger Elton Hill, Eddie Mallory's band, and Marion Hardy's Alabamans, with whom Calloway first came to New York.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Arrangers: Jimmy Mundy, Fred Norman, Buster Harding and Andy Gibson
segments.summary: Jackson names good arrangers he knew, many from Ohio, noting Andy Gibson wrote parts straight from his head for Cab.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Sy Oliver's method and style
segments.summary: Sy Oliver wrote parts from the head with Zack White, showed Jackson his layering method, and had a distinctive driving style.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Chappie Willett and Calvin Jackson
segments.summary: Chappie Willett arranged Cotton Club shows and dancers' music; Calvin Jackson was a pianist-arranger who wrote for films.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Jimmy Harrison, the trombonist who influenced others
segments.summary: Jackson names Harrison first among trombone influences, saying many stole from him including Benny Morton and Teagarden.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Jack Teagarden as a flexible trombonist and mechanic
segments.summary: Teagarden was very flexible and made his own mouthpieces and mutes.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Big Green, Bessie Smith and Dinah Washington's Play It Butter
segments.summary: Charlie Green played soulful blues on Bessie Smith's records; Jackson recorded Play That Slide Trombone with Dinah Washington, who called out his nickname.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Wilbur De Paris, Vic Dickinson, Floyd Brady and J. C. Higginbotham
segments.summary: Jackson recalls Wilbur De Paris, Vic Dickinson of Xenia, Stump Brady who taught him and whose place he took with Zack White, and Higginbotham.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Dickie Wells, who almost talked on the trombone
segments.summary: Wells came through Springfield with Cecil Scott, later played with Teddy Hill and Basie, and kidded Vic Dickinson.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Meeting Lawrence Brown with Les Hite; Hampton's vibraphone on Song of the Islands
segments.summary: Jackson met Brown at Sebastian's Cotton Club with Les Hite, who played behind Louis Armstrong, where Hampton first played vibraphone on a record.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Lawrence Brown's record Charlie's Idea
segments.summary: Brown's early record of Tiger Rag as Charlie's Idea with Paul Howard's band showed a trombone speed nobody had heard.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Lawrence Brown's soft playing and Duke taking him for three trombones
segments.summary: Brown strolled between tables playing quietly; McKinney would not hire him, so when Redman had three trombones Duke grabbed Brown.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Claude Jones at Wilberforce and the start of the septet
segments.summary: Claude Jones started on trombone at Wilberforce and joined the Synco Cinco Septet that became the Cotton Pickers.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: The septet at Manitou Beach, Goldkette and the Cottonpickers name (repeat)
segments.summary: Jackson retells how Goldkette heard the seven-piece band at Clark's Lake, had Redman enlarge it, and gave it the Cotton Pickers name and Victor contract in 1927.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Keg Johnson: nervous temperament, teacher and section mate
segments.summary: Keg Johnson played better in the dressing room than on stage, inspired others, sent Jackson to teachers in Chicago, and anchored a great Calloway trombone section.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Tyree Glenn: minstrel banjoist who learned from Jackson and Claude Jones
segments.summary: Glenn had played banjo in minstrels and came to Tommy Miles's band with little; Claude Jones taught him lip vibrato and Jackson mapped out solos for him.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Stage pranks in Calloway's band: Tyree, Dizzy and the football pass
segments.summary: Tyree kidded Jackson constantly; Hinton recalls Dizzy and Tyree pretending to pass and catch a football behind Cab's ballads while Cozy Cole tapped the bass drum.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: DePriest Wheeler and the bass trombone
segments.summary: Jackson never saw Wheeler's bass trombone, having only subbed in his place and joined after Wheeler left.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: J. J. Johnson as the revolutionary modern trombonist
segments.summary: Asked who did for trombone what Blanton did for bass, Jackson names J. J. Johnson, whom he first heard in Benny Carter's band at the Apollo.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: White trombonists: Miff Mole, Tommy Dorsey, Jack Jenney, Will Bradley, Buddy Morrow
segments.summary: Jackson recalls white trombonists he heard, from Miff Mole through Billy Rausch and Jack Jenney across from Redman's band, to Buddy Morrow the iron man.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Carl Fontana, Frank Rosolino and Urbie Green
segments.summary: He names Carl Fontana and Frank Rosolino as favorites, and calls Urbie Green the greatest all-around trombonist.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Bill Watrous and Jackson's reputation as super sideman
segments.summary: Jackson praises Bill Watrous, who calls him father and practices hours daily; Hinton says trombonists credit Jackson's influence.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Trummy Young and Eddie Bert
segments.summary: Trummy Young was noticed with Lunceford and Louis Armstrong but preferred Hawaii; Eddie Bert is a friend of Trummy's.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Sandy Williams and the Jimmy Harrison swing style
segments.summary: Williams was closest to Harrison's swinging, melody-based style, which Benny Morton also had; Jackson laments playing melody is now a lost art.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Snub Mosley and the slide saxophone
segments.summary: Mosley, with Alphonso Trent, played a unique slide saxophone and was an exciting salesman.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Which trombonists influenced him most
segments.summary: Asked who most impressed him, Jackson declines to name a greatest, crediting Claude Jones for starting him and something from each of the others.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Reel Four opening
segments.summary: The Reel Four header; Hinton restarts on trombone influences.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Claude Jones as his inspiration, and Lawrence Brown's later influence
segments.summary: Claude Jones talked him into trombone and was his model; Dickie Wells seemed too complicated, and Lawrence Brown influenced everyone after 1932.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: How white trombonists respected Black players
segments.summary: White trombonists such as Tommy Dorsey, Teagarden and Peewee Hunt admired Black players; Hinton stresses the mutual respect despite segregation.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: White patronage of Harlem, after-hours joints and copied riffs
segments.summary: In the early thirties whites flocked safely to Harlem clubs and after-hours spots, and downtown musicians wrote down riffs on their cuffs.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: White musicians studied; advice to take lessons
segments.summary: Jackson credits white musicians for studying hard and advises kids to learn technique so they can play with any feeling.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Pete Brown and Earle Warren, alto saxophonists
segments.summary: Pete Brown was a jolly swinging alto of the 52nd Street days; Jackson also praises his Springfield friend Earle Warren as an underrated first alto with Basie.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Charlie Holmes and the Hodges sound
segments.summary: Holmes had the nearest style to Johnny Hodges, avoided the comparison, and stayed in New York rather than join Ellington.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Tab Smith, alto influence
segments.summary: Tab Smith, whom he knew with Lucky Millinder, had a Hodges-like feel and later played with Basie alongside Earle Warren.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: New England alto stars and Hilton Jefferson
segments.summary: Hinton notes New England produced Hodges, Carney, Mondello and Jefferson; Jackson says Calloway kept Jefferson when Ellington wanted him.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Cuba Austin, McKinney's carnival drummer
segments.summary: Cuba Austin, hired from a carnival, was a colorful clowning dancer-drummer, cousin of Mantan Moreland; Lloyd Scott and Arnold Bolden are also mentioned.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: First hearing Big Sid Catlett in Milwaukee
segments.summary: In 1931 Catlett filled in for the sick Cuba Austin with McKinney's band and made everyone forget him.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Zutty Singleton on records and in Chicago
segments.summary: Jackson first heard Zutty on West End Blues and in person at the Three Deuces with Roy Eldridge about 1937.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Jamming after hours in Chicago until the union stopped it
segments.summary: With Redman's band he jammed at the Three Deuces and Tony's after the Regal Theater until the union banned unpaid jamming that club owners advertised.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Kaiser Marshall and the invention of the high-hat
segments.summary: Marshall was the first New York drummer with a high-hat; Jackson describes the earlier rat-trap foot cymbal Cuba Austin used.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Walter Johnson, the smoothest drummer
segments.summary: Walter Johnson never wilted a collar and still looked the same in his seventies.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Chick Webb the drummer who set a style
segments.summary: Webb couldn't read but knew every note and phrase, rolled one mallet on a cymbal, spent his money on music and talked about his band constantly.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Chick Webb's trumpet and reed sections
segments.summary: Jackson lists Webb's best band with Vance, Stark and Jordan and a sax section of Jefferson, Carver, Elmer Williams and Pete Clark.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Joe Jones and the Basie rhythm section
segments.summary: Joe Jones was the first drummer to drop bombs and set drumming styles; with Page, Green and Basie he formed the all-American rhythm section.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Cozy Cole, studious and rhythmic
segments.summary: Cozy Cole swung with Blanche Calloway, Willie Bryant and Stuff Smith, and practiced rudiments on a pad between Calloway shows.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Leroy Maxey and why Calloway replaced him with Cozy Cole
segments.summary: Maxey was a great Cotton Club show drummer but could not play solos once Krupa made them fashionable, so Calloway hired Cozy Cole.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Jimmy Crawford, Joe Marshall and the Lunceford rhythm section
segments.summary: Jimmy Crawford and the Lunceford rhythm section were superb; Crawford later became Broadway's busiest drummer and Joe Marshall followed him in the band.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: J. C. Heard and drummers who danced
segments.summary: J. C. Heard idolized Joe Jones and was a good show and swing drummer; many drummers were former dancers.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Panama Francis, Kansas Fields and drummers who went to Europe
segments.summary: Jackson recalls Panama Francis with Calloway, Kansas Fields and Hines's drummers who stayed in Europe, and Oliver Coleman.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Mel Lewis, Grady Tate and Osie Johnson
segments.summary: He calls Grady Tate today's drummer and Osie Johnson one of the greatest all-around drummers.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Sonny Greer, Ellington's colorful drummer
segments.summary: Greer was a colorful, expressive painter of feelings rather than a swing drummer and never needed a drum book.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Louis Bellson and Dave Black in Ellington's band
segments.summary: Bellson wrote drum parts from the horn parts; after him Duke wanted two bass drums, so Dave Black came in.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Sam Woodyard, the greatest Ellington drummer
segments.summary: Woodyard had Greer's color plus swing and memory, and could hawk a soloist to death as at Newport '56.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Montgomery Morrison and Billy Taylor, tuba and bass players
segments.summary: His first great bass player was Montgomery Morrison on upright tuba in Zack White's band; then Billy Taylor in McKinney's.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Bob Ysaguirre and Milt Hinton as bassists he played with
segments.summary: Ysaguirre was a foundation bass in Redman's band; Jackson says he learned from watching Hinton for eight and a half years.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Playing the two-bass part with Hinton and how he learned bass
segments.summary: Jackson took over Franz Jackson's two-bass part at the Strand after others failed, having learned bass by watching Billy Taylor, Ysaguirre and Hinton.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Why Hinton calls him a super sideman: knowing everybody's part
segments.summary: Jackson argues hearing and remembering notes is simple, and says in Ellington's band he knew the saxophone parts and filled in on bass.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Wendell Marshall, the gentleman bassist
segments.summary: Wendell Marshall, Blanton's cousin, lived in Jimmy's shadow, guarded his health, left Fiddler on the Roof to become a minister, and was a perfect gentleman.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Jimmy Blanton and Ben Webster
segments.summary: Blanton did not drink; Ben Webster loved him and nicknamed him Bear, inspiring Jack the Bear.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: John Kirby and the tuba fading out
segments.summary: Jackson first saw Kirby with Fletcher in 1930 playing both tuba and bass, and he was the first tuba player with lip vibrato.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Pops Foster, first string bassist in jazz
segments.summary: Jackson says Pops Foster brought the string bass to New York with Luis Russell, with Hinton noting Bill Johnson in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Oscar Pettiford, the phenomenal soloist
segments.summary: Pettiford hung out backstage with Hinton, nearly got Hinton fired by Calloway, and briefly filled in with Ellington after Blanton.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Wellman Braud and Billy Taylor in Ellington's band
segments.summary: Jackson explains Braud was soon forgotten after Billy Taylor arrived, and Taylor quit when Blanton came.
