segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Junior Raglin and Jimmy Woode joining Ellington
segments.summary: Junior Raglin was a lovable drinker who played guitar before bass; when he had to leave, Duke tried out Jimmy Woode in Boston.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Teaching introductions to Woode and Mingus
segments.summary: Jackson taught Jimmy Woode and Charles Mingus the Ellington introductions and Mingus never forgot it.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: His philosophy on teaching young musicians
segments.summary: Jackson says he happily shows anyone and criticizes teachers who keep students coming back without teaching them.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Adolphus Alsbrook, brilliant unsung bassist
segments.summary: Hinton and Jackson recall Alsbrook, a brilliant bassist, cellist and arranger who studied at Minnesota, had sleeping sickness and was a Golden Gloves boxer.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Richard Davis and bowed bass
segments.summary: Jackson praises Richard Davis's bowing that makes the bass sound like a cello.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Alsbrook with Basie and Lawrence Welk
segments.summary: Alsbrook did a few dates with Basie and Duke and eventually wrote music for Lawrence Welk.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Jimmy Woode sits with Hazel Scott and Oscar Pettiford sits in
segments.summary: At Birdland Woode had Pettiford sub for him; Duke called Jack the Bear and Oscar knew every cue, then Duke gently rebuked Woode.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Elmer James and Beverly Peer
segments.summary: Both bassists played with Chick Webb; Beverly Peer, from Boston, now plays with Bobby Short at the Carlyle.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Erskine Hawkins, the Bama State Collegians and Dud Bascomb's Tuxedo Junction solo
segments.summary: The Collegians came to the Savoy by school bus, Moe Gale billed Hawkins as the Twentieth Century Gabriel, but Dud Bascomb's solo made Tuxedo Junction.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Reel Five opening and Dud Bascomb's tone versus Erskine Hawkins's
segments.summary: Reel Five begins with Hinton returning to Dud Bascomb's Tuxedo Junction solo; Jackson contrasts Bascomb's broad tone with Hawkins's high-note sound.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Dud Bascomb's son on Fender bass
segments.summary: Bascomb's son is a fine New York bassist with a Fender; like father, like son.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: First pianists to impress him: Earl Hines and Fats Waller's pipe organ
segments.summary: He first heard Earl Hines with Louis Dippo's Pittsburgh orchestra, and had Fats Waller's 1926 Victor pipe organ record.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Art Tatum in Toledo and at the Rhythm Club (retold)
segments.summary: Jackson recounts hearing Tatum in 1931 in Toledo and at the Rhythm Club where Fats gathered pianists; then he moves to Herman Chittison.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Adelaide Hall's pianists and Joe Turner
segments.summary: They sort out that Tatum went to Europe with Adelaide Hall and then Joe Turner, the pianist who wrote Walking Through Heaven.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Herman Chittison with Zack White and on radio
segments.summary: Chittison, with long fingers, played with Zack White, was on radio in Newport, Kentucky, and became a society pianist.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Luckey Roberts, Ford Dabney and society pianists
segments.summary: Roberts and Dabney got the best society jobs for Black pianists, and Roberts wrote hit songs.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Leroy Smith's society band
segments.summary: Leroy Smith's Detroit-born violinist-led band played society jobs, its members were aloof gentlemen, and Wilbur De Paris played trombone.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Fats Waller the entertainer, his death and his swing organ
segments.summary: Waller would have been a TV star; he died on a train in 1943, and played swing organ at the Lafayette Theater and Connie's Inn.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Leola Carter, who replaced Fats on organ at Connie's Inn
segments.summary: Connie hired Leola Carter, a Black woman born in Bavaria, to play organ; she later became a vocal coach.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: The Alvin Hotel
segments.summary: Jackson recalls musicians at the Alvin Hotel, where Pres and later Shorty Baker died.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Hinton's St. Albans neighborhood and Fats Waller
segments.summary: Hinton explains that the Queens neighborhood where they record was white and Fats Waller, Basie and others later lived nearby.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Fats Waller at the Apollo: Hammond organ, wine bottles and appetite
segments.summary: The last time Jackson saw Fats was at the Apollo; Waller had a Hammond organ, gave every bandsman a bottle, and ate from serving dishes.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Jackson's love of the organ and Fats teaching Basie
segments.summary: Jackson played theater organs early in the morning; Fats taught Count Basie the organ in New York.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Great eaters: Chu Berry, Tyree Glenn, Redman, Calloway, Carter and Hawkins
segments.summary: Jackson and Hinton swap stories of big appetites, including Hawkins ordering two dinners from two Detroit restaurants.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Mom Sutton's in Atlanta and eating in Black homes
segments.summary: Hinton notes segregation forced musicians into private rooms and Black restaurants; they recall Mom Sutton's in Atlanta.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Mom Charleston and Mom Havelow in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Jackson recalls the big cook Mom Charleston and Mom Havelow's brownstone where bandleaders lived upstairs.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Pop Henry's, the Sterling Hotel in Cincinnati and Jerry the rat
segments.summary: In Cincinnati they ate at Pop Henry's near the Sterling Hotel, where an old rat named Jerry roamed the halls.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Black landladies as the best cooks
segments.summary: Jackson says the home cooking was better than white restaurants.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: The traveling kitchen in Calloway's band
segments.summary: The band carried a stove, took turns cooking, and once cooking cabbage in a Youngstown theater made the audience drool.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: RKO theater dressing rooms and Edwina's in Washington
segments.summary: Jackson again describes RKO backstage kitchens and recalls staying and eating at Edwina's near the Howard Theater.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Barbecue across the country and Jackson's love of food
segments.summary: Chicago barbecue was best, with Magnus Clark in Detroit and an Evansville pit; Jackson says food was his vice instead of drink.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Hilton Jefferson, a gentleman at the table
segments.summary: Jefferson was a left-handed gentleman raised by aunts in New England, carving chicken like a surgeon.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Billy Kyle and Lucky Millinder's band
segments.summary: Jackson first knew Billy Kyle in Lucky Millinder's thirties band with Andy Gibson, Sweets Edison, Charlie Shavers, Kirby and Tab Smith.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: George Matthews, melodic trombonist
segments.summary: Big George Matthews played melodic trombone, was still active, and played in the Apollo band under Reuben Phillips.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Billy Kyle's playing; Buster Bailey and Red Allen in Millinder's band
segments.summary: Kyle swung commandingly while sitting straight and was good-looking; Buster Bailey and Red Allen also played with Millinder.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Avery Parrish and Tippin' In
segments.summary: They discuss Erskine Hawkins's pianist Avery Parrish and who wrote Tippin' In and Tuxedo Junction; the band wrote them.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Donald Kirkpatrick, Redman's pianist and arranger
segments.summary: Kirkpatrick came to Redman from Chick Webb, wrote beautiful arrangements, loved to eat, and married Johnny Hodges's sister.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Benny Payne, the great accompanist
segments.summary: Payne accompanied singers and dancers brilliantly, Bojangles tried to hire him from Calloway, and Jackson wishes he had been a featured entertainer.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Benny Payne's Cotton Club trio and Mattie Hite
segments.summary: Before Calloway Payne sang in a trio at the Cotton Club and accompanied cabaret star Mattie Hite, earning big tips.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: How Cab Calloway got the Cotton Club job
segments.summary: With Ellington away filming, Duke recommended Calloway; gangsters Owney Madden and Herman Stark forced the Savoy manager to release his contract and turned the Missourians into Calloway's band.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Hank Jones, Oscar Peterson and Phineas Newborn
segments.summary: Jackson calls Hank Jones the complete pianist with a fine tone and rates Oscar Peterson and Phineas Newborn close to Tatum.

segments.chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
segments.title: Erroll Garner in Pittsburgh and Art Tatum's help
segments.summary: Jackson and Danny Barker took teenage Erroll Garner around Pittsburgh houses and urged him to come to New York, where Tatum looked after him.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Leaving Calloway, waiting for Duke, and being fired by Lucky Millinder
segments.summary: Ellington asked him to wait for him; meanwhile Millinder hired him then fired him after three weeks, the only firing of his life.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Lucky Millinder's band: personnel and constant firing
segments.summary: Millinder replaced Jackson with white trombonists Freddie Zito and Porky Cohen; Jackson lists the band, and Bullmoose Jackson said he played with a hundred saxophonists.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Waiting on unemployment and Duke's offer to replace Claude Jones
segments.summary: After Ellington returned from Europe he offered Jackson Claude Jones's chair; Jones was unhappy being made to play valve trombone.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Joining Ellington at the Duke Ellington Club in Washington
segments.summary: He joined on October 21, 1948, at a short-lived Washington club; Tyree Glenn had joined over a year earlier.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Ellington's band in 1948-49: personnel and Shelton Hemphill
segments.summary: Jackson lists the five trumpets, three trombones and saxophone section, remembers Scad Hemphill, and Ben Webster rejoins making six saxes.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: The Clique Club in Philadelphia
segments.summary: The Clique Club on Market Street had the longest bar and a turntable bandstand; Sears left and Ben Webster stayed until 1949.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: What Duke Ellington was to Jackson: psychologist and diplomat
segments.summary: Jackson calls Ellington a great psychologist who wrote parts knowing how each man would play them.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Third trombone, a lead part, and the name Monsieur du Beurre
segments.summary: Jackson, a famous low-note player, found a lead passage in his third part; Duke said he heard him on it, and in Paris in 1950 called him Monsieur du Beurre.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: How Duke wrote for individual players
segments.summary: Ellington gave each man particular notes in chords and made new arrangements when personnel changed; he used Hamilton, Procope and Carney expertly.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Duke writing constantly, untitled parts and calling him Edward
segments.summary: Ellington wrote on buses and bandstands, passing out untitled pieces that grew chorus by chorus, which confused substitutes.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: His relationship with Ellington and the two raises
segments.summary: Ellington talked quietly with Jackson, and when he tried to quit twice Duke kept him until he agreed to a raise, partly because Basie asked him to join.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Band changes in fall 1950: Cat Anderson back, trumpets
segments.summary: Al Killian left and Cat Anderson returned; Francis Williams and Nelson Williams are sorted out.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: The 1950 European tour: five trumpets and Butch Ballard
segments.summary: For Europe Duke took Ernie Royal as a fifth trumpet and Butch Ballard as extra drummer; Tyree stayed home and Jackson began the plunger role.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Alone on trombone in Italy
segments.summary: After Ted Kelley left to marry and Lawrence Brown's back gave out, Jackson covered all the trombone parts alone.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Tyree returns for the Masterpieces by Ellington album
segments.summary: Tyree Glenn only came back to record Masterpieces by Ellington with Mood Indigo and Sophisticated Lady, then returned to gigging and the Ted Steele show.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: The weird scene in the band: loners and non-talkers
segments.summary: Sections barely spoke; Ray Nance and Al Killian were loners, Shorty Baker liked everyone, the trombones were close.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Lawrence Brown, immaculate and nicknamed Sweety Brown
segments.summary: Brown shaved with two razors, dusted his cuffs, wiped his face with a sponge, and Ben Webster nicknamed him Sweety Brown.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: The early 1940s Ellington trombone section Jackson could only envy
segments.summary: Jackson sat in Tizol's seat after hours at the Hurricane and Strand and lists the 1942-43 band he heard.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Tricky Sam Nanton's plunger chair
segments.summary: Tricky Sam urged Jackson to take his chair; Jackson thought he never could but learned Tricky's solos from records.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Playing the plunger: Tricky Sam's ya-ya versus Tyree's wa
segments.summary: Jackson copied Tricky Sam's plunger sound, relaxing it, getting closer to the ya-ya than Tyree Glenn.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Duke's instruction not to play too pretty, and descriptive music
segments.summary: Duke told him the music was folklore; Jackson explains Ellington's black music, colors, and descriptive pieces.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: 1951: Hodges leaves and Britt Woodman and Tizol arrive
segments.summary: Hodges, Greer and Lawrence Brown left to form Hodges's band in 1951; Britt Woodman came from Los Angeles and Claude Jones briefly returned.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: The Oasis, Charlie Smith, and Louie Bellson, Tizol and Willie Smith arriving
segments.summary: On the road the replacements failed, until in Omaha Bellson, Tizol and Willie Smith joined and the band tightened.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: The 1952 Birdland opening against bebop and Symphony Sid
segments.summary: Procope challenged Birdland's bebop crowd, and the Ellington band's first Birdland night packed the club and delighted the audience.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Bellson's double-drum feature and Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue
segments.summary: Bellson's drum feature angered other drummers; Duke sent Paul Gonsalves out for the Diminuendo and Crescendo choruses and the crowd cheered.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Louie Bellson meets Pearl Bailey
segments.summary: Tizol introduced Bellson to Pearl Bailey in Washington and Bellson left the band to marry her in London.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Hilton Jefferson joins and leaves Ellington
segments.summary: Hodges's chair went to Jefferson, whom Procope and others wanted, but Jeff's foot injury and his wife's faked heart attacks got him home.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Saxophonists Bill Graham and Rick Henderson
segments.summary: Bill Graham got everyone drinking Thunderbird wine and was let go; Rick Henderson, a bebop-influenced alto from Washington, joined and Procope took more lead.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Duke tearing apart arrangements for continuity
segments.summary: Henderson wrote commercially despite playing bebop, and Duke reworked any arrangement, jumping between letters; he told Jackson he didn't like the continuity.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Billy Strayhorn and Ellington's writing marriage
segments.summary: Jackson calls Strayhorn and Ellington the greatest musical marriage; Strayhorn was tender, and arrangements were passed between them so you couldn't tell who wrote what.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: How Strayhorn joined in 1939 and the tunes he wrote
segments.summary: Ellington got Strayhorn in Pittsburgh in 1939; he wrote Chelsea Bridge, Passion Flower, Take the A Train and Lush Life.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Lush Life as a controversial lyric
segments.summary: Jackson and Hinton discuss the lyrics of Lush Life about gay spots as daring for its time, and also racy titles in Ellington's book.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Strayhorn as a gentleman who never made himself obvious
segments.summary: Hinton wonders whether gay admirers know Strayhorn; Jackson says he was a perfect gentleman beloved by all, nicknamed Sweet Pea by Ben Webster.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: And His Mother Called Him Bill and Strayhorn's Blood Count
segments.summary: Jackson A&R'd the Strayhorn tribute date because he knew all the music, and recalls Blood Count as Strayhorn's last piece, played by Hodges.

segments.chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
segments.title: Duke suggests the Fender bass; Jackson's memorized book
segments.summary: Ellington urged him to take up Fender bass when he couldn't play trombone; Jackson says he memorized every arrangement.

segments.chapter: Illness, comeback and shop talk
segments.title: The 1966 neck operation and Bell's palsy
segments.summary: After a lot of New York work, an operation on a neck growth left Jackson with Bell's palsy, and he could not play until 1969.

segments.chapter: Illness, comeback and shop talk
segments.title: Not blaming the surgeon, determined to play again
segments.summary: Doctors said the nerve surgery was tedious and not the surgeon's fault; Jackson vowed no one could stop his music and Hinton praises his comeback.

segments.chapter: Illness, comeback and shop talk
segments.title: Secretly practicing and Benny Powell's test
segments.summary: Working with Harlem Backstreet Youth, Jackson blew with a finger holding his cheek; Benny Powell surprised him and brought him to a record date.

segments.chapter: Illness, comeback and shop talk
segments.title: Tony Bennett and the Waldorf trombone section take him back
segments.summary: Tony Bennett had him sit in the Waldorf band despite his condition and the other trombonists supported him.

segments.chapter: Illness, comeback and shop talk
segments.title: The Waldorf house band with Charlie Terry; Russia with Thad and Mel
segments.summary: He played dance music in Charlie Terry's Waldorf house band until 1973, was allowed off to tour Russia with Thad Jones and Mel Lewis.

segments.chapter: Illness, comeback and shop talk
segments.title: Thad Jones, bass trombone and his teachers
segments.summary: Thad Jones got him back to tenor trombone; he had been the main Black bass trombonist, learning from Tommy Mitchell, Bart Varsalona and Tony Studd.

segments.chapter: Illness, comeback and shop talk
segments.title: Trombonists and bassists stay close; Tony Studd and George Roberts
segments.summary: Jackson says trombone and bass players love each other; Tony Studd taught him embouchure and attack, and George Roberts is his favorite bass trombonist.

segments.chapter: Illness, comeback and shop talk
segments.title: Melodic trombonist, plunger and the blues
segments.summary: Jackson says he is mainly melodic but gets soulful with the plunger, credits Duke for the blues, and calls Hodges the greatest blues saxophonist.

segments.chapter: Illness, comeback and shop talk
segments.title: Ben Webster's nicknames
segments.summary: Ben Webster nicknamed Hodges Rabbit, Calloway Twist, Basie Groundhog, and called Hinton Yo.

segments.chapter: Illness, comeback and shop talk
segments.title: Ben Webster's jazz language for money and people
segments.summary: Hinton recalls Ben's slang, such as a cow for a hundred dollars, a soft for a girl and a gray for a white guy.

segments.chapter: Illness, comeback and shop talk
segments.title: Band slang: McKinney's Synguadny and Basie's names
segments.summary: Jackson recalls McKinney's band language, calling women bear, tweed or period, and Basie's Janes and John Thomases.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: The 1955 Flushing Meadows water show without Ellington's regulars
segments.summary: Because many regulars lacked New York union cards, outside players filled in at the water and ice show, and Jackson played first trombone.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: Newport Jazz Festival 1956 and Paul Gonsalves's 27 choruses
segments.summary: At Newport 10,000 people went wild during Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue; George Wein told Duke to stop but Duke played on.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: The post-1955 band and Sam Woodyard lifting it
segments.summary: With Hodges back, Cook, Terry, Nance and Anderson in the trumpets, Jackson praises the impeccable trombone section with Britt Woodman and John Sanders, and Woodyard's drumming.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: Oscar Pettiford sits in at Stony Brook
segments.summary: Pettiford with his amplified bass sat in for Woode and drove Paul Gonsalves to 36 choruses; Woodyard told Jackson how Oscar laid it in your lap.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: Outswinging Stan Kenton at the Graystone
segments.summary: Woodyard rallied the band to put the pots on, and Ellington's band swung all night while Kenton's men stood astounded.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: Ellington at the piano and humming when the band cooked
segments.summary: Ellington hummed and hit chords behind soloists when he was pleased, and Jackson says he was a great accompanist who knew where you were.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: No one like Duke; Thad Jones as today's arranger
segments.summary: Jackson says there will be no one like Ellington and names Thad Jones as today's greatest arranger.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: Ellington denied the mass media and the Pulitzer Prize
segments.summary: Jackson and Hinton note Ellington never had a TV show or the Pulitzer despite honors; Duke said they didn't want him too famous too young.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: The Ellington band is a disease; Duke and Basie as friends
segments.summary: Jackson says anyone who played in the band can't forget it; Basie called Duke the master, and other bands' music felt mediocre afterward.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: Leaving Ellington for Quincy Jones's Free and Easy in Europe
segments.summary: Tired of traveling, Jackson left Ellington in Europe in October 1959 to join Quincy Jones's musical show with Clark Terry.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: Quincy Jones's Free and Easy band: personnel
segments.summary: Jackson lists the trombones, saxes, rhythm and trumpets, including Melba Liston, Jimmy Cleveland, Phil Woods, Budd Johnson and Benny Bailey.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: Rehearsing and memorizing the show in Brussels
segments.summary: The band rehearsed in the Brussels World's Fair American theater and memorized the whole Arlen-based show with no music stands, sounding like stereo.

segments.chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
segments.title: The tour after the show closed and the band's lack of style
segments.summary: When the show closed in Paris the band toured Europe with Nat Cole and the Platters, returned to no bookings, and lacked a distinct style.

segments.chapter: Count Basie's band
segments.title: Called to join Basie at Camp Kilmer
segments.summary: Henry Snodgrass asked him to sub for Al Gray with Basie in fifteen minutes; Jackson changed into brown and made the bus.

segments.chapter: Count Basie's band
segments.title: Joining Basie in January 1961 and the Kennedy Inaugural Ball
segments.summary: After a Reel Seven opening, he agrees to join Basie on money, and plays the Kennedy Inauguration Ball the next day.

segments.chapter: Count Basie's band
segments.title: Basie's band the most consistent he played with
segments.summary: Outside the 1943 Calloway band, Jackson calls Basie's the most consistently good, and Basie a tempo genius.

segments.chapter: Count Basie's band
segments.title: Basie's natural feel for tempo and people; Freddie Green
segments.summary: Hinton and Jackson say Basie set perfect dance tempos by natural feeling for the audience, with Freddie Green as Mr. Metronome.

segments.chapter: Count Basie's band
segments.title: Rhythm guitar: Basie's guitar and Clarence Holiday
segments.summary: Basie's band kept a guitar, which Jackson says adds to a rhythm section; Clarence Holiday was the greatest rhythm guitarist he heard.

segments.chapter: Count Basie's band
segments.title: Sam Herman and Barry Galbraith, rhythm guitarists
segments.summary: Jackson praises Sam Herman with Tommy Dorsey and Barry Galbraith, whom Redman used on every record date, as unsung rhythm guitarists.

segments.chapter: Count Basie's band
segments.title: Basie's 1961 personnel: trumpets, trombones, saxes and rhythm
segments.summary: He lists the trumpet section, trombones Coker, Powell and himself, the saxophone section, Sonny Payne and Ed Jones.

segments.chapter: Count Basie's band
segments.title: Leaving Basie in 1962 after 33 years on the road
segments.summary: After a year and nine months he left to stay home in New York, ending 33 years on the road.

segments.chapter: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
segments.title: Clark Terry introduces him to Jim and Andy's
segments.summary: Clark Terry brought him to Jim and Andy's bar to meet contractors and to Radio Registry; he met owner Jim Kulavaris.

segments.chapter: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
segments.title: Jim Kulavaris, bar owner and lender to musicians
segments.summary: Kulavaris acted as contractor and lent musicians money; many, like Ben Webster, repaid every dime, and Jim lent Jackson $100.

segments.chapter: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
segments.title: Mr. Collins's Harlem restaurant and rooming house
segments.summary: Musicians like Don Byas and Hinton roomed at Mr. Collins's place for a few dollars a week and owed him when he died.

segments.chapter: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
segments.title: The Woodside Hotel: kitchens and the basement jam room
segments.summary: The Woodside housed musicians and pimps; everyone cooked, Basie's band scuffled there, and after the Savoy musicians jammed with strict courtesy.

segments.chapter: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
segments.title: Courtesy, professionalism and learning from older musicians
segments.summary: Big-band musicians treated music as a profession, rehearsed for love, dressed as gentlemen, and learned from the older players.

segments.chapter: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
segments.title: No big bands left for apprentices; kids want to know now
segments.summary: Hinton notes young players have no big bands to learn in, but Jackson sees younger kids wanting to know how and why.

segments.chapter: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
segments.title: A talent is to be used; lucky with good bands
segments.summary: Jackson says God-given talent should be used wisely and he was lucky to play only in good bands.

segments.chapter: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
segments.title: Advice to young musicians
segments.summary: Jackson says to study technique, develop an individual style, listen widely, learn piano and have self-respect.

segments.chapter: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
segments.title: How to practice: long soft notes, scales, instrument before solos
segments.summary: Jackson recommends whole notes played softly on the trombone, scales slowly, and mastering the instrument before soloing.

segments.chapter: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
segments.title: Summing up his career and passing knowledge on
segments.summary: Hinton sums up Jackson's career from the Buckeye Melodians to the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band; both say passing knowledge on is a kind of immortality.

segments.chapter: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
segments.title: The Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band
segments.summary: Thad Jones asked him back to tenor trombone to play plunger; Jackson praises Jones's humorous writing and conducting but dislikes touring.

segments.chapter: Marriages and closing words
segments.title: First marriage to Lucille Forby in California
segments.summary: In 1931 he married a chorus girl, Lucille Forby, despite warnings from Eddie Anderson; it lasted only months.

segments.chapter: Marriages and closing words
segments.title: Meeting Odessa in Memphis
segments.summary: On tour with Calloway he met Odessa in a Memphis rooming house and sent for her to join him.

segments.chapter: Marriages and closing words
segments.title: Marrying Odessa in Boston on Decoration Day
segments.summary: On his $75 blackjack winnings he brought Odessa to Boston and tipped an elevator man to get the license so they could marry before leaving.

segments.chapter: Marriages and closing words
segments.title: Odessa's life in Chicago and the divorce
segments.summary: Odessa stayed in Chicago and finished high school while Jackson was on the road; they divorced about 1955 and he kept paying her rent.

segments.chapter: Marriages and closing words
segments.title: Odessa's Grocery and adopting Michael
segments.summary: Odessa saved enough to buy a grocery, now a self-service market, and they adopted a son, Michael, around 1955.

segments.chapter: Marriages and closing words
segments.title: First encounters with Jackie in 1933 and 1947
segments.summary: His future wife Jacqueline heard him sing in 1933 as a child, and he met her again in Boston in 1947 but didn't approach her.

segments.chapter: Marriages and closing words
segments.title: Meeting Jackie at Birdland and Thad Jones's introduction
segments.summary: He bumped into her backstage at Birdland and Thad Jones, who once almost married her, introduced them.

segments.chapter: Marriages and closing words
segments.title: Friendship, silent looks and jealousy over Osie Johnson
segments.summary: They kept meeting at Birdland while she was married and close to Osie Johnson, and Jackson grew jealous.

segments.chapter: Marriages and closing words
segments.title: Dinner at Junior's and the snowy night in Brooklyn
segments.summary: After a record date she talked with him over dinner; she visited his Brooklyn apartment in the snow and stayed, beginning their life together on February 15, 1964.

segments.chapter: Marriages and closing words
segments.title: Twelve years with Jackie and music as their bond
segments.summary: Hinton admires the couple; Jackson says his wife plays violin, they test each other's ear, and music underlies their closeness.

segments.chapter: Marriages and closing words
segments.title: Closing thoughts on love and thanks
segments.summary: Jackson says musicians should learn to love, which frees the mind and shows in the playing; Hinton thanks him and ends the interview.
